title: When menopause is mistaken for disability, women can miss the care they need
subtitle: Research highlighted ahead of World Menopause Day identifies communication and knowledge gaps affecting women with learning disabilities. Accessible information is part of the response—but women must also be heard in decisions about their care.
author: ATHENA
body:
Women with learning disabilities can have menopause symptoms misunderstood or overlooked because they resemble difficulties already associated with their disability, researchers at the University of Sunderland warned in an update published on 16 October.

The university is developing further support resources with NHS partners, including a video made with women with learning disabilities and their carers. The work brings an often-excluded group into the discussion around World Menopause Day on 18 October.

The problem is not simply a shortage of information about menopause. It is whether information reaches a woman in a form she can use—and whether a health professional recognises a change in her experience as something that deserves investigation.

## Listening beyond an existing diagnosis

The project involved interviews with 23 people with learning disabilities experiencing menopause and 15 carers, according to its public research abstract. Carers were interviewed in March and April 2025; interviews with participants with learning disabilities took place between October 2025 and February 2026.

Carers’ accounts informed the questions subsequently put to participants. The researchers identified communication, knowledge and individually tailored support among the major themes.

This is interview-based research about experiences, not a representative survey measuring how often menopause is missed. It cannot establish a national rate of delayed diagnosis or prove that a particular resource improves treatment. The full report is restricted in the university repository; the public abstract does not provide enough detail to assess recruitment or the full analysis.

The initial project was completed in March. October’s announcement describes its findings and next phase, rather than a newly completed clinical trial.

That distinction does not diminish the question it raises. If an existing diagnosis becomes the explanation for every new difficulty, a woman’s changing health needs can disappear behind it.

## A passport designed to make appointments more useful

One practical response already exists. The North East and Cumbria Learning Disability Network’s Easy Read Menopause Passport provides space to record symptoms, communication preferences and matters someone wants to discuss with a health professional.

It asks how information should be offered—through pictures, simple language, audio or support from another person—and includes options such as longer appointments and a quieter waiting area. Its opening pages address permission to share personal information with care staff.

These are small details with substantial implications. An appointment is not accessible merely because someone can physically attend it. She also needs time to understand, a way to describe what she is experiencing and an opportunity to express her preferences.

Dr Kathy Petersen, a GP and medical director at the North East and North Cumbria Integrated Care Board, said the regional network had co-produced the passport to support recognition of symptoms and discussion of management plans. She said the research would examine its usefulness and possible improvements.

That is an intention to evaluate the tool—not evidence that its effectiveness has already been demonstrated.

## Support must strengthen a woman’s voice

UNFPA’s World Menopause Day message identifies stigma and the expectation that women should simply endure symptoms as barriers to care. It lists sleep disturbance, hot flushes, persistent pain, anxiety and brain fog among possible experiences, while emphasising that symptoms vary.

For women who need communication support, awareness campaigns alone cannot resolve the problem. A carer may help explain changes or prepare for an appointment, but support should make the woman’s own account easier to hear, not replace it.

Nor should greater awareness turn every new symptom into a menopause diagnosis. Recognition should open a clinical conversation, not close off consideration of other explanations.

The next test for the Sunderland work is whether its resources change what happens during care: whether women understand the information, can express their needs and receive appropriate follow-up. Those outcomes matter more than how many leaflets or videos are produced.

Menopause care should not depend on a woman being able to present a fluent, medically familiar account of her symptoms. The service must be able to listen in more than one way.

title: Peru’s girls’ education prize puts the focus on finishing school—not just enrolling
subtitle: CARE Peru has won UNESCO recognition for a programme linking secondary education with health, financial skills and future planning. Its reported gains are encouraging; the next test is whether they can be sustained and independently measured.
author: ATHENA
body:
Original reporting date: 17 October 2026

CARE Peru has received a US$50,000 UNESCO prize for helping rural and Indigenous adolescent girls complete secondary school—a recognition that puts attention on what happens after a student secures a place in a classroom.

Its Girls with Opportunities programme was honoured in Paris on 9 October alongside Morocco’s Project Soar. UNESCO updated its announcement on 16 October. Each organisation received the same prize amount under an award funded by China’s government.

For the Peruvian programme, the central proposition is straightforward: keeping a girl in education involves more than recording her attendance. Health knowledge, financial skills, support from teachers and the ability to plan a future belong in the same conversation.

## What the results show—and what they cannot yet prove

CARE Peru says an evaluation covering 2022–2024 found that the share of female students completing the fifth year of secondary school rose from 65% to 82%. That is an increase of 17 percentage points.

It also reports that adolescent pregnancy cases at participating schools fell from 18 to nine.

Those figures warrant attention, but careful interpretation. The published announcement does not provide the evaluation’s sample size, a comparison group or enough methodological detail to establish how much of the change the programme caused. A fall in recorded cases is not, by itself, a measured reduction in pregnancy risk: that requires knowing the population being counted and whether reporting remained consistent.

Nor should pregnancy become a shorthand for a girl’s educational worth. A programme’s success should include whether pregnant students and young mothers can continue learning, not only whether fewer pregnancies are recorded.

CARE says it intends to use the award for programme continuity and an impact evaluation in 2027. That future assessment could help distinguish promising results from evidence strong enough to guide expansion.

![Schoolchildren from an Asháninka community in Peru sit in a classroom](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Ashaninca_children_in_school.jpg?width=1600)

Contextual photograph: Asháninka children at school in the Nuevos Unidos Tahuantinsuyo community, Puerto Inca Province, Huánuco, Peru, 10 October 2014. This is not a classroom in the CARE Peru programme. Photograph by Schönitzer. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ashaninca_children_in_school.jpg Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

## Education that connects with life beyond school

According to UNESCO, Girls with Opportunities combines emotional and social learning with comprehensive sexuality education, mentoring, financial education and science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics.

The design brings subjects often treated separately into one educational offer. Understanding money concerns the choices a student may make after school. Understanding her health concerns decisions she needs to make while still there. Neither should require abandoning academic ambition.

CARE’s country director, Marilú Martens, credited girls, teachers, families and communities for the recognition. Her emphasis matters: the achievement belongs partly to students who remained in education and completed their studies, not simply to the organisation supporting them.

CARE reports that 23 educational institutions incorporated programme sessions into their management instruments in 2025. It is also training teachers to sustain the approach beyond its direct involvement.

That is a more consequential test than whether an award attracts attention. A project can demonstrate an approach; an education system must make it dependable.

![Students use laptops in a classroom in Ferreñafe, Peru](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/One_Laptop_Per_Child_-_Ferrenafe_(by).jpg?width=1600)

Contextual photograph: students using laptops in a classroom in Ferreñafe, Peru, 1 May 2008. This is not the CARE Peru programme. Photograph by One Laptop per Child. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:One_Laptop_Per_Child_-_Ferrenafe_(by).jpg Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/

## The work after the ceremony

The prize’s other recipient, Project Soar, works through local women facilitators and combines education support with menstrual health provision, rights awareness and community participation. Its recognition alongside CARE Peru points to a shared concern: schooling does not operate separately from the conditions of girls’ daily lives.

Yet recognition is not a guarantee that a model will work equally well everywhere.

For Peru, the next questions are practical. What does delivery cost per student? Which girls are still leaving school? Can teachers maintain the sessions without additional support? And do students themselves find the programme useful when deciding what comes next?

Those questions need published answers before promising results become broad claims about national transformation.

The achievement is worth recognising without overstating it. More girls reportedly completed secondary school in the evaluated programme, and participating institutions have begun embedding its methods. The responsibility now is to preserve that progress while testing what made it possible.

A girl’s opportunity should not depend on whether her school happens to host an award-winning project. The lasting value of this prize will lie in what remains available to her after the celebration ends.

title: Afghanistan’s next hunger emergency is already forecast. Mothers and children need help before it arrives.
subtitle: More than four million young children are projected to need malnutrition treatment in 2027, alongside 1.27 million pregnant or breastfeeding women. A new warning exposes the distance between food being available and families being able to afford it.
author: ATHENA
body:
Original reporting date: 16 October 2026

More than four million children in Afghanistan are expected to need treatment for acute malnutrition in 2027, UNICEF and Action Against Hunger warned on 15 October, calling for sustained funding before services fall further behind need.

The underlying Integrated Food Security Phase Classification analysis puts the projected burden at 4.04 million children aged six months to under five, including nearly 1.1 million with severe acute malnutrition. Separately, approximately 1.27 million pregnant or breastfeeding women are expected to require treatment. These are projected needs across a year, not a count of people already receiving care.

https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1165463/?iso3=AFG

Women’s treatment needs are not an incidental addition to a children’s emergency. The assessment identifies malnutrition among pregnant and breastfeeding women and adolescent girls alongside poor child diets, illness and inadequate water and sanitation as factors driving the crisis.

For families already seeking care, the costs extend beyond food. In reporting published by the Associated Press, Zarmina described borrowing money to bring her two-year-old daughter Fatma from Logar to a Kabul hospital. While staying with her, she worried about her other children at home. Her account captures a problem a treatment total cannot: reaching one child can leave a parent struggling to protect the rest of the household.

https://apnews.com/article/afghanistan-malnutrition-hunger-taliban-wfp-poverty-49645d8ab1209844854d8aa7eb0b5acb

![A woman and three children walk along a street in Kabul.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/1a/An_Afghan_women_with_children_passing_by_ANA_Humvee.jpg)

Contextual archive photograph: a woman with three children crossing a street in Kabul, 19 March 2008. Photograph by Nasim Fekrat, CC BY 2.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:An_Afghan_women_with_children_passing_by_ANA_Humvee.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/

## A better harvest does not guarantee a better diet

FAO and the World Food Programme issued a separate warning on 15 October: around 19.2 million people are projected to face high levels of acute food insecurity during the November 2026–April 2027 lean season. About five million are expected to face emergency-level hunger.

The agencies say favourable rainfall supported crops and pasture this year. But unemployment, higher costs and reduced assistance are preventing many households from buying nutritious food. Winter also reduces opportunities for agricultural work. Their warning distinguishes a national supply of food from a family’s ability to obtain it.

https://www.wfp.org/news/food-insecurity-and-child-malnutrition-worsen-afghanistan-despite-strong-agricultural-season

That distinction matters for the response. Agricultural assistance can support future harvests, but it cannot substitute for immediate treatment. Food in a market offers little protection to a household without purchasing power.

Nor is malnutrition simply a matter of insufficient food. UNICEF and Action Against Hunger report that unsafe water, diarrhoeal disease, measles and disrupted nutrition supplies are increasing the pressure on families and services. Cobi Rietveld, Action Against Hunger’s country director, argued that success must include preventing children from becoming severely malnourished, rather than measuring treatment alone.

https://www.unicef.org/press-releases/afghanistan-face-sharp-rise-acute-malnutrition-2027-over-4-million-children

## Women must be able to deliver—and receive—assistance

Access also depends on who can work. In a 7 September statement, UN Women’s Afghanistan representative Susan Ferguson said restrictions preventing Afghan women staff from entering UN premises remained in place a year after their reinforcement.

She described women continuing to provide services and support grassroots organisations despite those restrictions, while warning that the constraints undermine the UN’s ability to reach women and girls. She called for unhindered access to workplaces and field sites. The statement provides no response from the Taliban authorities.

https://unwomen.org.au/a-year-since-afghan-women-staff-barred-from-entering-united-nations-premises-across-the-country/

Afghan women are therefore not only recipients of assistance. They are among the people whose work makes assistance reachable. Funding supplies without protecting their ability to deliver services leaves a critical part of the response insecure.

![Young Afghan girls at a women’s bazaar in Kabul.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8c/Women%27s_Bazaar_in_Kabul%2C_Afghanistan_130503-A-CV700-001.jpg)

Contextual archive photograph: young Afghan girls at a Women’s Bazaar in Kabul, 3 May 2013. U.S. Army photo by Maj. Meritt Phillips; public domain. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Women%27s_Bazaar_in_Kabul,_Afghanistan_130503-A-CV700-001.jpg

WFP describes a combination of nutrition treatment, food assistance and cash support for pregnant women and mothers, alongside livelihood training. These are programme descriptions, not evidence that every eligible household currently receives help.

https://www.wfp.org/countries/afghanistan

The practical accountability questions are now urgent: which clinics have reliable supplies, how many women and children complete treatment, and which communities cannot reach care? Donors need to distinguish money pledged from services sustained; agencies need to show where coverage is shrinking; authorities need to remove barriers that prevent women from providing and obtaining assistance.

The projections are a warning, not an unavoidable outcome. Their value lies in the opportunity to act before children become critically ill and before mothers must borrow for another journey to hospital.

Reporting note: The IPC malnutrition page is dated 13 October; the agency appeals were issued on 15 October. This report uses IPC’s explicit age groups and separate women’s estimate because some agency summaries use inconsistent wording. Food-insecurity and malnutrition figures measure different, overlapping needs and should not be added together. ATHENA conducted no field interviews.

title: Women farmers are taking up climate-resilient methods. Investment must follow.
subtitle: New evidence from Farm Africa highlights women’s adoption of farming practices that protect soil and livelihoods. The results strengthen the case for better access to resources, while leaving important questions about how the comparisons were measured.*
author: ATHENA
body:
Women participating in Farm Africa programmes are adopting climate-resilient agricultural practices and sustaining their use, the organisation says in a new publication calling for greater investment in female farmers across eastern Africa.

Published on 13 October, *Women lead the way* brings programme evidence into the debate around International Day of Rural Women on 15 October. Its central argument is practical: agricultural support should be designed around women’s access to resources and decision-making. Farm Africa’s publication announcement [1].

The organisation’s campaign describes women-led households in Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania continuing with climate-smart practices for longer than male-led households. These are findings about people participating in particular programmes, not a ranking of women’s and men’s farming ability across the region. Campaign findings [2].

One comparison in the booklet is striking. In its Strengthening Regenerative Agriculture in Kenya project, Farm Africa reports adoption of regenerative technologies among 56% of female-headed households, against 31% of male-headed households. The booklet also reports average crop production of 700kg and 430kg respectively.

Those production totals are not yields per hectare. Without comparable land areas, crops and growing conditions, they cannot by themselves establish that one group farmed more productively. The booklet does not supply sample sizes, detailed observation periods or statistical methods for these comparisons. Household headship also cannot tell us who performed every task or controlled the proceeds. Read the booklet [3].

The findings are therefore a useful signal for programme design, rather than proof that gender caused the differences. Farm Africa both implements the programmes and presents their results; fuller evaluation would help funders assess which interventions worked, for whom and at what cost.

![Women smallholder farmers standing in a field in Machakos, Kenya.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/Women_smallholder_farmers_in_Kenya.jpg/1280px-Women_smallholder_farmers_in_Kenya.jpg)
Women from the Mbini Self-Help Group in Machakos, Kenya, on 14 October 2010. Contextual archive photograph: McKay Savage. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Women_smallholder_farmers_in_Kenya.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0

For Judith Aumah in Muhooma, in Uganda’s Kamuli District, the practical value of support is easier to identify. Farm Africa’s May profile describes a farmer and mother of three who chairs a local women’s support organisation. Through an AGRA-funded project, she received savings and credit training, connections to seed suppliers and advice on farming and storage.

Judith grows crops including maize, beans and vegetables, and uses composted cow dung and mulch. The profile reports that improved post-harvest handling lets her store crops longer, giving her more choice over when to sell. This is Farm Africa’s account of her experience, not an ATHENA interview or an independent income assessment. Judith’s story [4].Her experience makes an important distinction visible: a farmer needs more than instructions on what to plant. Access to supplies, affordable finance and the ability to wait for a suitable buyer can determine whether agricultural knowledge becomes income.

The wider barriers are well documented. FAO’s 2023 global assessment identified women’s less secure access to land, credit and training, alongside technology poorly suited to their needs. It reported a 24% productivity gap between female- and male-managed farms of equal size. That older global estimate is background, not a measurement of Farm Africa’s participants or a fresh 2026 result. FAO’s assessment [5].

Farm Africa proposes practical changes including savings groups, childcare at training sessions, accessible scheduling and women’s participation in cooperatives and marketing. Such measures address whether a woman can use an opportunity, rather than simply whether a programme has offered it.

For governments and donors, the next questions should extend beyond enrolment and harvest totals. Do women retain control of additional earnings? Does a new practice reduce their workload or add to it? Can they keep using land and equipment after a project ends?

Higher production can benefit households, but women’s claim to investment should not depend on outperforming men or spending every additional shilling on others. They are farmers, business owners and decision-makers in their own right. The strongest response to these findings would give them the resources—and the authority—to shape what happens next.

title: When Control Is Written as Love
subtitle: Romance can make refusal look like an obstacle, jealousy like devotion and suffering like the price of being chosen. The question is what a story asks us to forgive—and whether it gives its heroine permission to leave.*
author: ATHENA
body:
A woman says no. The story hears: not yet.

He persists. He appears where she has not invited him. He decides that her hesitation conceals a desire she does not understand. In one kind of film, this is the beginning of danger. In another, it is the beginning of love. The difference lies partly in the instructions surrounding the encounter: the music, the comedy, the access to his wounded heart, the promised ending.

This is where a serious critique of romantic storytelling begins. A narrative can present a woman’s boundary as an obstacle to the hero’s happiness, then reward him for crossing it. By the final embrace, her earlier refusal has been rewritten as a mistake he was right to ignore.

Calling this “grooming” captures the fear that audiences are being taught to welcome what should trouble them. But the word implies deliberate preparation for exploitation, an intention we cannot assign to an entire genre or industry. The more defensible argument concerns romanticisation: the ways particular stories make control desirable, excuse cruelty and turn endurance into evidence of love.

In the 2004 film *The Notebook*, Noah hangs from a Ferris wheel and pressures Allie to agree to a date by threatening to let go. The scene makes his willingness to endanger himself part of his appeal. Yet the structure of the demand is coercive: she must agree or bear the immediate fear of what he might do. That encounter sits inside a film celebrated for lifelong devotion. Its tenderness does not make the pressure disappear. Scene discussed in TIME [1].

The troubling move is the conversion of intensity into moral authority. Because a character feels deeply, the audience is invited to grant him permissions that another person would not receive. Wanting her becomes a reason to overrule her. Jealousy becomes proof of how much she matters. His distress occupies the foreground; her freedom becomes negotiable.

A novel can accomplish the same conversion through interiority. We learn about his abandonment, his grief, the tenderness he cannot express. Explanation is one of literature’s great capacities. But explanation becomes an alibi when the narrative makes her responsible for repairing what happened to him, while treating the harm he does to her as a necessary stage of his recovery.

The fantasy of being the exception is especially powerful: he is ruthless with everyone, but gentle with her; incapable of intimacy, until she arrives. Within the story, her specialness appears to guarantee her safety. Outside it, nobody has an author ensuring that another person’s cruelty will stop at the bedroom door.

This fantasy also assigns her a job. She must interpret hostility correctly, remain through injury and recognise the goodness nobody else can see. If he changes, her patience is vindicated. If she leaves, the same narrative logic can make her look like someone who abandoned him just before the transformation. Love becomes an examination in how much she can bear.

Yet literature itself offers a warning against this reading. In Emily Brontë’s *Wuthering Heights*, Isabella imagines a desirable man in Heathcliff and discovers a brutal husband. Her letter to Nelly asks, “Is Mr. Heathcliff a man?” The question punctures any easy glamour surrounding him: here is the experience of the woman who must live inside the fantasy. *Wuthering Heights*, Chapter XIII [2].

To read the novel solely as a monument to overwhelming passion is to lose that witness. Heathcliff’s suffering and his cruelty coexist; one does not cancel the other. The book’s disturbing force depends on our confronting the damage, rather than extracting a desirable lover from it.

That distinction matters across the genre. A story may depict an unhealthy relationship in order to examine it, grieve it or expose its attractions. Depiction alone is not endorsement. The sharper questions concern narrative consequences: whose pain receives attention, whose excuses receive sympathy, and what conduct the ending rewards.

There is evidence that romantic framing can influence attitudes, although it supports a narrower claim than the accusation that romance trains women to accept abuse. Julia R. Lippman’s experiment, published online in 2015 and in a 2018 issue of *Communication Research*, recruited 426 undergraduate women and randomly assigned them film material portraying pursuit as romantic, frightening, or absent. Romanticised pursuit did not increase stalking-supportive beliefs across all participants. The effect appeared among viewers who found the material more realistic or felt more absorbed in its story. Frightening portrayals reduced such beliefs.

These were immediate responses from a university sample, not evidence that viewers subsequently entered or remained in abusive relationships. Different films also differed in features beyond their treatment of pursuit. The experiment supports taking narrative framing seriously; it cannot establish an entire genre’s long-term effects. Lippman’s study [3].

The quieter promise of romance deserves scrutiny too: that the right person will know us without explanation, that compatibility announces itself through instant recognition, that love can resolve every practical disagreement. Those expectations can make communication seem like evidence that something is missing. If he really loved her, why would she need to ask?

A 2013 study by Veronica Hefner and Barbara J. Wilson combined an analysis of 52 successful romantic comedies with a survey of 335 university students. Students who reported watching romantic comedies to learn about relationships endorsed romantic ideals more strongly. Because the audience study was a survey, it could not establish whether viewing produced those beliefs, whether those beliefs encouraged particular viewing habits, or both. Its findings concern a specific student population, not all readers and viewers. Hefner and Wilson’s study [4].

Art compresses time. A reconciliation can take a scene; rebuilding trust can take much longer. A declaration gives a story a climax, while the changed behaviour that would make it credible requires repetition. The danger in treating the declaration as sufficient is that eloquence begins to stand in for accountability.

Still, criticism must distinguish unrealistic spectacle from entirely reasonable desire. Wanting affection, sexual pleasure, reliability or a partner who takes one’s ambitions seriously is not asking too much because a novel made those possibilities vivid. Women should not be told to lower their expectations until disappointment looks mature. Sometimes the fantasy exposes how little they have been encouraged to expect.

Nor does enjoying a dangerous fictional lover establish a desire for danger outside the book. A reader can explore obsession, surrender or transgression while retaining control over the encounter: she can stop, skip, reread or close the cover. Consensual power exchange is also distinct from coercion. Neither a taste for dark romance nor an interest in kink is evidence that someone wants their real boundaries violated.

An argument that erases these distinctions reproduces the paternalism it claims to challenge. Women become impressionable consumers who must be protected from their own imaginations. Responsibility for abuse then risks drifting towards the books they read, instead of remaining with the person who harms them.

A more useful literary education would give readers language for what they already notice. We can be moved by a scene and question the bargain it offers. We can find a character compelling without appointing him a model partner. For younger audiences especially, a discussion of how a story produces desire is more illuminating than a verdict that the book is good or bad.

![Jane tries to take hold of Mr Rochester’s horse in an early Jane Eyre illustration.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d6/P107b.jpg)
Jane tries to take hold of Mr Rochester’s horse. Illustration by F. H. Townsend, published in an 1847 edition of Jane Eyre. Public domain.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:P107b.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/

Charlotte Brontë supplies a particularly demanding example. In *Jane Eyre*, Jane loves Rochester and refuses to remain with him after discovering that he is already married. Her feeling does not vanish conveniently to make the decision easier. She leaves while still wanting him. “I care for myself,” she tells herself. *Jane Eyre*, Chapter XXVII [5].

The novel eventually reunites them, and its treatment of Rochester’s wife, Bertha, makes that resolution ethically troubled. But Jane’s refusal remains significant. Her own judgement has authority even when desire argues against it. She does not have to become indifferent before she is entitled to go.

Romance need not abandon dangerous characters, impossible longing or extravagant pleasure. It can contain the whole unruly range of desire. What deserves resistance is the bargain that asks a woman to surrender her judgement in exchange for being chosen.

The most radical romantic ending may be one in which being loved leaves a woman fully able to say no—and the story knows she has lost none of her worth.

title: Women’s football is booming. Nearly half of surveyed players are considering leaving early
subtitle: A survey of 791 players across 40 countries finds that the women’s game is creating global stars faster than it is creating secure jobs. The warning is not that women lack ambition, but that professional expectations are still being imposed without professional protection.
author: ATHENA
body:
Nearly half of the women footballers surveyed for a new global employment report said they were considering leaving the game earlier than planned, even as salaries, audiences and commercial investment rise at the top of the sport.

The study by global players’ union FIFPRO gathered survey responses from 791 players in 40 countries during the 2025–26 season and conducted semi-structured interviews with 34 players across six regions. Forty-nine per cent of respondents said they were considering an early departure. Among that group, 59% cited their financial situation and 46% cited psychological stress; respondents could identify more than one reason, so those percentages should not be added together. [1], [2].

The result does not mean that half of all professional women footballers will retire soon. It records what this group was considering when surveyed, not completed retirements or a forecast. The sample is broad but not a random census of every league and player in the world, and FIFPRO is a union advocating for stronger labour standards. Its figures should be read as substantial evidence of insecurity among surveyed players, not a precise estimate for every woman who plays professionally.

The report nevertheless exposes a contradiction the industry cannot explain away. Women’s football increasingly presents itself as a major commercial product. Many of the women producing that product still cannot depend on it as stable employment.

## A rising average can conceal the player in the middle

FIFPRO reports that the inflation-adjusted average monthly club wage in its survey has tripled since its previous global study in 2017, reaching $2,601. The median is considerably lower at $1,669.

That difference matters. An average can be pulled upwards by a relatively small number of highly paid players in wealthy leagues. The median—the point at which half of reported salaries fall above and half below—better describes the centre of an unequal distribution. Neither figure is a universal wage: taxes, living costs, season length and whether players are paid throughout the year differ by country.

In ten Eastern European countries analysed, average pay remained below the relevant national minimum wage, FIFPRO said. Even in parts of Western Europe and Asia-Oceania containing prominent leagues, average player pay was not substantially higher than national minimums. These are regional comparisons within the report; they do not mean every club or player in those regions has the same conditions.

Employment security is also about more than the amount deposited each month. Only 56% of respondents had an employment contract, according to FIFPRO, while the average contract lasted 19 months. Just 13% received a pension from their club, and only eight of the 30 national leagues examined had a collective agreement negotiated with players through their unions.

A short contract can turn an injury, pregnancy, coaching change or missed renewal into an immediate housing and income problem. It also makes long-term financial planning unusually difficult for workers whose careers are already brief.

Calling a league professional does not by itself make every player’s job professional. That status should be visible in written employment rights, reliable pay, medical care, qualified staff and a procedure through which a player can challenge a club without sacrificing her career.

![A Persepolis women’s player trains with a football in Tehran in 2025](/images/athena-women-football-2025.jpg)
A Persepolis women’s player trains in Tehran on 1 February 2025. Archive photograph illustrating the global women’s game; it does not establish this player’s employment conditions. Photograph: Frenchman Valley / Wikimedia Commons. CC0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Persepolis_Women_Football_Team_Training_in_2025.jpg
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/deed.en

## Mental health cannot be separated from working conditions

Fifty-seven per cent of surveyed players reported having struggled with their mental health. Half of those players said their clubs had not provided support.

The survey does not diagnose a clinical condition, establish when each difficulty began or prove that football caused it. Financial insecurity, injury, personal circumstances and pressures outside the sport can overlap. FIFPRO’s player interviews did, however, identify workload and social-media abuse among the pressures accompanying the game’s expansion. [3].

Mental-health provision should therefore not be reduced to teaching players to tolerate an unstable workplace. Confidential care needs to be independent enough for a player to seek help without fearing that disclosures will affect team selection, contract renewal or how coaches assess her resilience.

FIFPRO points to the United States’ National Women’s Soccer League, where mental-health practitioners work alongside club staff and players have access to extended mental-health leave, as one possible model. A policy on paper still needs qualified clinicians, privacy protections and enough staffing to work in practice.

The staffing problem extends beyond counselling. Forty-seven per cent of respondents said their clubs lacked sufficient staff for players’ needs. FIFPRO’s interviews included accounts of inexperienced or underqualified support personnel. As teams demand more training, travel, media work and matches from players, medical, safeguarding and performance services have to grow with those obligations.

## Maternity protections show that rules can change expectations

The report also contains evidence of progress. Among players considering an early exit, the proportion citing starting a family fell from 47% in FIFPRO’s 2017 study to 19% in 2026.

FIFPRO connects that shift partly to global maternity protections introduced by FIFA in 2021 and expanded in 2024, as well as to the visibility of players combining parenthood with elite sport. FIFA’s rules include paid maternity leave and protections relating to adoption, non-biological motherhood, severe menstrual symptoms, pregnancy complications and returning to football. [4].

The comparison is encouraging, but it is not a controlled experiment. The 2017 and 2026 samples are not identical, the industry changed in other ways and a reduced intention to leave is not proof that every club implements the rules properly.

Individual cases demonstrate why enforcement matters. In a ruling publicised in June, the Court of Arbitration for Sport found that Lazio Women unlawfully ended Swedish defender Maja Gothberg’s employment after learning she was pregnant and awarded compensation. Lazio said the dispute arose from misunderstandings during a complex negotiation and promised to review its procedures. The decision showed that maternity rules can create a remedy, not merely a public commitment. [5], [6].

FIFPRO argues that another gap remains: pregnancy does not automatically extend a contract. With an average contract length of only 19 months, leave protections can be weakened if a player’s agreement simply expires during pregnancy or recovery.

New fertility benefits create a related question. Chelsea and Spain’s football federation have offered players access to services including egg freezing. Such programmes may expand reproductive choice, but employer-funded treatment must not become pressure to postpone motherhood for a club’s convenience. Access to fertility care and the right to become pregnant during a playing career should exist together. [7].

## Growth should be measured by the careers it sustains

The solution is not to ask supporters to feel guilty about sold-out stadiums or higher broadcast revenues. Commercial growth can finance better employment. The accountability question is where that money travels after it enters the sport.

League licensing can require minimum staffing, safe facilities, medical cover and written contracts. Collective bargaining can give players a role in determining salaries, leave, scheduling and dispute procedures. Governing bodies can make funding conditional on verified labour standards rather than accepting the word “professional” as proof of professional conditions.

Clubs should also publish enough information to make progress measurable: how many players are employees, whether wages arrive on time, which healthcare services are independent, how maternity rules are implemented and whether athletes have a protected route to report abuse or unsafe conditions.

Women players have already demonstrated the demand for their sport. They have also organised through unions, challenged discriminatory decisions and helped establish maternity rights that were once absent from the global rulebook.

The new report is not evidence that women are walking away because they cannot withstand elite competition. It is evidence that talent and commitment cannot indefinitely substitute for employment security.

A sport has not fully professionalised when its stars play in packed stadiums while the player beside them is one short contract, one injury or one unpaid month away from leaving. Women’s football should judge its growth not only by the audiences it attracts, but by how many women can build—and finish—the careers their ability earned.

title: Bumble agrees to a $1.3 billion sale. Its women-first promise is already being rewritten
subtitle: The agreed takeover arrives two months after Bumble retired the messaging rule that made it famous. The company’s decline also tests what happens when women-centred design becomes both a mission and a marketing asset.
author: ATHENA
body:
Publication update, 14 October 2026: This report has been revised to include the acquisition agreement announced on 13 October. Its original reporting date is retained.

Bumble announced on 13 October that it had agreed to be acquired by Ithaca Holdings in a $1.3 billion cash transaction. Class A shareholders are to receive $6.05 per share. This is an agreed transaction, not a completed takeover. [1]

The announcement followed Reuters’ 12 October report of talks at a roughly $1 billion valuation. Bumble’s shares closed almost 50% higher on Monday at $3.80, their largest one-day percentage gain. The company had been worth about $389 million on the stock market at Friday’s close. [2].

Bumble reported $451 million in debt and $154 million in cash at the end of June. A transaction’s headline value and a company’s stock-market value measure different things; neither should be treated as the amount each shareholder receives.

The agreed sale matters beyond one battered technology stock. Bumble built a global brand by arguing that the architecture of a dating app could redistribute power: in heterosexual matches, women—not men—had to initiate the conversation. That rule was never a complete answer to harassment or unequal relationships. But it made women’s experience the product’s most recognisable feature and turned a gendered social problem into a commercial distinction.

Now the company that sold that promise is preparing to leave the public market shortly after changing the promise itself.

## From market landmark to falling subscriptions

Wolfe Herd founded Bumble in 2014. When the company went public in February 2021, its initial offering priced the business at more than $7 billion. A first-day share surge then carried its market value to about $14 billion. Those are different valuation moments, often compressed into one dramatic number. At 31, Wolfe Herd became the youngest woman to take a US company public. [3], [4].

The decline since then is substantial, but it cannot be explained by a single branding decision. The wider dating-app business is confronting swipe fatigue, competition and difficulty persuading younger users to pay. Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, has faced related pressure.

Bumble’s own figures show the strain. In the second quarter of 2026, total revenue fell 15.2% from a year earlier to $210.5 million. Average monthly paying users across Bumble, Badoo and other included products fell 16.4%, from 3.8 million to 3.2 million. Revenue per paying user rose slightly, suggesting the company earned more from the customers who remained even as the paying population shrank.

The company also recorded a $127.9 million quarterly net loss, including a $169.3 million impairment charge. Its preferred adjusted measure, EBITDA, was positive at $72.9 million. Both figures belong in the picture: the first captures accounting costs the company says are not representative of its underlying operations; the second removes several expenses and is not the same as net profit. [5].

These numbers help explain the pressure behind the takeover. Private ownership can give management more room to rebuild without a public verdict every quarter. It can also reduce what users, workers and outside investors can see, because a private company generally discloses less financial information than one listed on Nasdaq.

## Was “women make the first move” freedom—or work?

In August, Bumble stopped reserving the first message for women in heterosexual matches. Anyone can now send one opening message, and the recipient has up to 72 hours to respond rather than 24.

The company said nearly two-thirds of women it surveyed would prefer men to message first, often because they wanted less pressure. It also said Canadian product tests produced more initiated chats, fewer expired matches and more mutual conversations. The public announcement did not provide enough methodological detail to establish whether the survey represents Bumble’s global female membership or whether the test results will persist at scale. These are company findings, not an independent evaluation. [6], [7].

The change need not be reduced to either liberation or betrayal. Requiring a woman to initiate gave her a clear gatekeeping choice after a match. It could also make her responsible for starting every exchange, under a deadline, on a platform used by people with different preferences, cultures and communication styles.

Giving women control does not always mean assigning women more work. Yet removing the rule also removes a filter that some users valued. The relevant test is not whether the new system sounds more flexible; it is whether it produces safer, more respectful and more useful conversations for women in practice.

That question is larger than who sends the first sentence. Harassment, impersonation, fraud and abuse can happen after a conversation begins or moves off the app. Bumble says it offers reporting tools, identity verification and automated systems intended to detect harmful conduct, and it publishes transparency information under the European Union’s Digital Services Act. Those safeguards should be judged by measurable outcomes: response times, repeat-offender detection, successful appeals, staffing and what happens when a woman reports conduct that crosses platforms. [8], [9].

## A private buyer inherits more than an app

Ithaca Holdings was founded by former Instacart finance chief Ravi Gupta and former Meta advertising executive John Hegeman. Reuters reported that the holding company invests in technology businesses; the Wall Street Journal reported that it intends to apply artificial intelligence across its investments. Bumble says Gupta and Hegeman will become its co-chief executives when the transaction closes, with Wolfe Herd remaining involved. [1]

AI has already become part of Bumble’s attempted turnaround. The company has discussed new matching and guidance tools designed to move users away from repetitive swiping and towards in-person dates. But AI cannot be assessed only by whether it lifts engagement. Dating profiles contain intimate information about identity, sexuality, location, preferences and relationships. Any buyer should have to explain what data its AI uses, how long that data is retained, whether it trains shared models, and how users can refuse without losing basic access.

There is also a structural conflict at the centre of dating-app economics. A successful match may cause two paying customers to leave. That does not prove platforms deliberately keep people single, but it does mean companies should publish better evidence for claims that product changes create meaningful relationships rather than merely more messages, longer sessions or higher subscription revenue.

For women, the lesson of Bumble’s fall is not that a women-focused company was commercially naive. Its original rule was a serious product intervention and a powerful marketing idea; it also could not by itself solve the economics of online dating or the behaviour of people using it.

If the agreed transaction closes, the decisive question will not be whether Bumble preserves the exact ritual of women messaging first. It will be whether new owners continue to invest in women’s safety, agency and privacy when those priorities compete with cost cuts, data extraction and growth targets—and whether the company supplies enough evidence for users to judge the answer.

title: She carried her daughter for three days. Somalia’s malnutrition emergency is also a crisis of distance
subtitle: An estimated 1.92 million Somali children may require treatment for acute malnutrition by June 2027. Halima Abdullahi Ibrahim’s journey to hospital with her three-year-old daughter shows why food alone cannot solve an emergency when clinics, transport, clean water and humanitarian funding are disappearing together.
author: ATHENA
body:
For three days, Halima Abdullahi Ibrahim carried her three-year-old daughter almost 90 kilometres from their village to a hospital in the southern Somali city of Kismayo.

Asho Hassan Abdi’s body was swelling. The specialised care she needed was unavailable closer to home. At Kismayo Referral Hospital, clinicians diagnosed oedema associated with severe acute malnutrition and admitted her to a stabilisation centre, according to Associated Press journalists reporting from the city. AP photographed mother and daughter there on 22 September and published their story on 12 October. The report did not state Asho’s subsequent condition or whether she had been discharged. [1]

Halima’s journey is one family’s experience, not a representative study of every Somali household. But the barrier it exposes—specialised treatment separated from a sick child by days of travel—is consistent with national warnings about closed services and reduced access.

Somalia’s latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification analysis estimates that 1.92 million children aged six to 59 months will suffer or are expected to suffer acute malnutrition and require treatment during the 12 months from July 2026 to June 2027. Of those cases, 433,000 are projected to involve severe acute malnutrition, the most dangerous form. [2]

The 1.92 million figure is a projected treatment burden across a year—not a count of children simultaneously malnourished on one particular day. Nor does it mean each child has already been clinically diagnosed. The estimate combines current conditions and projected cases across assessed areas; changing rainfall, disease, displacement and aid delivery can alter what happens.

## Mothers need care too

The same IPC analysis estimates that 157,000 pregnant and breastfeeding women will suffer or are expected to suffer acute malnutrition over the period. That figure is easily lost when an emergency is described only through children.

Maternal and child nutrition are connected, but mothers should not appear in the story solely as vehicles for their children’s survival. A pregnant or breastfeeding woman requires treatment for her own health. When a clinic closes, she may also absorb the cost of transport, days away from other children, lost income and the physical labour of carrying a sick child to care.

That labour can be narrated as devotion. It should also be recognised as evidence of an inaccessible system. A three-day walk to hospital is not a healthcare pathway.

In August, UNICEF said 205 health and nutrition facilities had already closed following humanitarian funding cuts and warned that as many as 618 could close nationwide. The agency also reported a 32% rise in admissions of children suffering severe acute malnutrition with medical complications. Those figures were reported by Reuters from a UNICEF briefing; they describe service contraction and admissions, not proof that every closure caused a particular child’s condition. [3]

At Kismayo Referral Hospital, 152 children with severe acute malnutrition were admitted in August and four died, Jubbaland Health Minister Ismail Garas told AP. A hospital total cannot measure all cases in the surrounding region: children who never reach the ward are absent from it. [1]

![A medical officer checks a woman’s blood pressure in Kismayo in 2013](/images/athena-kismayo-care-2013.jpg)
A Kenyan medical officer checks a woman’s blood pressure at an AMISOM clinic in Kismayo on 19 August 2013. Archive photograph; it does not depict the 2026 malnutrition cases described in this report. Photograph: Ramadaan Mohamed Hassan / AU–UN IST / AMISOM Public Information. CC0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:2013_08_19_AMISOM_Sector_Two_Health_Clinic_010_%289649640387%29.jpg
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/deed.en

## Hunger is only one part of the diagnosis

Acute malnutrition is not produced by a single cause. The IPC identifies disease outbreaks, acute food insecurity, poor access to clean water and sanitation, and reduced health and nutrition services among the pressures concentrated in southern Somalia.

Infection and malnutrition can reinforce each other: illness can reduce appetite and the body’s ability to use nutrients, while malnutrition can make a child more vulnerable to disease. UNICEF’s Somalia representative, Sandra Lattouf, told AP that illnesses including measles were intensifying the danger.

This is why delivering food, although essential, is not a complete response. A child with severe malnutrition and complications may need clinical monitoring, therapeutic feeding and treatment for infection. Families also need safe water, sanitation and functioning local services capable of identifying deterioration before hospital stabilisation becomes necessary.

An ICRC account from the same Kismayo centre in 2025 described therapeutic milk, medical care and nutrition and breastfeeding counselling for caregivers. It said recovery commonly took seven to 14 days at that programme. That earlier operational account shows what treatment can involve; it is not evidence of Asho’s outcome or a guarantee that every child will recover on the same timetable. [4]

## Flood warnings arrive as the response contracts

The danger is expected to increase during the October-to-December rainy season. Somalia’s government and UN agencies warn that El Niño-associated flooding could expose 2.5 million to 3.5 million people and displace about one million, damaging crops and livestock while cutting roads to markets, clinics and aid deliveries.

These are forecasts, not completed events. Their value is precisely that action can still change the outcome. Agencies have called for food, therapeutic supplies and emergency support to be positioned in vulnerable areas before roads become impassable. [5]

The IPC classified 19 assessed areas at its Critical acute-malnutrition level for June to September and projected displaced people in Beletweyne to reach the Extremely Critical category during October to December. It also warns that displaced communities in Baidoa could face famine under a plausible worst-case scenario. The Baidoa assessment was based on data collected in April, and authorities said a follow-up assessment was planned for October. That limitation matters: famine-risk statements must be updated as new evidence becomes available rather than repeated as a settled present-tense finding.

## The question is not how far a mother will walk

At the Luglow displacement settlement outside Kismayo, a regional official told AP that many families had received no humanitarian assistance since 2023 because organisations lacked funding. Dirty standing water and makeshift shelters already create conditions in which disease and hunger can spread; further displacement would add pressure to the settlement’s clinic and to Kismayo’s hospital.

The institutional response therefore has to be measured at the beginning of the care chain, not only at its most visible end. How many community health workers can screen children? Which outpatient centres remain open? Are therapeutic foods and medicines continuously stocked? Can pregnant and breastfeeding women receive treatment nearby? What transport exists when a child develops complications?

Halima reached a hospital. Her determination should not become the standard against which other mothers are judged. Families who cannot cross 90 kilometres have not failed their children; a system that places lifesaving care beyond a family’s reach has failed them.

Somalia’s emergency needs food and money, but it also needs proximity. Treatment must exist before a child becomes too weak to travel—and before a mother has to turn an impossible journey into her only remaining form of healthcare.

title: Four minors face irreversible injuries as France reviews its policing of student protests
subtitle: Twenty-four cases are now before France’s police watchdog, and one stun-grenade model has been suspended. The test is whether accountability reaches beyond a single weapon—and whether children can protest their school conditions without risking lifelong harm.
author: ATHENA
body:
France’s internal police watchdog is examining 24 cases connected to the policing of nationwide school protests, after teenagers suffered injuries that include the loss of a hand, possible permanent damage to an eye and severe facial trauma.

Sebastian Roché, a policing researcher at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research, told Reuters that four minors had sustained irreversible injuries within 12 days. Reuters said it independently documented 28 injuries through interviews and legal records, 15 of them among the cases referred to the Inspectorate General of the National Police, or IGPN. The investigations are not findings that officers acted unlawfully; they are the mechanism through which that question should be tested. [1]

The injuries have shifted the public argument. The protests began over overcrowded classrooms, missing teachers, deteriorating buildings and long school days. They are now also a test of whether France’s public-order system treats teenagers as rights-holders whose age increases the state’s duty of care—not as smaller adults in a hostile crowd.

## A 14-year-old, a launcher and two competing accounts

In Saint-Ouen-l’Aumône, 14-year-old Eden suffered a broken jaw and smashed teeth after a tear-gas canister struck his face. His family’s lawyer said he had been sitting away from the protest and looking at his phone before an officer approached. The local prosecutor gave a more complicated sequence: an officer struck Eden with a baton, Eden kicked an officer and was then struck by a canister fired by a second officer using a Cougar launcher.

Eden’s family has filed a complaint alleging attempted murder. The officer who fired the canister has been placed under formal investigation for assault by a public official resulting in permanent disability or disfigurement. That legal status does not establish guilt. Associated Press reported that the officer was suspended, barred from carrying a gun and prohibited from public contact while the case proceeds. Police declined Reuters’ request to comment on the active investigation. [2]

The case matters beyond the eventual charge. Even if investigators conclude that some force was justified after Eden kicked an officer, they must separately determine whether firing a gas projectile towards a child’s face at close range was necessary and proportionate—and whether emergency assistance was provided promptly.

Other cases make it harder to dismiss the concern as a single operational failure. A 15-year-old in Lens lost a hand in an explosion that Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said was probably caused by a stun grenade. In Argenteuil, a 16-year-old suffered an eye injury that his lawyer says may be permanent; the precise projectile has not been established. Police said he resembled a young person who had fired fireworks at officers, an account his lawyer disputes. Those competing accounts require evidence, not social-media verdicts.

## “Less lethal” does not mean harmless

Nuñez suspended the relevant stun-grenade model from use during the student protests pending investigation. Amnesty International France said the temporary measure was insufficient and called for a permanent ban on stun grenades in demonstrations. Amnesty is an advocacy organisation; its position is not a judicial finding. [3]

![French police at a 2023 demonstration, with a Cougar launcher visible](/images/athena-france-cougar-launcher-2023.jpg)
A police officer carries a Cougar launcher during a pension-reform demonstration in Lille on 13 April 2023. Archive photograph illustrating the equipment; the officers pictured are not identified as involved in the 2026 cases. Photograph: RedRRR / Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Policier_d%27une_Brigade_Sp%C3%A9cialis%C3%A9e_de_Terrain.jpg
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0

The label “less lethal” describes an alternative to firearms, not a promise of safety. United Nations guidance says kinetic-impact projectiles should be reserved for an imminent threat of injury, generally aimed at the lower abdomen or legs, and never targeted at the head, face or neck. It warns that facial strikes can cause skull fractures, brain injury, blindness or death. [4]

That guidance does not decide any French case. It does provide a standard against which weapon design, training, targeting, distance and command decisions can be examined. A review limited to whether one grenade malfunctioned would be too narrow if the deeper problem lies in when such weapons are authorised around children, how officers distinguish violent individuals from bystanders and whether supervisors can reconstruct every discharge.

## The violence against police is part of the record

The government says around 200 students and 700 police officers have been injured during the unrest. Schools have been burned or ransacked, teachers and public workers attacked, and 6,877 people arrested, most of them minors. Nuñez has said students were only rarely injured by police and has defended the overall response as proportionate.

Thierry Clair of the UNSA Police union told Reuters that officers need intermediate-force weapons when confronted with violence; without them, he argued, the remaining option could be lethal force. That concern cannot simply be waved away. Police have a duty to protect people and property, and an officer facing fireworks or an assault is not required to absorb violence without responding.

But necessity is not a blank cheque. It must be assessed for each use of force, against the conduct of the person targeted—not against the disorder of a crowd as a whole. Children who commit offences can be investigated without making every student near a blockade a permissible target.

The scale of arrests also needs scrutiny. “Mostly minors” is not a minor detail. Authorities should publish how many children were released without charge, how long they were held, whether guardians and lawyers were notified promptly, and what safeguarding rules governed custody. Arrest totals measure police activity; they do not, by themselves, measure justified enforcement.

## What credible accountability would require

The 24 IGPN cases should produce more than private files and eventual statistics. Credible investigation means preserving body-camera and street video, launcher and ammunition logs, radio instructions, medical records and witness accounts. It means identifying which officer fired, what threat was present, what distance and angle were used, and whether aid followed. Where misconduct is substantiated, consequences should reach command decisions and training failures as well as the individual act.

The government should also explain whether the suspension applies only to one grenade model or reflects a wider child-specific public-order policy. Nuñez has acknowledged that children must be handled differently. That principle needs operational meaning: clearer restrictions on projectile weapons around schools, trained de-escalation teams, routes for peaceful protest and independent publication of injury and investigation outcomes.

Students have agency in this story. They organised because they say their education is being diminished by shortages and inequality; the acts of violence around some demonstrations do not erase those demands. Nor should serious police injuries be used to erase the rights of teenagers who protested peacefully.

France’s immediate task is to establish what happened in each disputed encounter. Its larger obligation is to ensure that a child asking for a functioning classroom does not leave a demonstration with an injury that shapes the rest of her or his life.

title: Navi Pillay wins the Peace Nobel as the courts she helped build come under attack
subtitle: The South African jurist helped establish that rape can constitute genocide. Her Nobel Prize honours a career spent turning survivors’ testimony into law—but sanctions imposed on the International Criminal Court hours later reveal how fragile that legal protection remains.
author: ATHENA
body:
South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for advancing peace and international law, recognition that reaches beyond one woman’s historic career. It affirms a principle with direct consequences for women in war: sexual violence is not an inevitable side effect to be recorded after the fighting, but conduct that can be investigated and prosecuted as an international crime.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced the award on 9 October. Pillay, 85, will receive 12 million Swedish kronor at a ceremony in Oslo on 10 December. The committee said international law and the institutions that uphold it are under severe pressure. [1], [2].

The timing sharpened that message. Hours after the Nobel announcement, the United States imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court, where Pillay served as an appeals judge from 2003 to 2008. The measures potentially restrict banks, insurers, software providers and other US-linked companies from serving the court, although Washington introduced a six-month grace period and some exemptions.

The two announcements falling on the same day does not establish that the sanctions were a response to Pillay’s award. The Trump administration had already sanctioned individual ICC officials and threatened broader action. Their convergence nevertheless exposed the argument at the centre of this year’s prize: whether international courts can function when powerful governments decide accountability has gone too far.

## She helped make the law hear what women endured

Pillay’s most consequential contribution to women’s rights came before the permanent ICC existed.

She was one of the three judges in the 1998 trial of Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former Rwandan mayor. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda convicted him of genocide and crimes against humanity, including rape. It was the first judgment by an international court for genocide.

More importantly for the development of international law, the chamber held that rape and sexual violence could constitute acts of genocide when committed with the intention of destroying a protected group. It also articulated a definition of rape centred on coercive circumstances rather than requiring proof of physical force.

The finding did not belong to Pillay alone: the three-judge chamber reached it unanimously, after hearing evidence that included testimony from women subjected to sexual violence. But the UN body that now preserves the tribunal’s legacy credits Pillay with an essential role in the case. She was the tribunal’s only woman judge during its first four years and later served as its president. [3], [4].

That distinction matters because women’s accounts of wartime rape have historically been minimised as private injury, treated as an unavoidable consequence of conflict or excluded from the central legal story of mass violence. The Akayesu judgment did not end those failures. It created legal language through which prosecutors could name the conduct and connect it to a campaign of group destruction.

A precedent is not the same as universal justice. Survivors still face stigma, unsafe reporting systems, weak investigations and courts that cannot reach suspects. But recognition changes what institutions are expected to investigate—and what they can no longer credibly dismiss as incidental.

## A career built against exclusion

Pillay began practising law under apartheid. In 1967, she became the first woman to open a law practice in South Africa’s Natal province. After apartheid ended, she became the first non-white woman appointed to South Africa’s High Court.

Her path matters without being turned into a simple triumph-over-adversity story. A woman of Indian Tamil heritage practising under a state built on racial hierarchy encountered institutional barriers that shaped who could enter court, represent political defendants and become a judge. Her career moved from defending anti-apartheid activists to adjudicating genocide cases, serving at the ICC and leading the UN human-rights office from 2008 to 2014. [2], [5].

She is now serving as a judge in proceedings at the International Court of Justice concerning Myanmar, which is accused of genocide against the Rohingya. An allegation before a court is not an established finding of guilt; the case remains a legal proceeding.

Pillay dedicated the Nobel to survivors of international crimes and to those defending international justice. That places survivors at the centre of the award’s meaning, but recognition cannot substitute for accessible legal support, witness protection, reparations or enforcement.

## Gaza makes the honour fiercely contested

The Nobel also recognises a figure whose recent work is politically disputed.

Pillay chaired the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Israel rejected that finding and responded to the Nobel decision by accusing the committee of abandoning its moral judgment.

The commission’s conclusion must be attributed precisely. It is a finding by a UN investigative body, not a final judgment by the International Court of Justice or a criminal conviction by the ICC. Israel denies the allegation of genocide.

This controversy is not peripheral to the prize. It demonstrates why institutions need evidentiary procedures—and why their findings should be scrutinised without turning disagreement into punishment of judges or disabling the courts themselves.

International law does not become legitimate only when its conclusions are convenient. Nor should a prestigious award place any jurist’s work beyond examination.

![The International Criminal Court building in The Hague in 2022](/images/athena-icc-2022.jpg)
The International Criminal Court in The Hague on 6 August 2022. Archive photograph. Photograph: Choinowski / Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:International_Criminal_Court_2022.jpg
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0

## A Nobel cannot execute an arrest warrant

The ICC has no police force. It depends on countries to arrest suspects, transfer them to The Hague, protect witnesses, freeze assets and enforce sentences. [6].

That dependence is why sanctions on the institution matter. Washington says the ICC has overreached and describes it as a threat to US sovereignty. The court says the sanctions attack the rule of law. European officials have signalled support for protecting its operations. [7].

For women and girls living through conflict, this dispute is not an abstract contest between diplomats. If investigators lose secure technology, banking services or access to evidence, cases involving rape, forced pregnancy, sexual slavery and gender persecution may become harder to build. A court’s weakness can become a survivor’s closed door.

Pillay’s Nobel marks how much international law changed when women’s testimony was treated as evidence of the crime itself. The next test is whether states will protect the institutions required to act on that law—or celebrate the principle while allowing its machinery to fail.
