title: Anne Carson wins literature Nobel, bringing ancient voices into a new spotlight
subtitle: The Canadian poet and translator has won literature’s highest-profile international prize for work that crosses poetry, scholarship and performance. For readers, her books offer a way to reconsider whose voices survive—and who gets to interpret them.
author: ATHENA
body:
Anne Carson, the Canadian poet, essayist and translator whose books move between ancient literature and contemporary experience, won the Nobel Prize in Literature on 8 October. The Swedish Academy recognised her inventive dialogue with the classical tradition and her creation of new literary forms. Reuters:
https://www.reuters.com/lifestyle/canadian-writer-anne-carson-wins-2026-nobel-prize-literature-2026-10-08/

The award makes Carson the 19th woman among 123 literature laureates, according to the University of Toronto, where she studied classics. She is the second Canadian woman to receive it, after Alice Munro. The presentation is scheduled for 10 December in Stockholm, with a prize of 12 million Swedish kronor. University of Toronto:
https://www.utoronto.ca/news/anne-carson-wins-nobel-prize

Those milestones matter. But they do not explain the particular achievement being recognised: a writer who treats translation as creative work and allows scholarship, intimacy and visual form to occupy the same page.

For ATHENA’s readers, one compelling route into that work begins with another woman’s words, preserved only in pieces.

## Letting Sappho’s fragments remain fragments

In If Not, Winter, Carson presents Sappho’s surviving fragments in Greek and English. The publisher describes a translation that retains their broken condition rather than turning them into apparently complete modern poems. The Vintage paperback was published in August 2003; the work first appeared in 2002. Penguin Random House:
https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/160692/if-not-winter-by-sappho-translated-by-anne-carson/
 University of Toronto:
https://www.utoronto.ca/news/anne-carson-wins-nobel-prize

![Papyrus fragment preserving part of Sappho’s Ode to Aphrodite.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/04/P.Oxy.v0021.n2288.jpg)
Historical manuscript: Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 2288, dated to the second century CE, preserves part of Sappho’s Ode to Aphrodite. Digital reproduction from the Oxyrhynchus papyri collection, via Wikimedia Commons; photographer not identified. Public domain. This is contextual imagery, not a page from Carson’s edition.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:P.Oxy.v0021.n2288.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/

That choice has significance beyond typography. A fragment asks readers to distinguish the words that survive from the words they might wish were there. It leaves room for uncertainty.

Read through ATHENA’s concern with women’s cultural inheritance, this becomes a useful discipline: bringing a woman’s voice to new readers need not mean filling every silence on her behalf. The missing text remains missing. Its absence is part of the encounter.

This is an interpretation of the work’s form, not a claim that Carson’s translation supplies a complete history of why Sappho’s writings were lost. Preservation and interpretation are different questions.

## Helen of Troy meets Marilyn Monroe

Carson’s Norma Jeane Baker of Troy makes a more explicit intervention in the stories told about famous women. It brings Helen of Troy and Marilyn Monroe into the same dramatic work, examining beauty and the destructive attention it can attract.

New Directions describes the work as reconsidering the two women from their own perspectives. Its stage production opened at New York’s Shed in spring 2019, performed by Ben Whishaw and Renée Fleming and directed by Katie Mitchell. The publisher lists the paperback edition as February 2020. New Directions:
https://www.ndbooks.com/book/norma-jeane-baker-of-troy/

![Marilyn Monroe in a 1953 studio publicity portrait.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3b/Monroe_1953_publicity.jpg)
Archive publicity portrait: Marilyn Monroe, 1953. Photograph: Frank Powolny / 20th Century Fox, via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain in the United States because copyright was not renewed. Context for Carson’s literary treatment of Monroe; not a photograph of the stage production. Displayed to fit.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Monroe_1953_publicity.jpg

The distinction between performance and publication dates matters, but so does the distance between the women themselves. Monroe was a historical person; Helen belongs to an ancient literary and mythological tradition. Bringing them together is an artistic comparison, not evidence that their lives were equivalent.

The pairing nevertheless invites a contemporary question: what happens when a woman’s public image becomes more powerful than anything she can say about herself?

Carson’s approach offers readers a way to examine inherited stories without accepting their familiar framing as final. The beautiful woman can become a subject of interpretation rather than simply its object.

## A book can also be an object of mourning

Her experiments reach beyond retelling classical women. Nox, created after her brother’s death, reproduces a handmade work combining letters, family photographs, sketches and poetry. It unfolds like an accordion inside a box and incorporates her translation of Catullus’s poem mourning his own brother. New Directions:
https://www.ndbooks.com/book/nox/

Here, the physical arrangement matters. Readers encounter a collection of traces rather than a conventional continuous account. Ancient writing sits beside family material; translation becomes one way of approaching personal loss.

These books make the Nobel’s emphasis on form concrete. Experimentation can change how a reader meets a voice, an image or an absence—not simply make a familiar story harder to follow.

## What recognition can—and cannot—do

The prize brings commercial attention as well as prestige. Asked about its effect on sales, Carson joked that her books would gain a sticker. The Associated Press noted that previous laureates, including Munro, experienced increased sales after winning. That history does not establish how many additional Carson books will sell. Associated Press:
https://apnews.com/article/nobel-prize-literature-sweden-swedish-academy-05a268ffc76827d273f9d986c5a5a65e

Publishers now have an opportunity to introduce new readers to an already substantial body of work. Libraries, booksellers and teachers can help make that encounter less intimidating by explaining what each book asks of its reader.

For women’s literary recognition, the award offers something more substantial than a celebratory count. Carson is being honoured for intellectual and artistic invention: for changing the possibilities of the work itself.

The invitation to readers is equally substantial. Return to an old story. Notice who speaks. Notice what survives. And leave space for a woman’s writing to be strange, demanding, playful or unresolved.

title: “I am Jane Doe”: The Cornell case turning women’s solidarity into a demand for accountability
subtitle: An alleged fraternity-house assault, a group chat reportedly containing 57 men, and questions about an abandoned criminal inquiry have sparked a wave of support for a former Cornell student. As women rally around her, the institutions responsible for investigating face scrutiny of their own.
author: ATHENA
body:
Women are posting the same name across social media: Jane Doe. Some are sharing accounts of their own assaults. Others are trying to protect the privacy of the former Cornell University student whose lawsuit has brought renewed scrutiny to an alleged gang rape and the institutions she approached afterwards.

The campaign has grown alongside concrete official action. On 1 October, New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor. Five days later, Cornell trustees commissioned former US deputy attorney general Sally Yates to examine the university’s handling of sexual misconduct, including this case. Neither appointment establishes the guilt of the accused. Both reflect serious questions about how the original allegations were handled. Governor’s order: https://www.governor.ny.gov/executive-order/no-64-appointing-special-prosecutor-investigate-and-if-warranted-prosecute-matters, Cornell’s announcement: https://statements.cornell.edu/2026/20261006-special-committee.cfm.

For ATHENA, the story extends beyond a viral case name. It concerns a woman’s ability to seek an investigation without surrendering her privacy—and why other women have felt compelled to create the protection they believe institutions failed to provide.

## What “Cornell 57” means—and what it does not

Jane Doe filed her civil complaint in New York County on 16 September 2026. She alleges that members of Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity sexually assaulted her during the night of 19–20 October 2024, after she had been drinking and was pressured into taking additional substances. The lawsuit names seven men, alongside the university, fraternity organisations and other defendants.

The complaint reproduces a message allegedly sent to the “Chi Phi Actives” Snapchat group at approximately 1.42am, presenting her as sexually available to others upstairs. It alleges that more men then entered the room. These are allegations in a legal pleading, not findings from a criminal trial. Filed complaint: https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/doe-cornell-new-york-supreme.pdf.

The number 57 refers to the reported membership of that group chat, according to CBS reporting cited by SBS. It is not a count of people accused in the lawsuit of physically assaulting her. Nor does group membership establish when each person read a message, what they understood, where they were or how they responded. SBS: https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/were-fed-up-the-cornell-case-reigniting-the-metoo-conversation/j9ikbt9bd.

That distinction strengthens the questions investigators should ask. Who sent or received the messages? Who saw them in time to act? Did anyone encourage others, check on her welfare or seek help? What records remain to establish the answers?

The language described in the complaint is central to the public anger: it appears to turn a woman into something a man can offer to other men. Investigating that alleged conduct requires individual evidence. A viral label cannot supply it.

Lawyers for three of the named men have denied the allegations against their clients, SBS reported. No criminal charges had been reported in the sources reviewed through 8 October. The civil allegations remain contested.

![Letitia James speaking at a City Hall press conference in 2008.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8a/NLN_Letitia_James_%28cropped%29.jpg)
Archive photograph: Letitia James, then a New York City Council member, at City Hall on 5 October 2008. This photograph predates the Cornell case. Photo: Thomas Good / Next Left Notes (NLN), via Wikimedia Commons. Existing crop by Reppop; displayed to fit. CC BY-SA 4.0.
Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NLN_Letitia_James_(cropped).jpg
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

## The account that reached prosecutors

Hochul’s executive order identifies a specific concern: the local district attorney declined prosecution in November 2024 without speaking to Jane Doe, relying partly on a police statement that reportedly omitted her unequivocal assertion that she had been assaulted. The governor ordered an independent investigation of the underlying incident and prosecution if warranted. Executive Order 64: https://www.governor.ny.gov/executive-order/no-64-appointing-special-prosecutor-investigate-and-if-warranted-prosecute-matters.

District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has said the original account described consensual conduct and that he relied on the campus police investigation. Doe’s lawyer disputes that characterisation. SBS reported that the interview transcript obtained by CBS included her description of rape later in the night, alongside an earlier encounter she described differently. Consent to one encounter cannot simply be assumed to cover everything that follows. SBS: https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/were-fed-up-the-cornell-case-reigniting-the-metoo-conversation/j9ikbt9bd.

On 7 October, her lawyer Thomas Giuffra told AP that Doe had been misled into believing the criminal inquiry continued. Cornell declined comment on behalf of campus police, citing litigation. Separately, one defendant petitioned to remove James, alleging bias in her earlier public comments; her spokesperson declined comment. That challenge is a request to a court, not a ruling. AP: https://apnews.com/article/cornell-university-rape-investigation-sitin-protest-e5d3182af81fff6efc86d700516e171a.

The accountability question is therefore about more than whether somebody filed a report. It is whether the record preserved what she said, whether investigators pursued the available evidence and whether she was accurately told what authorities were doing.

## Why women are saying “I am Jane Doe”

AP documented supporters posting videos, photographs and written messages across platforms. Some hoped that repeating the name would frustrate attempts to identify the plaintiff; others used it to discuss experiences they had struggled to make heard.

Wendy Lea Brewer, a singer interviewed by AP, described finding community after feeling that her earlier efforts to speak about abuse had gone unheard. Photographer Kelsey Combe participated partly to protect Doe’s identity—but later discovered an AI system had incorrectly identified Combe as the plaintiff. She told AP she secured its removal. AP’s report on the movement: https://abc7ny.com/post/cornell-7-case-updates-am-jane-doe-movement-social-media-supports-alleged-gang-rape-victim-suing-university/19906901/.

These accounts show the campaign’s emotional force and its technical limits. There is no verified evidence here that mass posting reliably prevents identification or “confuses” AI in a protective way. Combe’s experience demonstrates that mistaken identification can create a different risk.

The Verge reported that Doe’s lawyers said three other women had been falsely identified and harassed. Its investigation also documented attempts to expose the plaintiff on mainstream platforms. Public curiosity about a complainant’s identity is not the same as legitimate scrutiny of evidence. The Verge: https://www.theverge.com/report/1006636/jane-doe-cornell-dox.

Support does not require sharing suspected names, personal photographs or identifying clues—even to denounce the people circulating them. Nor should another survivor feel obliged to recount her own assault publicly to demonstrate solidarity. Privacy is something the movement can defend without asking women to surrender more of it.

![Official portrait of Sally Yates.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b4/Sally_Q._Yates.jpg)
Archive portrait: Sally Yates as US Deputy Attorney General, 30 January 2016, according to the source metadata. US Department of Justice / US Government, via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain as a US federal government work; displayed to fit. This is not a photograph of the 2026 review.
Source and public-domain notice: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sally_Q._Yates.jpg

## What Cornell’s review must answer

Cornell has defended its investigation, saying it barred the fraternity and imposed sanctions including expulsions. President Michael Kotlikoff has also promised to examine fraternities’ and sororities’ role on campus and acknowledged that the university must improve. Reuters: https://www.reuters.com/world/us/cornell-president-vows-serious-look-fraternities-sororities-wake-rape-2026-10-04/.

The Yates review has a broad remit: student support, investigations, hearings, sanctions, appeals, campus police, coordination with prosecutors and the trustees’ own oversight. Cornell says reviewers will have access to relevant records and personnel, subject to law and privacy requirements, and report directly to a special board committee. The board intends to share findings and recommendations. Its announcement gives no fixed completion date. Cornell’s 6 October statement: https://statements.cornell.edu/2026/20261006-special-committee.cfm.

This university-commissioned review is separate from James’s criminal investigation and Doe’s civil lawsuit. It can identify failures and recommend reforms; it cannot convict anyone. Its independence will be judged by the work it is allowed to do and what the university eventually discloses.

Students have already carried the demand into public space. At the 5 October protest, demonstrators sought changes to disciplinary procedures and greater accountability. Student Athena Holloway told the crowd: “How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?” AP: https://apnews.com/article/cornell-university-rape-investigation-70d74249bc779480975f3b2a4166ee97.

The answer should be visible in records, decisions and support: who acted on the complaint, what evidence reached prosecutors, how sanctions were determined and what assistance allowed—or failed to allow—the complainant to continue her education. Protecting her privacy need not mean concealing institutional decisions.

Social media can make a case impossible to ignore. It cannot safely replace investigators, courts or services that support someone after she reports an assault. The solidarity surrounding Jane Doe matters because it challenges isolation. Its lasting value will depend on whether institutions respond before the next woman needs a national movement to obtain a thorough investigation.

Reporting note: Based on the filed civil complaint, New York’s executive order and official statements, Cornell’s review announcement, and reporting by AP, Reuters, SBS and The Verge. ATHENA has not interviewed the parties or independently authenticated the complete chat history. The “57” figure is attributed reporting, not an established count of perpetrators or knowing bystanders. No reliable total for the solidarity campaign’s reach was available. Images are clearly dated archive photographs of the institution and public officials; none depicts the anonymous plaintiff or the October 2026 protests.

title: The Valkyries crossed $100 million in revenue. Women’s sport has moved beyond proving there is a market.
subtitle: In only their second season, Golden State have reportedly become the first women’s professional sports team to cross $100 million in annual revenue. The milestone breaks an old argument about demand—but revenue, profit, valuation and player pay are four different measures of success.
author: ATHENA
body:
The Golden State Valkyries have exceeded $100 million in annual revenue, according to a Sportico figure reported by Reuters on 8 October, becoming the first WNBA franchise—and reportedly the first women’s professional sports team—to pass that threshold.

The number is a landmark because women’s sport has spent decades being asked to prove that an audience exists before receiving the investment routinely used to create audiences in men’s sport. Golden State’s second season offers a different sequence: build a recognisable team, place it in a major arena, market it seriously, give supporters an experience worth returning to and let the demand become measurable.

But $100 million is gross revenue, not profit. The team has not released an independently audited public financial statement showing its expenses or net income, and the figure reaches the public through Sportico rather than a regulatory filing. Reuters reported that a run to the WNBA Finals could push gross revenue above $130 million. That projection is not money already earned. Reuters, 8 October 2026: https://www.reuters.com/sports/valkyries-first-wnba-franchise-hit-100m-annual-revenue--flm-2026-10-08/
.

## The demand was built—not suddenly discovered

The Valkyries sold out all 22 regular-season games at San Francisco’s Chase Center this year. Their 32–12 record was the WNBA’s second best, and they followed it by winning their first-round playoff series against the Dallas Wings. Competitive success matters commercially: it creates additional home games, television attention and merchandise opportunities. It does not, however, explain why supporters filled the arena before the postseason began.

The foundation was visible in the team’s first year. Golden State says it received 15,000 season-ticket deposits within two months of revealing its brand and started with more than 10,000 founding season-ticket holders. The club says its merchandise was sold in all 50 US states and 70 countries during 2025, while average attendance reached 18,064 across 22 sellouts. Those are company figures, but the sellout record and visible crowds support the central finding: this was not a niche audience waiting to be rescued by a winning streak. Golden State Valkyries’ 2025–26 brand report: https://valkyries.wnba.com/news/golden-state-valkyries-awarded-silver-effie-for-brand-creation-and-2025-launch-campaign-20260618
.

For 2026, the club sold more than 12,000 season tickets before the season opened, a league record, and moved additional supporters onto a paid waitlist. That converted interest into predictable income before single-game tickets, sponsorships, food, hospitality and merchandise were counted. Golden State Valkyries season-ticket announcement: https://valkyries.wnba.com/news/valkyries-announce-season-tickets-sold-out-with-over-12000-season-ticket-holders-20260423
.

The brand was also designed as more than a smaller extension of the NBA’s Golden State Warriors. Violet, “Ballhalla” and a programme of public launches and community events gave the club its own vocabulary. Corporate partners were placed visibly across the uniform and arena, while campaigns connected merchandise to the history of women’s basketball in the Bay Area. None of that makes the product authentic by itself; it shows what happens when a women’s team receives professional brand investment instead of being expected to survive on goodwill.

![Violet and guests on the court at Chase Center.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/62/Indiana_Fever_at_Golden_State_Valkyries_-_August_2025_-_Sarah_Stierch_06.jpg)
Archive photograph: Violet with guests at the Indiana Fever–Golden State Valkyries game, Chase Center, 31 August 2025. From left: Kyle Juszczyk, Kristin Juszczyk, Claire Kittle, Violet, George Kittle, Tori Moraga and Ricky Pearsall. Photo: Sarah Stierch (Missvain). CC0 1.0; original photograph displayed to fit.
Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Indiana_Fever_at_Golden_State_Valkyries_-_August_2025_-_Sarah_Stierch_06.jpg
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/

## An important case study—not a universal blueprint

Golden State is an unusually well-positioned expansion franchise. The ownership group paid a reported $50 million expansion fee in 2023 and could build within the Warriors’ established business operation. The Valkyries play in a modern arena in one of the wealthiest US markets and can draw on existing ticketing, sponsorship, media and event expertise.

Those advantages do not diminish what the team has achieved. They do limit what can be inferred from it. A women’s club without an NBA-linked owner, a major arena, Bay Area corporate partners or capital to spend before revenue arrives cannot simply reproduce this result through enthusiasm.

The more useful lesson is not that every team should already be worth hundreds of millions. It is that underinvestment cannot be used as evidence of weak demand when the test itself withheld the conditions needed for demand to grow.

Nielsen’s wider data show that the market is larger than one club. The measurement company reports 28.3 billion minutes of women’s sport viewed in the United States during the first half of 2026 and 122.5 million Americans interested in women’s sport. Advertising investment has risen 120% since 2022. These are Nielsen’s commercial audience measurements, not a census of every supporter worldwide, and they do not establish that all leagues or markets will grow at the same rate. They do show that the Valkyries are an exceptional expression of a broader shift, not an isolated curiosity. Nielsen’s 2026 women and sport report: https://www.nielsen.com/insights/2026/women-sports/
.

## Revenue is not profit. Valuation is not cash.

The milestone arrives alongside eye-catching valuations. Sportico estimated the franchise at $850 million in May, while CNBC placed it at $1 billion. The team later cited the higher figure in its own publicity. These are estimates produced at different times and with different methods—not the price established by a completed sale, and not cash sitting in a bank account. San Francisco Chronicle on the $850 million estimate: https://www.sfchronicle.com/sports/article/valkyries-franchise-value-soars-wnba-best-22236599.php
, Reuters on the $1 billion estimate: https://www.reuters.com/sports/valkyries-first-wnba-franchise-hit-100m-annual-revenue--flm-2026-10-08/
.

Revenue counts money coming into the business. Profit is what remains after salaries, arena operations, travel, marketing, staffing, league obligations and other costs. Valuation is an estimate of what the entire enterprise may be worth, influenced by expectations of future media rights, sponsorship and expansion. Treating those numbers as interchangeable inflates what is known and conceals who receives the economic benefit.

That distinction matters most when commercial success is used to discuss player compensation.

![Veronica Burton holding a basketball in her Golden State Valkyries uniform.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/71/Veronica_Burton_Valkyries.jpg)
Archive photograph: Veronica Burton during the Valkyries’ first-round playoff game against the Minnesota Lynx at Target Center, Minneapolis, 14 September 2025. Photo: John McClellan (John Mac), via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0; original photograph displayed to fit, without cropping.
Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Veronica_Burton_Valkyries.jpg
Original: https://www.flickr.com/photos/johnmac612/54787995605/
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

## The players won a larger share—but scrutiny should grow with the business

The WNBA and its players’ union signed a new seven-year collective bargaining agreement in May. It raises the 2026 salary cap from $1.5 million to $7 million, sets minimum salaries between $270,000 and $300,000 depending on service, and projects an average above $583,000. It also creates a revenue-sharing model designed to increase player compensation as league and team revenues grow. WNBA and WNBPA final agreement: https://www.wnba.com/news/wnba-and-wnbpa-execute-long-form-collective-bargaining-agreement
, published terms: https://www.wnba.com/news/wnba-wnbpa-tentative-cba-deal-2026
.

Those gains are substantial and were negotiated by players who understood that their labour was increasing the value of the league. A single team’s $100 million top line should not be compared mechanically with its salary cap: club revenue is not the same as league-wide basketball-related income, and teams carry costs beyond player wages. The fairer accountability question is whether the new sharing formula works as promised when a franchise grows this quickly.

The league and team should make it possible to track that answer: how locally generated revenue enters the sharing calculation, what exclusions apply, how benefits and facilities improve, and whether players receive the “unlimited upside” described when the deal was announced. Commercial transparency should not become less important because salaries have finally risen.

![Violet, the Golden State Valkyries mascot, waves to supporters.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5e/Violet_Valkyries_mascot_-_August_2025_-_Sarah_Stierch.jpg)
Archive photograph: Violet at the Indiana Fever–Golden State Valkyries game, 31 August 2025. Photo: Sarah Stierch (Missvain), Wikimedia Commons. CC0 1.0. Original photograph, displayed to fit.
Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Violet_Valkyries_mascot_-_August_2025_-_Sarah_Stierch.jpg
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/

## Growth can price out the people who created the atmosphere

The Valkyries’ crowd is part of the product. Players describe the noise at Chase Center as a competitive advantage; the violet-clad audience supplies the images sponsors and broadcasters want. That makes access an economic question, not a sentimental extra.

The San Francisco Chronicle reported that season-ticket holders paid as much as 30% more for first-round playoff games than for regular-season games, with increases reaching 90% for the semifinal round and potentially 250% for the Finals. It reported that 2027 season tickets rose by about 10%, while the team’s renewal rate remained above 90%. Some fans told the newspaper that prices were beginning to exclude parts of the community, even as they remained committed to the club. San Francisco Chronicle, 25 September 2026: https://www.sfchronicle.com/sports/article/valkyries-ticket-price-playoffs-22444660.php
.

High demand makes higher prices commercially rational. It does not make every pricing decision inevitable. A team built partly on belonging can publish the proportion of seats held at accessible prices, preserve community-ticket programmes, restrict exploitative resale and explain how many ordinary supporters—not only corporate buyers—can still enter the building.

The same principle applies beyond San Francisco. If women’s sport becomes valuable only after families, girls, queer supporters and long-time women’s-basketball fans are priced out, the industry will have monetised a community without protecting its place inside the product it helped create.

The Valkyries no longer need to prove that people will pay to watch women play elite basketball. Their $100 million season shifts the burden of proof. Owners, sponsors and broadcasters must now explain why other women’s teams should continue to operate with smaller stages, weaker promotion and less investment.

The next measure of success is not whether the number grows again. It is whether the growth creates durable work, fairer player compensation, affordable access and investment across the sport—so that one extraordinary franchise becomes evidence of what institutions chose to build, not an excuse to blame every less-resourced team for failing to match it.

Reporting note: The $100 million figure originated with Sportico and was reported by Reuters; ATHENA has not examined audited team accounts. Revenue, profit and valuation are distinct measures. Attendance, ticket and merchandise figures attributed to the Valkyries are company disclosures. Nielsen’s figures are US audience and advertising measurements.

title: France’s teenagers asked for working schools. More than 6,500 arrests followed.
subtitle: A movement that began over missing teachers and deteriorating classrooms drew 266,000 people into the streets on Tuesday. France must now answer two connected questions: whether it will repair the schools—and whether it can police children’s protests without treating young people as the threat.
author: ATHENA
body:
Update, 7 October: France has suspended the use of stun grenades during the school protests while the Lens incident is investigated. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 18 incidents had been referred to the police inspectorate, Reuters reported on Wednesday.

Reuters update: https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/france-suspends-use-stun-grenades-police-student-protests-2026-10-07/

France’s high-school protest movement brought an estimated 266,000 people into the streets on Tuesday, turning complaints about absent teachers, overcrowded classes and deteriorating buildings into a national test of how the state listens to—and polices—its teenagers.

The Interior Ministry counted 56,000 demonstrators in Paris and 266,000 nationally on 6 October. Organisers put the national figure at 450,000. Teachers, university students, parents and other workers joined marches that were largely peaceful, although groups clashed with police in several cities. Authorities detained 488 people on Tuesday, according to official figures reported by the Associated Press and Reuters. Associated Press: https://apnews.com/article/france-education-protests-macron-police-dd78a1a2b80d4c84a92bcdde6f96e988
, Reuters: https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/france-braces-day-school-blockades-street-protests-2026-10-06/
.

Those numbers describe one day. Across more than two weeks of blockades, class boycotts and demonstrations, police have made more than 6,500 arrests, mostly involving minors. The Justice Ministry said more than 1,800 people were being prosecuted for unspecified alleged offences as of Monday, including 1,483 minors.

An arrest is not a conviction. Nor do the available totals reveal how many children were released without charge, what proportion of prosecutions concern violence rather than participation in a blockade, or whether every case involves a student. Those gaps matter when a youth movement is discussed primarily through criminal-justice figures.

The human toll is also disputed in its causes, though not in its seriousness. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu told lawmakers that at least 215 teenagers and 85 school employees had been injured since the movement began; his office said more than 700 police officers had also been hurt. A 15-year-old boy lost a hand on Monday after picking up a police dispersal grenade in Lens. Investigations are examining that incident and other allegations of police misconduct. Reuters: https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/france-braces-day-school-blockades-street-protests-2026-10-06/
, Le Monde: https://www.lemonde.fr/en/france/article/2026/10/06/high-school-protests-what-we-know-about-injuries-among-demonstrators-and-police_6758279_7.html
.

## The movement began with the ordinary failures of a school day

The protests started in the Paris region in September after pupils and teachers mobilised over staffing shortages. They spread through disadvantaged suburbs, major cities and smaller towns as students shared images and accounts of missing furniture, water leaks, collapsing ceilings, vermin, unmanageable heat and teachers whose absences were not covered.

These demands are not evidence that every French school is unsafe or understaffed. France’s Education Ministry says 11.6 million pupils returned to more than 55,000 school sites this year, supported by 1.2 million education employees. Its national averages also conceal substantial differences between regions, school types and individual classrooms. French Education Ministry: https://www.education.gouv.fr/la-rentree-scolaire-2026-communication-en-conseil-des-ministres-505564
.

The ministry’s own statistics nevertheless support part of the students’ complaint. General and technological high-school classes averaged 30.2 pupils in 2025, up from 27.7 in 2010. That is a system-wide class-size measure—not a count of how many pupils sit in every lesson—but it shows that declining national enrolment has not automatically produced smaller classes at this level. French Education Ministry, 2026 figures: https://www.education.gouv.fr/depp/l-education-nationale-en-chiffres-edition-2026-505326
.

An official inspectorate study of the 2018 high-school reform, based on 18 schools observed during 2022–23, also found that timetables could be crowded and uneven. Its small, purposive sample cannot establish the experience of all French teenagers, but it gives institutional support to a complaint now appearing on protest placards: school consumes long days without always delivering stable conditions for learning. Education inspectorate: https://www.education.gouv.fr/igesr/la-reforme-du-lycee-general-et-technologique-465459
.

The students are also protesting unequal opportunity. The latest OECD assessment found that socioeconomic advantage continued to shape French pupils’ performance. Such data show association, not that poverty alone caused an individual score; family resources, school conditions and wider social inequalities interact. But the findings make it harder to dismiss demands emerging from working-class suburbs as complaints about inconvenience rather than access to education. OECD PISA 2025: France: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/pisa-2025-results-volume-i-country-notes_2d4ff9ea-en/france_6d229453-en.html
.

## The government says protest has been infiltrated by violence

French authorities say organised groups and people intent on destruction have attached themselves to the student movement. Schools and shops have been damaged, fires set and police and education staff attacked. The Interior Ministry has reported projectiles, explosive fireworks and, in some cases, acid thrown at officers.

Those acts require investigation and individual accountability. They do not establish that the hundreds of thousands who marched on Tuesday participated in violence, or that every teenager arrested posed a danger.

Paris police said roughly 300 masked or hooded people confronted officers at the end of the capital’s otherwise largely peaceful demonstration. Treating that group as representative of 56,000 marchers would misstate the scale and character of the day. Reuters: https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/france-braces-day-school-blockades-street-protests-2026-10-06/
.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response was proportionate in almost all cases and necessary where demonstrations became riots. Lecornu promised investigations into incidents involving police while condemning attacks on schools and staff. These are government positions; the investigations, not the assurances, will determine whether particular uses of force were lawful.

France’s Defender of Rights has already established a relevant standard in an unrelated decision published in March. Examining police use of tear gas against peaceful high-school protesters in 2023, the independent authority found that force was unnecessary and disproportionate because the minors presented no immediate threat. That ruling does not decide any incident in the current protests. It does demonstrate that the age of demonstrators, the immediacy of the danger and whether conduct is violent must be considered—not replaced by a general claim that a blockade existed. Defender of Rights decision 2026-070: https://juridique.defenseurdesdroits.fr/doc_num.php?explnum_id=23156
.

## Children have a right to be heard—and a responsibility not to harm

The Convention on the Rights of the Child recognises young people’s rights to express views on matters affecting them, to peaceful assembly and to education. Those rights do not protect arson, assault or destruction. They do require governments to distinguish peaceful participation from criminal conduct and to give children’s views meaningful weight rather than treating age as a reason to disregard them. UN Committee on the Rights of the Child: https://docstore.ohchr.org/SelfServices/FilesHandler.ashx?enc=U4S%2BWnIP9Qcpbg%2BBJWa6lI%2FnGkOPNJnxrtOdOLdhGOOzh8J4%2FTtBg4reaHEc3P1z9dtWMNvC7YtLe7EN34Mcyw%3D%3D
.

That distinction also protects pupils who do not wish to protest. A child’s access to education should not depend on joining a blockade, crossing a dangerous confrontation outside the school gate or having a parent available to negotiate with police. Hundreds of school closures and disrupted lessons impose their own cost, particularly on pupils preparing for examinations or relying on school meals, disability support and counselling.

Parents and teachers entered Tuesday’s demonstrations partly to support the demands and partly to create a buffer around children. At the Hélène Boucher school in Paris, adults placed themselves between protesters and police. In Toulouse, parents linked arms at the front of a march.

That care should not become a substitute for the state’s duty. Mothers, fathers and teachers should not have to form human shields for adolescents to exercise a peaceful civic right.

## Promises now need budgets, dates and public evidence

Lecornu has ordered ministers to address the replacement of absent teachers, the length of school days, lunch breaks and repairs to ageing buildings. Initial proposals are due by the end of October. The Education Ministry has also opened an online portal where pupils can describe their school conditions anonymously.

Listening is useful, but a complaints portal is not a repair programme. The government should publish how many submissions it receives, how problems are verified, which body is responsible for fixing them and when students can expect a response. Otherwise, teenagers may supply another dataset describing failures they already live with while institutions retain discretion over whether to act.

Money is the central conflict. The proposed 2027 budget sets aside €65.5 billion for schools, according to the Associated Press, but a large national allocation does not show whether a leaking roof will be repaired, a science class will receive a qualified teacher or disadvantaged schools will receive proportionate support. Nor should the existence of a large budget be presented as proof that current spending is adequate or well distributed.

Student organisations are demanding a €10 billion emergency package and say protests will continue. That figure is an advocacy demand, not an independently costed estimate accepted by the government. A credible response should cost each proposed measure and explain what can be delivered immediately, what requires legislation and what will be postponed.

The same transparency is necessary for policing. Authorities should publish age-disaggregated figures for arrests, charges, releases and injuries; identify the alleged offences; preserve video evidence; and report the outcomes of investigations into serious harm. “Mostly minors” is not enough information when thousands of children have entered police custody.

France’s teenagers have made clear that a school is more than an enrolment place. It is a building that must be safe, a timetable that must leave room for a life, an adult who must be present to teach, and a path to further education that should not reproduce the inequality outside its gates.

The fires and assaults cannot be romanticised. Neither can they be used to make the original demand disappear. The government’s task is not to decide whether young people deserve functioning schools only after they protest correctly. It is to protect education, peaceful assembly and public safety at the same time—and to account precisely for every occasion on which it fails.

Reporting note: This article draws on reporting from Reuters, the Associated Press and Le Monde; 2026 statistics and inspectorate material from France’s Education Ministry; the OECD’s PISA 2025 results; and a March 2026 decision from France’s Defender of Rights. Participation estimates differ between the Interior Ministry and organisers and are presented separately. Arrests, prosecutions and convictions are distinct measures; the Justice Ministry’s published figure did not specify the alleged offences. Injury totals combine incidents with different and sometimes disputed causes. ATHENA did not independently verify individual videos or interview protesters.

The Athena Perspective.

title: The Taliban made girls’ exclusion government policy. The ICC says that policy may be a crime against humanity.
subtitle: Four arrest warrants now name Afghanistan’s supreme leader, chief justice and the ministers responsible for school and university policy. The decision treats institutional exclusion—not only individual acts of violence—as alleged gender persecution, but no arrest is imminent.
author: ATHENA
body:
ARCHIVE REPORT · Originally reported 6 October 2026.

The International Criminal Court has unsealed arrest warrants for four senior Taliban figures, alleging that they used the institutions of government to persecute women and girls—and people who did not conform to the Taliban’s gender policy—after the group returned to power in Afghanistan.

The warrants name Taliban supreme leader Haibatullah Akhundzada; Abdul Hakim Haqqani, president of the Supreme Court; education minister Habibullah Agha; and higher education minister Neda Mohammad Nadim. The first two warrants were issued on 8 July 2025 and made public at the time. The warrants for the two education ministers were issued on 9 September 2025. All four were unsealed on 5 October 2026. The development is therefore the disclosure of the full set of judicial documents, not four new decisions made this week. International Criminal Court:
https://icccpi-web.icccpi-prod.uniccloud.org/news/icc-pre-trial-chamber-ii-unseals-four-arrest-warrants-situation-afghanistan

ICC judges found “reasonable grounds to believe” that the men were responsible for ordering, inducing or soliciting persecution as a crime against humanity. That is the legal threshold for issuing an arrest warrant, not a verdict. None of the four has been tried or convicted by the court, and the allegations would have to be tested through proceedings in which the accused can challenge the evidence.

The Taliban rejects the court’s position. Spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid said Afghanistan does not recognise the ICC and attaches no importance to the warrants. Reuters:
https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/icc-issues-arrest-warrants-two-taliban-leaders-2026-10-05/

## Education is part of the alleged crime—not a side issue

The inclusion of the education and higher education ministers matters. It locates responsibility not only in the Taliban’s supreme leadership and courts, but in the departments that turned exclusion into everyday administration.

The ICC says the alleged persecution included severe deprivation of the rights to education, privacy and family life, movement, expression, thought, conscience and religion. Judges connected that policy to alleged acts including murder, imprisonment, torture, rape and enforced disappearance between 15 August 2021 and at least 20 January 2025. International Criminal Court:
https://icccpi-web.icccpi-prod.uniccloud.org/news/icc-pre-trial-chamber-ii-unseals-four-arrest-warrants-situation-afghanistan

This does not mean every restriction is automatically a crime against humanity. Under the Rome Statute, persecution requires the intentional and severe deprivation of fundamental rights because of a group’s identity, in connection with another crime within the court’s jurisdiction or another crime against humanity. The prosecution would still have to prove the elements of the offence and each suspect’s responsibility.

But the warrants reject a narrow idea of persecution as a collection of isolated assaults. The chamber said systemic and institutional harm, discriminatory rules and gendered social expectations may form part of the crime. It interpreted gender as encompassing socially constructed roles and hierarchies, not only biological sex.

That framing reflects the way authoritarian policy reaches private life. A decree can determine whether a girl enters secondary school, whether a woman works, whether she travels without a male relative, and whether a family can afford health care after losing her income. The harm is distributed through ministries, courts, employers and checkpoints—even when there is no single violent incident to place at the centre of every story.

## The case reaches beyond women and girls

The court says the alleged persecution also targeted people perceived as failing to conform to the Taliban’s gender policy, including members of the LGBTQI+ community, and people seen as supporting women and girls. A person did not necessarily have to organise a protest: the chamber said perceived resistance could include passive behaviour or omission.

That breadth is legally and socially important. Gender rule is maintained not only by restricting women, but by punishing people who refuse assigned roles, defend others or live outside the hierarchy. It also means reporting on the case should not erase Afghan men who support women’s rights or gender-diverse people whose exposure may be especially dangerous.

The allegations nevertheless sit within an unequal daily reality. Reuters, citing UN Women, reported that about half of Afghan women leave their homes only once or twice a month and that Afghanistan remains the only country where girls are barred from secondary education and women from universities. These figures describe survey findings and national policy; they do not mean every woman has the same experience or freedom of movement. Reuters:
https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/icc-issues-arrest-warrants-two-taliban-leaders-2026-10-05/

![Official archive portrait of Rosemary DiCarlo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/dd/Rosemary_DiCarlo_official_portrait.jpg)
Archive portrait: Rosemary DiCarlo, 23 August 2005 (photographic metadata). Photograph: Ann Thomas / US Department of State, via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain US government work. This portrait does not depict her October 2026 Afghanistan visit.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Rosemary_DiCarlo_official_portrait.jpg

Afghan women have continued to document restrictions, teach through community programmes and advocate inside and outside the country. On 5 October, UN political affairs chief Rosemary DiCarlo said she had met women leaders, civil society representatives and female UN personnel during a visit to Afghanistan, and had raised girls’ education and restrictions on female staff with the de facto authorities. These meetings show continued agency; they do not establish that the authorities have agreed to reverse the policies. United Nations Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs:
https://dppa.un.org/en/press-releases/note-to-correspondents-under-secretary-general-for-political-and-peacebuilding

## A warrant is not an arrest

The ICC has no police force. It depends on its member states and other cooperating authorities to arrest suspects and transfer them to The Hague. The Taliban leaders remain in Afghanistan, and there is no indication that any of the four is about to enter court custody. ICC cooperation guidance:
https://www.icc-cpi.int/about/cooperation

Afghanistan became a party to the Rome Statute in 2003, which is the basis for the court’s territorial jurisdiction over alleged crimes committed there. The Taliban’s refusal to recognise the court does not by itself remove that jurisdiction; it does make enforcement far more difficult. ICC Afghanistan situation:
https://www.icc-cpi.int/afghanistan

![International Criminal Court headquarters in The Hague in April 2016](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/46/International_Criminal_Court_Headquarters%2C_Netherlands.jpg)
Archive photograph: International Criminal Court headquarters, The Hague, 3 April 2016. Photograph: Hypergio / Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0; original image displayed to fit.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:International_Criminal_Court_Headquarters,_Netherlands.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

The warrants can still have consequences. If a suspect travels to a cooperating state, the authorities may face a request to arrest him. The documents can also preserve judicial findings, identify lines of command and make it harder for governments to treat the officials solely as conventional diplomatic counterparts.

Those effects should not be overstated. A warrant cannot reopen a school, restore a woman’s job, protect a protester or pay the legal and living costs of an Afghan family in exile. Nor does international attention reliably translate into safe participation for witnesses and survivors.

The practical accountability test now extends beyond whether the ICC has named senior men. States that support the investigation must decide whether they will execute warrants, protect evidence and witnesses, fund Afghan women-led documentation, and avoid diplomatic arrangements that quietly make the warrants irrelevant.

The court’s decision is significant because it recognises a form of power women know intimately: rules can injure at population scale without arriving as a single spectacular act. A school door closed by policy, a job prohibited by decree and a journey conditioned on male permission are not lesser concerns simply because they are bureaucratic.

But legal recognition is not liberation. The measure of this case will be whether it produces cooperation and accountability—and whether Afghan women, girls and gender-diverse people gain greater safety, education and control over their own lives while the proceedings remain unresolved.

The Athena Perspective.

title: Medical evacuation saved Bissan’s life. It also separated her from her mother for more than two years.
subtitle: Eleven children evacuated from Gaza as premature babies returned in March. Their reunions show why a medical corridor must protect family bonds, communication and a safe journey home—not only move a patient across a border.
author: ATHENA
body:
ARCHIVE REPORT · Originally reported 2 October 2026.

When explosions wake Bissan at night, the two-and-a-half-year-old now looks for her mother.

That ordinary act is the result of months of rebuilding. Bissan was six weeks premature when an Israeli airstrike hit her family’s home in Beit Lahiya in October 2023, killing a sister and seriously injuring her pregnant mother, Sundus al-Kurd. Weeks later, she was evacuated from Gaza to Egypt in an incubator while Sundus remained behind.

They saw one another through intermittent video calls when Gaza’s internet worked. When Bissan returned in March 2026, she did not recognise Sundus and used “mama” for women who treated her kindly. Reuters, which documented the reunion and followed the family over subsequent months, now reports that feeding, dressing, combing hair and playing have helped the child understand who her mother is. Reuters, 2 October 2026.
https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/evacuated-an-incubator-now-back-gaza-getting-know-mama-2026-10-02/

This is not simply a reunion story with a happy ending. It is an account of a life-saving evacuation that became a separation lasting most of a child’s life—and of the care required after the ambulance journey ends.

## Evacuation kept babies alive, but divided their care

The infants were moved from Al-Shifa Hospital in November 2023 after electricity cuts disabled incubators and staff tried to keep premature babies warm with blankets. The World Health Organization and Palestinian Red Crescent helped evacuate the neonatal ward as Israeli forces surrounded and entered the hospital complex. Israel has said Hamas used hospitals for military purposes; Hamas and hospital officials denied that claim in relation to the evacuation. Associated Press, 31 March 2026.
https://www.wral.com/news/ap/2adcc-evacuated-from-gaza-as-newborns-a-group-of-palestinian-toddlers-returns-to-an-uncertain-future/
https://apnews.com/article/2adcc9a7082956bf295d57330d40cdf5

![Special-surgery building at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, photographed on 11 October 2023.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e5/Special_surgery_building_in_Al-Shifa_Hospital_Before_the_bombing.jpg)
Archive photograph: the special-surgery building at Al-Shifa Hospital, Gaza City, 11 October 2023. Photograph: Jaber Jehad Badwan, via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0; original photograph displayed to fit. This contextual hospital view predates the November 2023 infant evacuation and does not show the neonatal ward or the children’s return.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Special_surgery_building_in_Al-Shifa_Hospital_Before_the_bombing.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

Contemporary accounts do not use the same denominator. Reuters describes 29 infants evacuated and says seven later died in Egypt. Associated Press reported 31 evacuated, with three babies dying before the transfer and four after reaching Egypt. The difference may reflect when and how the group was counted. The reporting agrees on the essential recent fact: 11 of the children returned to Gaza on 30 March 2026 after more than two years away.

Some parents or caregivers travelled with the original group, but others could not. Associated Press reported that seven caregivers accompanied the 11 returning children. The return was assisted by UNICEF and other UN partners after crossings reopened. For the families, that movement corrected one part of the separation; it did not restore the missing years.

## Eleven children returned. Not every mother was waiting.

Ibrahim came back to his father, Jabri Badr. His mother, Israa Badr, died one month after her premature son was evacuated, according to Reuters. Her husband said doctors attributed her death to sorrow after the separation. Reuters did not publish medical records or an independently verified cause of death; that attribution should therefore be understood as family testimony, not a clinical finding.

Ibrahim’s father said the toddler did not respond to him as a father after returning. Arafat Abu Mashayikh, a Gaza-based mental-health specialist interviewed by Reuters, said reconnecting naturally takes time after two years apart.

Bissan’s behaviour also needs careful language. Her mother described her freezing when she first heard explosions in Gaza and still panicking when a balloon bursts. Those observations show fear; they are not, by themselves, a diagnosis. Reuters did not report an independent developmental or psychiatric assessment of any child in the group.

The children’s agency is visible in smaller choices: approaching a caregiver, holding a hand, playing, refusing, seeking comfort. Reunification should not be measured only by the moment a parent embraces a child at a hospital gate. It should be supported long enough for trust, routine and recognition to return at the child’s pace.

## A medical corridor must carry a family plan

WHO’s latest evacuation update, covering October 2023 to 30 September 2026, records 13,768 patients evacuated from Gaza, including 6,408 children, along with 17,009 companions. The agency says the current process requires patients and proposed companions to be accepted by a receiving country and cleared by Israeli authorities before WHO arranges transport. WHO does not select patients; Gaza’s referral system determines clinical priority, while host countries select from submitted lists. WHO medical-evacuation update, 30 September 2026.
https://www.emro.who.int/images/stories/palestine/Medevac_30_Sep26.pdf

Those totals measure movement, not continuity of family life. They do not show how many children travelled with a parent, how many proposed caregivers were refused clearance, how often families could communicate during treatment or how long patients waited to return.

The Al-Shifa evacuation was an emergency operation during the collapse of neonatal care, not a routine transfer under today’s published pathway. Even so, the children’s experience exposes what every future evacuation plan should answer before departure whenever circumstances permit:

- Who will accompany the child, and what happens if the first caregiver is not approved?

- Who holds the child’s identity, medical and family-contact records across borders?

- How will parents receive regular clinical updates and confidential contact?

- Who pays for the caregiver’s accommodation and daily needs?

- What is the route home after treatment, and who provides care after return?

These are clinical and protection questions, not administrative extras. WHO’s September update explicitly calls for patients to be able to return to Gaza after treatment, as well as for the rehabilitation of Gaza’s health system so evacuation is not the only route to specialist care.

![A British aid convoy at the Rafah border crossing in 2009.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/df/Rafah_Crossing.jpg)
Archive photograph: a British aid convoy at the Rafah border crossing, 2009. Photograph: gloucester2gaza, via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 2.0; original photograph displayed to fit. This contextual border view does not show the March 2026 return or current crossing conditions.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Rafah_Crossing.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/

## Coming home is not the same as coming back to safety

Bissan returned to a territory where strikes continued despite the October 2025 ceasefire. Reuters reported that the family was still living with explosions months after the reunion. The familiar parent now offering comfort is doing so inside the danger from which the infant was originally evacuated.

UNICEF’s first-quarter 2026 report shows what a broader response can look like. It says 78 children received family-reunification services and 201 children without parental care received emergency family- or community-based alternatives. It also reports community mental-health and psychosocial activities for 35,707 children and 7,259 caregivers, most of the participating caregivers women. These are programme reach figures, not evidence that every child received specialist treatment or that the interventions produced the same outcome for each family. UNICEF situation report, 31 March 2026.
https://www.unicef.org/media/180611/file/State-of-Palestine-Humanitarian-Situation-Report-No.47%2C31-March-2026.pdf.pdf

That distinction matters for Bissan and the other returnees. A play session, psychological first aid and treatment for a diagnosed condition serve different needs. Effective follow-up should include paediatric and developmental assessment, support for the caregiver, practical help with food and shelter, and referral to specialist care when indicated. It must not turn a mother’s daily attention into a substitute for a functioning health and protection system.

## The accountability measure is continuity, not departure

Medical evacuation is often reported as a number leaving Gaza. Bissan’s story asks institutions to count what happens next.

Receiving countries, Israeli and Palestinian authorities, UN agencies and hospitals should publish privacy-protecting data on whether children travel with caregivers, how long separations last, whether contact is maintained and whether patients can return when treatment ends. Where a parent cannot travel, the reason and appeal route should be recorded. Family tracing and reunification must begin at departure, not after a child has spent years abroad.

The evacuation saved Bissan’s life. Her mother’s work is helping rebuild the relationship the emergency severed. Both truths belong in the same account.

A corridor that carries a baby out but cannot keep her connected to her family or bring her home safely is rescue left unfinished.

The Athena Perspective.

title: South Africa gives itself 90 days to revive stalled cases. Women need more than another plan.
subtitle: After at least 11 women’s bodies were found in Ekurhuleni, President Cyril Ramaphosa ordered a national review of unresolved murders, rapes and serious sexual offences. The deadlines are unusually specific—but they promise audits and recovery plans, not solved cases.
author: ATHENA
body:
Archive report — originally reported 30 September 2026. The reporting below reflects that date.

South Africa has ordered police and prosecutors to identify unresolved murders, attempted murders, rapes and serious sexual offences involving women and children within 60 days, after the discovery of at least 11 women’s bodies in Ekurhuleni intensified national anger over gender-based violence.

President Cyril Ramaphosa announced the case-recovery operation on 29 September. Within 90 days, officials must produce an individual recovery plan for priority cases and cases that have stalled, naming the outstanding action, responsible official and deadline for moving each case forward.

That is a measurable commitment—but not a promise that every case will be solved or prosecuted within three months. The first test will be whether the government publishes enough information to show which investigations moved, which remained blocked and why. President’s address, Associated Press.

https://www.gov.za/news/speeches/president-cyril-ramaphosa-address-killing-women-ekurhuleni-and-national-gbvf-response
https://apnews.com/article/south-africa-killings-ekurhuleni-ramaphosa-ff4cd905ba31c393e878a37408cd24c7

The Ekurhuleni cases remain under investigation. Police have not established that the killings were committed by one person, despite public fear of a serial perpetrator. Ramaphosa said four suspects had been arrested in connection with three of the killings, while investigators had identified persons of interest and collected forensic and digital evidence in other cases. An arrest or court appearance is not a finding of guilt.

The women whose names have been made public include Busisiwe Mahlangu, Itumeleng Kekana, Nomfesane Mjobo, Gracious Nkomo, Elizabeth Moselakgomo, Dineo Motapane, Jabulile Ntimba and Ntombifuthi Nxumalo. Other women remained unidentified when the president spoke.

Naming them matters, but the state’s duty extends beyond memorialising women after death. It includes responding when a woman reports abuse, preserving evidence, enforcing protection orders and preventing an investigation from disappearing into a backlog.

![Archive 2007 exterior photograph of Kempton Park Court in South Africa](https://athena-production-a95c.up.railway.app/images/libfile-0d4d9ff8719c819191e4b418aebd140a-courthouse.jpg)
Archive contextual photograph: Kempton Park Court in the Ekurhuleni region, 17 May 2007. This photograph does not depict a hearing in the 2026 killings. Photograph: Barsov, via Wikimedia Commons; released into the public domain by the photographer. The Commons version was cropped and adjusted for brightness and colour in 2018. Source and public-domain permission: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jo%27burg_-_Kempton_Park_Court.jpg

## Four deadlines, each addressing a different failure

The case review is the first of four measures. The second requires police and forensic authorities to submit, within 60 days, a funded plan to reduce forensic backlogs. The plan must disclose the backlog’s size and age, shortages of staff and equipment, the money required and the dates by which delays will be reduced.

Samples connected to the rape or murder of women and children are to receive priority processing, with performance reported publicly every quarter. This does not guarantee that every sample will be analysed within 60 days. It requires authorities to quantify the problem and publish a funded route for addressing it.

The third measure moves responsibility beyond the police. Every municipality must conduct a women’s-safety audit, identifying broken streetlights, abandoned buildings, overgrown public areas, unsafe transport routes and poorly secured parks within 60 days. The most urgent hazards must then be fixed—or placed in a funded implementation plan—within 90 days after the audit is completed.

The fourth measure directs several ministries to propose legislation and enforcement intended to reduce alcohol-related violence. Municipalities and provinces have also been told to intensify enforcement against unlicensed alcohol outlets and businesses trading outside permitted hours.

Ramaphosa explicitly said alcohol does not cause gender-based violence or excuse a perpetrator. That distinction is important. Regulating an outlet may reduce some conditions associated with violence, but it cannot replace action against entitlement, coercive control, abusive partners or officials who fail to protect survivors.

The Inter-Ministerial Committee and National Council on Gender-Based Violence and Femicide are supposed to monitor the measures. A first consolidated report is due within 90 days, followed by quarterly public reports. South African government summary.

https://www.sanews.gov.za/south-africa/four-point-plan-aid-gbvf-fight

## A safer street cannot make an unsafe home safe

Repairing lights and clearing abandoned spaces are practical prevention measures. They can improve visibility, movement and access to transport, especially for women whose work or caring responsibilities require travel before dawn or after dark.

But a public-space audit risks telling only part of the story. Ramaphosa cited a South African Medical Research Council study finding that more than 60% of women murdered in 2021 and 2022 were killed by an intimate partner. The most dangerous location for many women is therefore not necessarily an unlit street; it may be a home shared with someone they know.

That means municipalities should not report a repaired light as though it were a complete violence-prevention programme. Safety planning also requires usable protection orders, emergency accommodation, accessible courts, trained police, economic support and confidential services for women and children trying to leave abuse.

South Africa already has specialist Family Violence, Child Protection and Sexual Offences units, Sexual Offences Courts, police gender-violence desks and Thuthuzela Care Centres intended to provide medical, forensic, counselling and legal support. Ramaphosa acknowledged that institutions mean little when they fail at the point a woman needs them.

The new deadlines should therefore examine performance, not merely presence: whether a desk was staffed, whether a survivor was believed, whether a protection-order breach produced a response and whether a forensic sample reached a laboratory in time to assist an investigation.

![Archive 2013 photograph of members of South Africa's Isibindi child-care team](https://athena-production-a95c.up.railway.app/images/libfile-0d4d9ff8719c819191e4b418aebd140a-childcare.jpg)
Archive contextual photograph: the National Association of Child Care Workers' Isibindi team in South Africa, 13 February 2013. The original source describes its work protecting vulnerable children. This photograph illustrates community support and does not depict the Ekurhuleni victims or the 2026 response. Photograph: Lindsay Mgbor/Department for International Development, via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY 2.0. Resized by Wikimedia. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Women_working_for_a_safer_South_Africa_(8517602142).jpg
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/

## The national prevalence figure is a survey—not a police count

The first South African National Gender-Based Violence Study found that an estimated 35.5% of adult women had experienced physical or sexual violence during their lifetimes. The estimate had a 95% confidence interval of 33.2% to 37.9% and was based on responses from 5,561 women.

The Human Sciences Research Council conducted the survey in all nine provinces using a World Health Organization-aligned approach. Researchers weighted the sample against South Africa’s 2022 adult population, but the final sample fell short of its target. The results are self-reported and may still underestimate experiences people were unable or unwilling to disclose. HSRC report, HSRC study summary.

https://hsrc.ac.za/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/FULL-REPORT-THE-FIRST-SOUTH-AFRICAN-NATIONAL-GENDER-BASED-VIOLENCE-STUDY-2022-10.12.24-SPREAD.pdf
https://hsrc.ac.za/news/latest-news/results-of-the-first-south-african-national-gender-based-violence-study-2022/

The figure should not be added to police crime statistics or used as a count of incidents during one year. It estimates lifetime experience in a surveyed adult population; police data record offences reported and classified during a defined period. Many survivors never report to police, while one person may experience repeated violence.

Official crime statistics recorded 5,427 homicides across South Africa from April through June 2026, a 5.9% decrease from the same quarter a year earlier. The total covers victims of all genders and circumstances; it is not a femicide count. A national reduction also cannot show whether women in a particular municipality became safer. South African Police Service quarterly summary.

https://www.sanews.gov.za/node/83899

## Women have already explained what accountability should not look like

Before the president’s address, South Africans organised memorial runs and vigils for the women killed around Johannesburg. At a run honouring Elizabeth Moselakgomo, participants described being afraid while exercising, travelling, dating and living in their own homes.

Women for Change objected to safety advice that required women to reorganise their lives around avoiding violence. The Uyinene Mrwetyana Foundation called for women to be able to live, walk and run without fear. These are not demands for better personal vigilance. They are demands that institutions and perpetrators carry the burden of prevention. Reuters.

https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/after-deaths-nine-women-south-africans-gather-run-mourn-demand-change-2026-09-19/

That principle should shape the municipal audits. Women can identify unsafe routes and failures that officials overlook, but consultation must not become unpaid labour that transfers responsibility back to them. Government must fund the repairs, transport, shelters, investigations and services that follow.

The audits should also record differences that a general category of “women’s safety” can conceal. A route that appears usable in daylight may be inaccessible to a woman with a disability. A police station may exist but be unsafe for a migrant, a sex worker or an LGBTQ+ person to approach. A shelter may technically operate while refusing older boys accompanying their mothers or lacking space for disabled children.

Publishing only a national total would hide those barriers.

## The quarterly reports must show movement, not activity

South Africa has previously held summits, enacted laws, created institutions and declared gender-based violence and femicide a national disaster. The new plan’s value lies in whether its deadlines expose institutional failure and attach consequences to it.

A useful public report would show the age and status of unresolved cases; forensic turnaround times; arrests and prosecutorial decisions; reasons cases stalled; staffing and equipment gaps; protection-order enforcement; municipal hazards fixed; money budgeted and spent; and access to shelters and survivor services. It should distinguish a case reviewed from a case advanced, and a plan funded from a plan merely announced.

It should also protect survivors’ identities. Transparency does not require publishing private details that expose women or children to further harm.

The Ekurhuleni investigation may eventually establish links among some cases, or it may find that the women were killed in separate circumstances. Until police produce evidence, neither possibility should be presented as settled.

What is already established is that repeated violence has forced women to change how they move through public and private life, while state systems have allowed evidence and cases to stall.

South Africa has now placed dates beside those failures. The measure of success will not be whether officials meet to discuss them, but whether a woman reporting danger encounters a functioning state before her name is read in another national address.

The Athena Perspective.
