title: Two women are steering an $8.2 billion bet on AI that can see the world
subtitle: AMD’s agreement to buy Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs would place one of artificial intelligence’s most influential scientists beside chief executive Lisa Su. The leadership matters in a male-dominated industry—but the larger test is whether the company can turn ambitious “world models” into useful, accountable technology.
author: ATHENA
body:
AMD has agreed to acquire World Labs, the artificial-intelligence company led by computer-vision pioneer Fei-Fei Li, in an all-stock transaction valued at approximately $8.2 billion. If regulators approve the deal and it closes as expected by the end of 2026, Li will become AMD’s executive vice-president and chief scientist, reporting directly to chair and chief executive Lisa Su.

The agreement, announced on 28 September, gives AMD a research team developing AI systems intended to generate, reconstruct and simulate three-dimensional environments. It also brings two of the technology industry’s most prominent women into the same leadership structure at a moment when the infrastructure beneath AI—not only the chatbots consumers see—is becoming a central commercial battleground. [1], [2].

That is significant, but it should not be mistaken for evidence that the industry has solved its gender imbalance. LinkedIn data analysed by the World Economic Forum indicate that women hold 25.3% of top-management positions in AI firms, compared with 27.7% in non-AI firms. Women’s visibility at the top can expand ideas about who builds and directs technology; it cannot by itself change who is hired, promoted, funded or affected by the systems those companies sell. [3].

## A chip company is buying a view of AI’s next workload

AMD’s immediate interest is strategic. It competes with Nvidia in the processors and computing systems used to train and run AI. World Labs gives AMD closer access to researchers building a different class of model, allowing the chipmaker to study what future systems may require from hardware, software, memory and data-centre infrastructure.

The relationship did not begin with the acquisition. World Labs says the companies started a technical partnership in 2025, working on model training and inference optimisation using AMD graphics processors. AMD was also among the investors in a $1 billion World Labs funding round announced in February 2026; Nvidia, Autodesk, Emerson Collective, Fidelity Management & Research Company and Sea were also named as investors. [4], [5].

The new transaction is all-stock: AMD would pay with its shares rather than $8.2 billion in cash. The headline valuation does not mean Li personally receives that amount. How the shares will be divided among founders, employees and investors has not been publicly disclosed, nor has AMD stated how many World Labs employees will join it.

World Labs was founded in 2024. Its leap from a newly created research company to an $8.2 billion acquisition target reflects the sums established technology companies are prepared to commit for scarce AI talent and a possible lead in the next computing market. It does not establish that World Labs’ models will generate revenue at the scale implied by the price.

## What a “world model” is—and what has actually been shown

Large language models learn patterns in text and other data to generate responses. World models aim to represent how environments look, change and behave in space and time. In practical terms, that could allow a system to create an explorable 3D scene from images, simulate a factory before equipment is moved, or provide a virtual environment in which a robot can learn without every trial taking place in the physical world.

World Labs’ first commercial product, Marble, generates persistent 3D environments from text, images, video or 360-degree panoramas. Its newer research model, Atlas, can create new camera views from a small number of images, reconstruct scenes and produce simulations for robotics workflows. Those descriptions come from the company itself. [6], [7].

World Labs says Atlas outperformed selected specialist models in camera-controlled generation and 3D reconstruction. It also acknowledges that no single benchmark captures the model’s broad capabilities and that other systems might perform better with more sophisticated prompts. Its published results were produced by the World Labs team, not an independent evaluator, and Atlas is in early access with selected partners.

The distinction matters because generating a visually convincing scene is not the same as accurately modelling physical cause and effect. A model used to plan a film shot can tolerate an invented detail that would be unacceptable in a surgical simulator, a warehouse robot or a system making decisions around children. The closer AI moves from images on a screen to machines acting around people, the more safety depends on knowing when the model is reconstructing evidence and when it is plausibly filling a gap.

![Fei-Fei Li speaking at the AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva in 2017](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c7/Fei-Fei_Li_at_AI_for_Good_2017.jpg)
Computer scientist Fei-Fei Li speaks at the AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva on 8 June 2017. Contextual archive photograph. Photograph: ITU Pictures / Wikimedia Commons. CC BY 2.0.
Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fei-Fei_Li_at_AI_for_Good_2017.jpg
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0

## The woman whose database changed computer vision

Li’s scientific importance predates the current generative-AI boom. Her laboratory’s ImageNet project assembled and labelled millions of images, creating a large dataset that helped researchers demonstrate the power of deep neural networks in visual recognition. She later served as chief scientist for AI and machine learning at Google Cloud and became the founding co-director of Stanford’s Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence.

In her account of the acquisition, Li argues that language alone is insufficient for AI because the world is made of physical objects and relationships, not only words. She says joining AMD will bring research closer to the hardware and provide the scale needed to develop spatial intelligence. Those are her strategic claims; the acquisition itself is not proof that world models have reached reliable physical understanding. [8].

The reporting line is notable. Li will not enter AMD as a ceremonial adviser: the announced role places her in the company’s executive ranks and gives its chief scientist direct access to Su. World Labs says co-founders Justin Johnson and Ben Mildenhall will continue leading its team with Li inside AMD.

This is a real concentration of scientific and corporate authority in women’s hands. The useful question for ATHENA is not whether that symbolism should be celebrated or dismissed. It is what these leaders do with the authority: which problems receive investment, which risks are measured, whose labour and data make the models possible, and who shares in their benefits.

## “Open” will need a definition the public can test

Both companies say the combination will strengthen an “open AI ecosystem” and promise widely accessible models and platforms. The announcement does not define which model weights, code, training data or evaluation methods will be released, under what licences, or on what timetable.

That gap is important. World Labs says Atlas was trained from scratch on a large and diverse collection of multimodal data, but its public technical post does not identify the full sources, licensing status or demographic composition of that corpus. Images and video can contain people, homes, streets, artworks and copyrighted commercial material. Systems designed to reconstruct real places also raise questions about privacy, surveillance and consent that cannot be answered by a general promise of human benefit.

The commercial incentives are equally clear. Better world models may create demand for more AMD processors and systems; access to AMD’s engineering resources may allow World Labs to train larger models. Li’s team says Atlas improves as training compute increases. More scale, however, also means more infrastructure, energy and capital. The companies have not published an acquisition-specific estimate of the computing, electricity or water demands expected from the research programme.

None of those omissions proves misconduct. They identify the evidence still needed to judge claims about openness and public benefit.

## What happens next

The transaction remains subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions. Until it closes, World Labs and AMD remain separate companies, and Li has not yet taken up the announced AMD role.

Regulators and shareholders will examine competition and financial questions. Researchers, workers and the public need a wider set of answers: Will benchmark results be independently reproducible? Will creators and communities be able to discover whether their material trained the models? What safeguards will apply when simulations guide robots in workplaces, schools, clinics or homes? Will AMD report the environmental cost of scaling this branch of AI? And will a deal led by two exceptional women create more routes for other women into technical and decision-making roles?

The acquisition deserves attention because women are directing it. It deserves scrutiny because the technology could shape physical spaces in which women, children and workers live.

Representation changes who is seen holding power. Accountability determines what that power builds.

## Sources

[1] AMD announcement
https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/09/28/3370256/0/en/amd-to-acquire-world-labs-to-advance-the-future-of-ai-compute.html

[2] Reuters
https://www.reuters.com/technology/amd-acquire-fei-fei-lis-world-labs-82-billion-deal-2026-09-28/

[3] World Economic Forum, Global Gender Gap Report 2026
https://www.weforum.org/publications/global-gender-gap-report-2026/in-full/trends-and-pathways-shaping-the-future-of-parity/

[4] World Labs funding announcement
https://www.worldlabs.ai/blog/funding-2026

[5] World Labs acquisition statement
https://www.worldlabs.ai/blog/amd-announcement

[6] World Labs product overview
https://www.worldlabs.ai/

[7] Atlas technical post
https://www.worldlabs.ai/blog/atlas

[8] Li’s 28 September statement
https://drfeifei.substack.com/p/worldlabs-joining-amd

Reporting note: This article draws on AMD’s transaction announcement; World Labs’ funding, product and acquisition statements; Fei-Fei Li’s account; World Economic Forum analysis of LinkedIn data; Reuters reporting; and World Labs’ published Atlas evaluation. World Labs’ performance claims have not been independently tested by ATHENA.

The Athena Perspective.

title: The offices created to defend women’s rights are losing their budgets—and their power
subtitle: A new UN assessment says one in three national gender-equality mechanisms has lost institutional authority in two years. The danger is not only that women disappear from government—but that the offices meant to turn rights into services remain visible while losing the power to act.
author: ATHENA
body:
One in three government bodies established to advance gender equality has lost institutional power during the past two years, according to a new assessment from UN Women and the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs.

Around one in four experienced an operating-budget cut, while nearly one in ten lost control over its own budget. International funding directed towards gender equality fell by 13% between 2023 and 2024, and funding for women’s-rights organisations fell by 28%. The UN says gender-equality financing is now at its lowest level since 2021. [1], [2].

These institutions can be ministries of women or gender, equality commissions, government directorates and other state bodies given responsibility for advancing women’s and girls’ rights. Their work may include reviewing discriminatory laws, coordinating responses to gender-based violence, influencing budgets, collecting sex-disaggregated data and checking whether employment, health and education policies reach women equitably.

An institution can therefore continue to have a minister, office and website while becoming less capable of changing what happens in a police station, hospital, school or national budget. The loss is easy to overlook because it may occur through administrative decisions rather than the public repeal of a right.

## What does “losing power” mean?

The Gender Snapshot was released on 17 September and draws together international datasets covering all 17 Sustainable Development Goals. Its new institutional finding comes from a 2026 survey of national gender-equality mechanisms.

UN Women describes the loss of power as changes affecting an institution’s authority, position, mandate, influence or resources. A ministry may be absorbed into a larger department; a commission’s staff may be reduced; an office may lose direct access to cabinet or finance officials; or its budget may be controlled elsewhere.

These changes are not interchangeable. A smaller budget is measurable, but political access can be harder to quantify. The one-in-three figure is a global survey result—not evidence that every third country has abolished its women’s ministry, and not a ranking of individual governments.

At the report’s launch, UN Women policy director Sarah Hendriks said the analysis was intended to identify systemic trends rather than grade particular countries. That limitation matters. A global proportion cannot establish the reason for every restructuring, nor can it show from the headline alone whether services deteriorated in each country. [3].

It does, however, reveal a pattern that deserves scrutiny: the institutions assigned to correct gender inequality are being weakened while the inequality itself remains deeply embedded.

![Women leaders and policy experts at a United Nations event on digital inclusion in 2017](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/91/Valentine_Rugwabiza_at_left_Digital_Inclusion-_Towards_Equal_access%2C_skills_and_leadership_for_women_and_girls.jpg)
Women leaders and policy experts discuss equal access, skills and leadership at a United Nations Commission on the Status of Women event in New York on 21 March 2017. Contextual archive photograph. Photograph: ITU Pictures / Wikimedia Commons. CC BY 2.0.
Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Valentine_Rugwabiza_at_left_Digital_Inclusion-_Towards_Equal_access,_skills_and_leadership_for_women_and_girls.jpg
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0

## Representation increased in some places. Control did not follow.

The report is not a claim that nothing has improved. Between 2019 and 2024, governments adopted 99 legal reforms removing discriminatory provisions or strengthening gender-equality frameworks. Women’s financial-account ownership in low- and middle-income countries increased from 50% in 2014 to 73% in 2024. Women’s labour-force participation improved in 128 of 186 countries between 2015 and 2026, according to UN DESA. [4].

There are also more women heads of state or government than in 2020: 28 at the start of 2026, compared with 20 six years earlier. Yet six out of seven countries are still led by men, and women’s share of parliamentary seats declined in 54 countries between 2020 and 2026.

Access to office is not the same as access to the decisions with the largest budgets and coercive powers. Women hold roughly 22% of cabinet positions worldwide, down from more than 23% two years earlier. Nearly nine in ten defence ministers and more than eight in ten finance ministers are men. Women occupy only 6% of corporate chief-executive positions and fewer than one fifth of the presidencies of countries’ highest courts. [5], [6].

That distribution matters because an equality office cannot implement national priorities alone. A plan to prevent maternal deaths depends on health financing and transport. Protection from domestic violence depends on police, prosecutors, courts and shelters. Equal pay requires labour enforcement, employer data and remedies that workers can use. Girls’ education can be affected by sanitation, safety, family income and school funding.

If the finance, justice, health and interior ministries do not share responsibility, “women’s issues” can be confined to a comparatively small office without the budget or authority to compel action elsewhere.

## The evidence links women’s power with public outcomes—but does not prove a simple cause

UN Women says countries where women hold more than 20% of parliamentary seats record childhood immunisation rates about 12 percentage points higher, alongside better child-survival outcomes. The report also cites research across 70 countries over four decades finding a statistically significant association between the presence of a national gender-equality mechanism and higher levels of democracy.

These findings support the case for women’s representation and functioning equality institutions. They do not prove that adding women to a parliament automatically vaccinates children or that creating one office causes democracy.

Countries differ in income, healthcare systems, conflict exposure, state capacity and many other conditions. During the launch briefing, a journalist pointed to Mozambique, which has high representation of women in parliament but also high child mortality. UN officials acknowledged that the relationship is correlational and that representation cannot compensate for inadequate public revenue, aid or health investment. [7].

That clarification strengthens rather than weakens the central argument. Women need more than seats; they need institutions, money and authority capable of converting representation into decisions.

## The 171-year warning is a trajectory, not a deadline written in stone

The report says that, at the current pace, full gender equality remains 171 years away—equivalent to the year 2197. Not one target under Sustainable Development Goal 5 is on track to be achieved by 2030.

The date should be read as a projection of present rates across multiple indicators, not a prediction that equality will suddenly arrive in a particular year. Policies can accelerate progress, and conflict, austerity or political backlash can reverse it. The purpose of the estimate is to show how far the current trajectory sits from governments’ 2030 promise.

The report’s institutional findings make the delay less abstract. Governments cannot plausibly promise equality while reducing the authority of the bodies assigned to deliver it. The UN itself is not outside that criticism: 42% of UN entities reported that funding cuts had weakened their gender-equality work. No woman has served as UN secretary-general during the organisation’s 80-year history.

## What women should be able to see in a government budget

A government’s commitment should be judged through more than the name of a ministry or the number of women appointed to ceremonial posts.

The important questions are concrete: Does the equality institution have a legal mandate? Can it review legislation and national budgets before decisions are final? Does it control its own funding? Are its staff and regional offices increasing or shrinking? Can it require other ministries to publish sex-disaggregated data? Are grants reaching independent women’s organisations? Are recommendations answered publicly, and can parliament audit implementation?

Women’s organisations also need protection from being treated as a cheap replacement for the state. Community groups may operate shelters, accompany survivors, document discrimination and reach women whom government services miss. But dependence on short-term grants forces them to spend time chasing funding and can leave essential support vulnerable to changes in donor politics.

The 28% decline in funding for women’s-rights organisations between 2023 and 2024 therefore affects more than advocacy campaigns. It can reduce legal assistance, safe spaces, economic programmes, research and the ability of women to participate in public decisions.

The new report’s most useful warning is that equality can be dismantled administratively. A law may remain on the books while its enforcement unit loses staff. A national plan may survive while its budget disappears. A woman may hold office while the financial and security portfolios remain elsewhere.

Progress should be measured not only by who is visible at the podium, but by who can direct money, demand evidence, enforce a remedy and survive a change of government.

An institution created for women’s rights should not have to ask permission to exercise the powers it was established to hold.

title: A World Cup final should not force young women to choose between club and country
subtitle: Spain and DPR Korea meet for the U-20 Women’s World Cup title in Poland today. But the tournament’s exclusion from FIFA’s protected women’s calendar has left clubs free to withhold players—and exposed how quickly a development opportunity can become a workplace risk.
author: ATHENA
body:
ARCHIVE UPDATE · 14 October 2026: Spain won the 27 September final 4–3 on penalties after a 0–0 draw with DPR Korea, becoming FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup champions. FIFA match report:
https://www.fifa.com/en/tournaments/womens/u20womensworldcup/poland-2026/articles/spain-dpr-korea-final-match-report-highlights

Spain and DPR Korea will contest the FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup final in Łódź on Sunday, bringing together the 2022 champions and the holders. Spain reached the decider by beating Italy 2–0; DPR Korea defeated Colombia 3–0 and will attempt to become the competition’s first consecutive champion. The final begins at 18:00 local time. [1].

It should be a celebration of the next generation. It is also the clearest possible moment to examine whether the institutions governing women’s football have made it unnecessarily difficult for that generation to appear.

The tournament, held from 5 to 27 September, does not sit inside a protected window on FIFA’s women’s international match calendar. Under FIFA’s player-status rules, clubs must release women for listed international windows and specified senior competitions, including the Women’s World Cup, Olympic tournament and confederation championships. The U-20 Women’s World Cup is not among those protected competitions. Outside the listed windows and competitions, the rules state that release is not compulsory. [2].

That legal distinction has practical consequences. Some clubs can decline a call-up; others may agree to release a player while still needing her for preseason or league matches. A young woman trying to establish herself professionally may therefore be asked to weigh a rare World Cup against the everyday job on which her career depends.

## The players have asked FIFA to change the calendar

On 15 September, current and former players including Marta, Alex Morgan, Crystal Dunn and Sophia Wilson supported an open letter asking FIFA to align future U-20 Women’s World Cups with the international match calendar. US youth captain Kennedy Fuller and other young players also signed it. The request was not to make development football more prestigious in language alone, but to give its most important tournament the protection that allows eligible players to attend. [3].

The problem is not confined to one league or one country. In Europe’s autumn-to-spring competitions, September overlaps with the beginning of the club season, when a young player may be trying to earn a first-team place after preseason. In the United States’ spring-to-autumn National Women’s Soccer League, it falls during the regular season. College players may face classes and their own competitive calendar.

The Guardian reported that several age-eligible US players were absent, including Lily Yohannes, Claire Hutton, Jordyn Bugg and Melanie Barcenas. Their absence illustrates the talent outside the tournament, but it does not by itself prove why each player was not selected or who made the decision. Injury, form, workload, education and personal circumstances can all affect availability. The documented structural fact is narrower and more important: FIFA’s rules did not guarantee their release. [4].

![Spain’s senior women play Japan at the 2023 FIFA Women’s World Cup](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e0/Japan_vs_Spain_%E2%80%93_2023_FIFA_Women%27s_World_Cup_Group_C_%E2%80%93_3.jpg)
Spain’s senior women play Japan at the FIFA Women’s World Cup in Wellington on 31 July 2023. Contextual archive photograph illustrating the pathway into the senior game; it does not show the 2026 U-20 tournament. Photograph: JaumeBG / Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0.
Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Japan_vs_Spain_%E2%80%93_2023_FIFA_Women%27s_World_Cup_Group_C_%E2%80%93_3.jpg
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0

## Development is work, not a favour

Youth tournaments are often described as opportunities, as though a player should simply be grateful to receive one. But elite development is labour. A footballer trains, travels, risks injury and is evaluated by club and national-team employers while attempting to turn potential into a durable career.

When two calendars collide, the cost is not distributed evenly. An established senior international may have the status to negotiate. A teenager or newly contracted professional has less power to challenge a club that controls her minutes, development plan and future employment. Even where nobody issues an explicit threat, the structure can make the consequences of leaving feel obvious.

This is why the calendar question is larger than whether a particular national team fielded its strongest squad. It concerns who carries the risk created by poor coordination. At present, much of it falls on the young player: miss the World Cup, or leave her club at a decisive point and hope the absence does not narrow her opportunities.

The tournament itself shows what protected access can produce. DPR Korea entered the final on a run of 13 consecutive U-20 World Cup victories, a competition record, after nine tournament matches without conceding. Spain arrived having won the 2022 title and reached another final four years later. These programmes are offering players sustained international experience—not merely a series of exhibition matches. [5], [6].

## FIFA’s stated purpose meets its own rules

FIFA says its international calendar should be “fit-for-purpose,” improve the quality of players, clubs and national teams, and create opportunities to identify and develop talent beyond a small group of countries. Poland 2026 expanded the U-20 field to 24 teams, including debutants Benin, New Caledonia, Portugal and Tanzania. [7], [8].

Those ambitions are difficult to reconcile with a premier development tournament that lacks protected release. Expansion creates more places at the World Cup; calendar protection helps determine whether the players who earned them can attend.

FIFA and the global players’ union FIFPRO signed a cooperation agreement in June that promises player involvement in decisions concerning welfare, rest and the international match calendar. That creates a route for reform, but not a completed reform. The next test is whether the agreement gives young women—many of whom are not yet established senior professionals—an effective voice in the dates that shape their careers. [9].

ATHENA found no public FIFA response addressing the players’ September letter. The governing body’s tournament coverage has celebrated the finalists and the development value of the competition, but its published calendar rules still leave the U-20 event outside mandatory release protection.

## What meaningful reform would look like

The immediate solution is not to compel young players to play more football. It is to coordinate the football they are already expected to play.

Future U-20 Women’s World Cups could be placed inside a clearly identified protected period, with release dates, travel time and return-to-club requirements published far enough in advance for domestic leagues and colleges to plan around them. FIFA should also disclose how players, unions, clubs, leagues and national associations were consulted—and explain any decision that leaves a youth World Cup unprotected.

Protection must include workload safeguards. A calendar window should not become permission to move a player directly from a club match to an international camp and back again without recovery. National associations need minimum standards for medical care, insurance and reintegration, while clubs need predictable dates. Players need the final say over their bodies without being punished for declining a call-up or requesting rest.

Spain and DPR Korea’s players have earned the attention that comes with a world final. The women who did not reach Poland because the calendar offered them no secure path deserve attention too.

A development system should not test a young player’s loyalty before it tests her talent. If FIFA regards the U-20 Women’s World Cup as essential to the future of the sport, its rules should make attendance possible without asking a teenager to gamble with her present.

[3] ESPN’s report on the letter

https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/16/usa-brazil-u20-womens-world-cup

https://www.fifa.com/en/tournaments/womens/u20womensworldcup/poland-2026/articles/dpr-korea-dominance-fifa-youth-womens-tournaments

ATHENA did not independently establish the reason for every player’s absence.

title: Zimbabwe refused to exchange sensitive health data for US aid. Patients will feel the cutoff first.
subtitle: Washington will end its health funding for Zimbabwe when September closes, after Harare rejected a five-year agreement over patient data, biological samples and unequal access to future medical discoveries. The sovereignty dispute is between governments; the immediate uncertainty belongs to people relying on HIV, maternal and child-health services.
author: ATHENA
body:
ARCHIVE UPDATE · 14 October 2026: The United States ended its global-health funding to Zimbabwe on 30 September after the proposed bilateral agreement was rejected. No replacement US–Zimbabwe health agreement had been announced by this update.
https://donortracker.org/policy_updates?policy=us-ends-global-health-funding-to-zimbabwe

The United States will end funding for its health programmes in Zimbabwe at the close of September, converting a months-long dispute over data sovereignty into an immediate question for clinics, health workers and approximately 1.2 million people receiving HIV treatment through US-supported services.

The US Embassy confirmed the deadline on 25 September. Ambassador Pamela Tremont said Zimbabwe’s refusal to sign a bilateral health memorandum meant the relationship would move away from health and humanitarian assistance and towards trade and investment. The announcement does not establish that every patient will lose medication on 1 October. It does mean that US financing for the systems surrounding treatment—including health workers, laboratories, disease surveillance and community programmes—is ending without a replacement package being publicly identified. [1].

The agreement Washington offered was worth $367 million over five years and covered HIV and AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, maternal and child health and outbreak preparedness. Zimbabwe rejected it in February, saying the conditions sought extensive access to citizens’ health data, virus samples and epidemiological information without reciprocal access to US data or a guarantee that Zimbabweans would receive vaccines, diagnostics or treatments developed from what they supplied. [2].

US officials presented the proposal as the largest prospective health investment offered by any international partner and part of a model intended to reduce donor dependence. Zimbabwe presented the same bargain as an unequal exchange. Those positions are not mutually exclusive: the money could support essential care while the conditions attached to it could still raise legitimate questions about privacy, ownership and who benefits from medical research.

## Health data are not an abstract bargaining chip

Patient records and pathogen samples can help researchers track outbreaks, design diagnostic tests and develop medicines or vaccines. Sharing them across borders can serve the public interest. But the terms matter: who may use the information, whether individuals can be identified, how consent is protected, where samples are stored, who profits from resulting products and whether the country providing the data receives affordable access to them.

Zimbabwe government spokesperson Nick Mangwana said the proposed agreement offered no reciprocal sharing of US epidemiological data and no assurance of access to innovations resulting from Zimbabwean material. That is the government’s description of the terms. The complete proposed memorandum has not been made public through the sources reviewed for this article, limiting independent assessment of its safeguards and obligations.

The dispute therefore should not be reduced to a government refusing free healthcare. Nor should the language of sovereignty obscure the state’s responsibility to maintain lifesaving services when it rejects external financing.

Zimbabwean officials say they will prioritise domestic funding. The important measure is now not the announcement but the budget: how much money has been committed, when it becomes available, which workers and programmes it covers, and whether patients will pay more out of pocket.

![USAID and PEPFAR-supported HIV treatment services in 2015](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/15/HIV_and_AIDS_Treatment_%2823749151771%29.jpg)
USAID and PEPFAR-supported antiretroviral treatment work on 18 December 2015. Contextual archive photograph; the people pictured are not identified as patients affected by Zimbabwe’s 2026 cutoff. Photograph: Oris Chimenya/USAID, via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain in the United States.
Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HIV_and_AIDS_Treatment_(23749151771).jpg
Licence: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Template:PD-USGov-USAID

## The first losses may occur around the medicine bottle

Antiretroviral medicines are central to HIV care, but a functioning treatment programme also requires testing, counselling, viral-load monitoring, reliable records, medicine distribution and workers who can find and support patients at risk of dropping out of care.

When US funding was abruptly disrupted in 2025, UNAIDS reported that Zimbabwe’s public facilities continued providing core services and that antiretroviral stocks remained available. It also recorded staffing losses affecting medicine distribution, patient management and monitoring, as well as disruption to condom distribution, HIV testing, counselling and access to pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP. The Global Fund supported services in 21 of Zimbabwe’s 64 districts, according to that assessment. [3].

That history explains why counting tablets alone can conceal a weakening system. A medicine may be in a national warehouse while a clinic lacks the worker, test kit, transport or functioning database needed to deliver and monitor it.

It also shows why the outcome of the new cutoff cannot yet be stated as a precise number of interrupted treatments or deaths. The final effect will depend on existing medicine stocks, the Global Fund and other partners, Zimbabwe’s replacement financing and how quickly affected staff and services are absorbed. Predictions should not be presented as completed harm.

## Women and girls lose prevention before they lose headlines

The risks are not distributed evenly. UNAIDS reported in March 2025 that funding disruptions in Zimbabwe affected HIV testing during prenatal care, early diagnosis for infants, paediatric treatment and the system used to transport medical samples. Across eastern and southern Africa, the suspension of the PEPFAR-funded DREAMS programme removed combined HIV prevention, sexual and reproductive healthcare, education and violence-prevention support that had served two million adolescent girls and young women. [4].

Those findings document the earlier funding shock; they are not proof that every service will fail in the same way after September. They identify where continuity plans must now be tested.

For a pregnant woman living with HIV, continuity involves more than her own treatment. Timely testing and effective medication can sharply reduce transmission during pregnancy, birth and breastfeeding. Globally, 87% of pregnant women living with HIV had access to antiretroviral medicines for that purpose in 2025, while treatment coverage for children remained markedly lower than for adults. [5].

Adolescent girls and young women also face risks that a clinic-only response can miss. Prevention programmes may provide PrEP, contraception, testing, counselling and referrals after violence. When community organisations close, a government may keep medicines on a shelf while losing the network that helps young women reach them privately and safely.

The US Embassy’s figure of 1.2 million people in supported HIV treatment does not mean the United States bought every dose or paid every cost for every person. It indicates the reach of programmes touching their care. That is why the withdrawal’s consequences must be measured service by service rather than converted into a single dramatic claim.

## “Health sovereignty” requires money, not only refusal

Zimbabwe’s decision forms part of a wider African argument about who controls health policy, data and biological resources. Africa CDC says development assistance for health across the continent has fallen from about $25.8 billion to $13 billion in four years, while debt burdens are restricting public spending. Its September call for stronger primary healthcare describes sovereignty in practical terms: what a family can reliably receive from its health system in an ordinary week and during a crisis. [6].

That definition places obligations on donors and African governments alike. Washington should explain the data protections, benefit-sharing rules and scientific access embedded in the agreements it offers. Harare should publish a funded transition plan rather than asking patients to accept sovereignty as a substitute for a laboratory test or clinic appointment.

The Global Fund and other partners may soften the impact, but replacing a long-standing donor is not a clerical transfer. US support has financed HIV prevention and treatment, tuberculosis and malaria work, laboratories, supplies, health workers and community services over many years. Some functions can be integrated into public facilities; others may disappear if no institution assumes their cost.

The most useful public reporting after the cutoff will therefore track concrete indicators: clinic closures and staffing, waiting times, HIV and tuberculosis testing volumes, viral-load monitoring, PrEP availability, prenatal testing, early infant diagnosis, medicine stockouts and new charges imposed on patients.

Women should not be made responsible for holding the system together through unpaid care, extra travel and improvisation when services move or disappear. Young people should not have to disclose sensitive information in less private settings because a specialised programme closed. And people living with HIV should not become leverage in a diplomatic contest over who owns data.

Zimbabwe was entitled to interrogate an agreement affecting its citizens’ medical information and biological material. The United States was entitled to define the conditions under which it would spend public money abroad. Neither principle resolves what happens to a patient when negotiations fail.

The test now is whether Zimbabwe can defend control over its health data while also defending access to healthcare—and whether Washington can pursue accountable partnerships without making continuity of lifesaving services the price of accepting its terms.

https://apnews.com/article/us-health-funding-ends-data-sharing-dispute-c272b37d589c313c886c35d52bc93382

[2] Associated Press on the breakdown of negotiations
https://apnews.com/article/b2d3fce8b9a340c53d117675319be120

[3] UNAIDS country assessment
https://www.unaids.org/en/resources/presscentre/featurestories/2025/march/20250317_Zimbabwe_fs

[4] UNAIDS regional assessment
https://unaids.org/en/resources/presscentre/featurestories/2025/march/20250331_ESA-region_fs

[5] UNAIDS global factsheet
https://unaids.org/en/resources/fact-sheet

[6] Africa CDC’s Arusha Call for Action
https://africacdc.org/news-item/the-arusha-call-for-action-primary-health-care-transformation/

Reporting note: This article draws on the US Embassy’s position as reported by the Associated Press on 25 September 2026, Zimbabwe’s February explanation for rejecting the proposed agreement, UNAIDS assessments of earlier funding disruptions and Africa CDC’s current health-financing framework. The proposed memorandum has not been publicly available in full through the sources reviewed. The exact programme-level consequences after September remain uncertain and should be monitored rather than assumed.

title: India is drawing a 50-metre line around school food. Children need more than a ban.
subtitle: A proposed national definition of foods high in added fat, sugar or salt could make India’s school-food rules enforceable. Whether it improves children’s diets will depend on what replaces the restricted products—and whether small shops can adapt.
author: ATHENA
body:
India is moving to put numbers behind a promise made six years ago: keep foods high in added fat, sugar or salt from being sold or promoted to schoolchildren inside schools and within 50 metres of their gates.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India published a draft amendment in August defining what counts as “high”. For solid foods, the proposed thresholds are more than 4.2 grams of added fat, 3 grams of added sugar or 0.625 grams of salt per 100 grams. Separate, lower thresholds would apply to drinks. The proposal is open to objections and suggestions for 60 days; it is not yet a final nationwide rule. [1].

That distinction matters. India’s 2020 regulations already told school authorities not to sell or advertise these foods to pupils on campus or within the surrounding 50-metre zone. The missing numerical definition made the category harder to apply consistently. The draft would not create an unrestricted national power to close every nearby shop or prevent sales to every adult customer. It would supply measurable thresholds for rules focused on sales and marketing to schoolchildren. [2], [3].

The policy is significant because it treats children’s food choices as something shaped by their environment, not simply by willpower or a mother’s packed lunch. But a line on a map will not by itself make a nourishing snack affordable, appealing or available.

## The numbers create a test that inspectors can use

The proposed thresholds are drawn from the Indian Council of Medical Research’s 2024 dietary guidelines. They could give regulators, schools and manufacturers a common test instead of relying on the imprecise label “junk food”. A product would fall within the rules because of its composition, not because it belongs to a familiar category such as crisps, sweets or samosas.

That is both the draft’s strength and an implementation challenge. Packaged-food manufacturers can analyse recipes and change formulations. A small stall selling unpackaged food may not have laboratory data for every item. Inspectors will need clear methods for sampling and classification, and businesses will need guidance they can actually use. Otherwise, enforcement could be strict in some districts, absent in others and easiest to direct at the smallest sellers.

Maharashtra is already taking a harder approach. Its food-safety authority issued a statewide compliance order in July covering government, aided and private schools. State commissioner Tukaram Mundhe told Reuters that shops within 50 metres cannot stock the restricted products because distinguishing a sale to a pupil from a sale to another customer would be impractical. State data reviewed by Reuters showed violations at 133 shops and orders for 51 to discontinue business. [4], [5].

That state action illustrates the unresolved question beneath the federal proposal: is the rule about particular transactions involving children, or about what a shop is allowed to stock? Those are very different burdens for a family business serving an entire neighbourhood.

![Children receive lunch at a rural school in Uttar Pradesh, India, in 2007](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b8/Children_at_a_rural_school_provided_with_lunch_Uttar_Pradesh_India.jpg)
Children receive lunch at a rural school in Uttar Pradesh, India, on 22 October 2007. Contextual archive photograph. Photograph: Ajay Tallam / Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 2.0.
Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Children_at_a_rural_school_provided_with_lunch_Uttar_Pradesh_India.jpg
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0

## Children’s health is the purpose—but the evidence needs careful reading

The World Obesity Federation estimates that the number of Indian children aged five to 19 living with overweight or obesity rose from 28 million in 2015 to 41 million in 2025 and could reach 56 million by 2040, according to Reuters. The 2040 figure is a projection, not a count, and rising prevalence cannot be attributed to snacks sold near schools alone. Diet, physical activity, household income, urban design, sleep, genetics and access to care all matter.

Nor should children in larger bodies be made into warnings for everyone else. The public-health case for better school food is broader: frequent exposure to heavily marketed products high in added sugar, salt or fat can displace more varied foods and shape habits during years when children are still developing.

International evidence suggests that comprehensive rules can change the market, although India should not assume another country’s result will transfer unchanged. Chile combined front-of-package warning labels, marketing restrictions and limits on sales in schools. A 2026 study cited by Reuters associated 18 months of exposure to that package with a 2.85% lower probability of excess weight among girls and 2.4% among boys. Because several policies operated together, those figures do not isolate the effect of a 50-metre sales zone. The result was also not identical across socioeconomic groups.

That is the most useful lesson: a school-gate restriction works as part of a system, not as a substitute for one.

## The food industry can reformulate; small shops need a route to adapt

FSSAI chief executive Rajit Punhani told Reuters that the rules are intended to discourage unhealthy habits and push companies to reformulate. He said shops could sell products that do not breach the thresholds. That creates a commercial incentive: a manufacturer that reduces added sugar, fat or salt may preserve access to a large market around India’s roughly 1.5 million schools.

Companies offered different levels of detail about their policies. PepsiCo referred Reuters to its global policy limiting which products it permits to be sold in schools. Nestlé said products sold in primary and secondary schools must meet its nutritional criteria. Coca-Cola and Mondelez did not respond to Reuters’ questions. Corporate standards are relevant, but they are not a substitute for a public rule that applies equally and can be independently enforced.

The Confederation of Indian Food Trade and Industry argued in a draft submission reviewed by Reuters that a 50-metre restriction would be difficult in dense markets and could cost livelihoods. The group did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment. Shopkeepers interviewed in Bhubaneswar estimated that their sales could fall by a third or more; those estimates reflect the expectations of a small local group, not a national economic study.

Their concern should not be dismissed. If government expects a kiosk to replace profitable packets and drinks, it should help answer with what: safe drinking water, fruit, unsalted nuts where allergy controls permit, lower-sugar dairy products, or affordable cooked foods that meet the standards. Transition guidance, supplier access and a reasonable compliance period could protect children without pretending that every small retailer can redesign a business overnight.

## Mothers cannot be the enforcement system

Reuters reported that one 15-year-old boy bought packets of crisps for recess because he preferred them to the rice and lentil stew his mother had packed. It is an ordinary scene with an important implication. A caregiver can prepare food, explain nutrition and set rules at home, yet still compete with price, branding, convenience and the social pull of what friends buy at the school gate.

The answer is not to shame the child or judge the mother’s lunch. Nor is it to transfer surveillance to mothers and teachers. Schools must provide decent food and water; regulators must make classifications intelligible; companies must comply in marketing and formulation; and governments must publish inspection and outcome data.

India should measure more than the number of warnings or closures. It should track what foods replace restricted products, whether prices rise, whether enforcement differs between wealthy and low-income areas, whether girls and boys experience the policy differently, and whether children’s diets improve without increasing hunger during the school day.

A 50-metre boundary can reduce one source of pressure. It cannot repair an unaffordable school meal, a lack of clean water or a neighbourhood where the healthier option is missing. The draft’s promise lies in making the food environment share responsibility with families. Its success will depend on ensuring that, once a packet is removed, a child is not left with nothing.

title: A blood test may find cancers mammograms cannot. It must not replace the screening women already have.
subtitle: US advisers have backed Galleri, a test designed to look for signals from more than 50 cancers. Its promise is greatest where routine screening does not exist, including ovarian cancer—but a divided effectiveness vote, missed cancers and a $949 list price make this an endorsement with serious conditions.
author: ATHENA
body:
A panel of independent advisers to the US Food and Drug Administration has concluded that the potential benefits of Galleri, a blood test intended to screen adults aged 50 and over for multiple cancers, outweigh its risks. The 7–2 vote, with one abstention, moves the first test of its kind considered by an FDA advisory committee closer to possible approval—but it does not amount to approval, and the panel was far less united on whether the evidence proves the test works.

The advisers voted unanimously that Galleri appeared sufficiently safe, but split 6–4 on effectiveness. The FDA is not bound by their recommendations and is expected to make its own decision in the coming months. Until then, Galleri remains available in the United States as a laboratory-developed test rather than an FDA-approved screening device. [1], [2].

For women, the appeal is easy to understand. Mammograms and cervical screening target particular cancers, but there is no routine population-screening programme for ovarian cancer. Galleri is designed to search one blood sample for methylation patterns—chemical marks on fragments of DNA—that may indicate cancer and suggest where in the body the signal originated.

The same breadth that makes the test attractive also makes its limitations harder to explain. It does not diagnose cancer. A positive result begins a diagnostic investigation; a negative result does not rule cancer out.

## The strongest promise is where screening does not exist

FDA reviewers noted that most US cancer deaths are caused by cancer types for which there is no screening recommendation from the US Preventive Services Task Force. A test capable of detecting some of those cancers could address a genuine gap.

In the first screening round of the large NHS-Galleri study, the test detected 12 of 16 ovarian or fallopian-tube cancers diagnosed within 12 months, producing a sensitivity estimate of 75%. That figure is promising, but the sample was small: the FDA calculated a wide 95% confidence interval of 50.5% to 89.8%. In practical terms, the data are compatible with materially lower or higher performance than the headline estimate. [3].

The test performed differently across cancer types. In the same NHS dataset, its estimated sensitivity was 80% for liver and intrahepatic bile-duct cancers, 65.4% for oesophageal cancer and 38.7% for a combined category covering pancreatic, extrahepatic bile-duct and gallbladder cancers. The variation means “screens for more than 50 cancers” should never be understood as “detects those cancers equally well.”

Nor does finding a signal automatically show that screening saves lives. GRAIL’s large randomised NHS trial did not meet its primary endpoint: after three annual screening rounds, adding Galleri to usual care did not produce a statistically significant reduction in the combined number of stage III and IV cancers among the trial’s 12 prespecified cancer types. Secondary findings, including fewer stage IV diagnoses, may be encouraging, but they do not erase the failed primary outcome. Mortality data require longer follow-up. [4], [5].

![A National Cancer Institute scientist pipettes DNA samples in 2014](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/04/Female_scientist_with_DNA_sample_pippetting.jpg)
National Cancer Institute scientist Chanelle Case Borden pipettes DNA samples for PCR in August 2014. Contextual archive photograph; the procedure is not the Galleri test. Photograph: Daniel Sone / National Cancer Institute, via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain in the United States.
Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Female_scientist_with_DNA_sample_pippetting.jpg
Licence: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/

## The test missed about two-thirds of cancers overall

Two pivotal studies formed the core of the FDA review. In the US PATHFINDER 2 analysis, Galleri detected 35% of cancers diagnosed within 12 months. In the first NHS-Galleri screening round, it detected 31.6%. Put plainly, the test missed roughly two out of every three cancers that were diagnosed during the follow-up period.

Its specificity was high: 99.85% in PATHFINDER 2 and 99.74% in the NHS analysis. Specificity measures how often a test correctly returns a negative result among people who do not have the disease being assessed. High specificity limits false alarms, but it does not compensate for limited sensitivity—the proportion of actual cancers detected.

Among female participants in the NHS analysis, sensitivity was 32.9%, specificity 99.81% and positive predictive value 69.8%. The female subgroup included a weighted population of more than 25,000, but these measures combine many cancers with very different detection rates. They should not be read as a woman’s personal probability of receiving an accurate result. Age, cancer type, stage and prevalence all affect interpretation. [6].

Breast cancer demonstrates why Galleri cannot replace established screening. In the NHS analysis, it detected 21 of 110 breast cancers diagnosed within 12 months—an estimated sensitivity of 19.1%. Among women eligible for recommended breast screening, the estimate was 16.1%. The FDA also reported that PATHFINDER 2 detected five of 20 breast cancers in women who were up to date with breast screening and were subsequently diagnosed between scheduled screenings.

Those findings suggest the blood test may occasionally identify an interval cancer, but they do not support abandoning mammography. The panel resisted describing Galleri broadly as an “early detection” test and emphasised that it should be an addition to established screening, not a substitute. [7], [8].

## A positive result is the start of a medical journey

Galleri reports either “Cancer Signal Detected” or “No Cancer Signal Detected.” When it finds a signal, it also predicts a likely site of origin to guide further investigation. Confirmation may require scans, specialist appointments, biopsies or other procedures.

In PATHFINDER 2, 77% of participants with a positive result were diagnosed with cancer within the study’s 12-month window; in the NHS analysis, the proportion was 66.2%. The remaining positive results were not confirmed as cancer within that period. Some may represent false positives; in other cases, the available investigation may not have found the source.

The possible harms therefore extend beyond a misleading laboratory result. They include invasive follow-up, radiation exposure from imaging, financial cost and the distress of living with an unresolved cancer signal. The opposite error also matters: a negative result may create false reassurance, particularly if someone delays seeking care for symptoms or skips a mammogram, cervical test or colonoscopy.

The FDA’s proposed warnings state that Galleri does not detect every cancer, can produce false-positive and false-negative results and must not replace recommended single-cancer screening or diagnostic care. GRAIL gives the same central warning in its patient information. [9], [10].

## Approval would not settle the access question

Galleri’s current US list price is $949, although GRAIL advertises temporary or negotiated discounts. The company says most health-insurance plans do not cover it. FDA approval could influence future coverage and clinical adoption, but it would not by itself guarantee that every eligible person could afford the test—or the investigations that follow a positive result. [11].

That creates a second test of the technology’s value. A screening programme is not equitable merely because the initial procedure requires one vial of blood. Patients need access to primary care, imaging, specialists and biopsy services, and they need enough paid time, transport and childcare to complete the diagnostic pathway. A result without a reachable next step can convert scientific possibility into prolonged uncertainty.

Women should also be wary of commercial language that compresses a complicated performance profile into the promise of “one blood test for more than 50 cancers.” The number of cancers a laboratory attempts to detect is not the same as the number it reliably finds, and detecting a molecular signal is not the same as proving that screening reduces deaths.

Galleri may become a useful additional tool, particularly for cancers that medicine currently struggles to find before symptoms appear. The advisory panel’s vote recognises that possibility. Its division on effectiveness is equally important. If the FDA approves the test, clear labelling, post-approval studies and repeated measurement of stage at diagnosis, unnecessary procedures and mortality will be essential.

For now, the practical message is precise: a future Galleri result may add information, but it must not be treated as permission to ignore symptoms or abandon mammograms, cervical screening and other proven care.

title: A place for her story. And the bigger picture.
subtitle: Introducing ATHENA: women and children at the centre of the story.
author: ATHENA
body:
EDITOR’S NOTE

ATHENA is a media initiative centred on women and children. This is a space for news, culture and the questions that deserve more room than a headline can give them.

Our focus reaches across borders and subjects: health, education, justice, the economy, creativity and everyday life. Women’s lives do not fit inside one news category. Neither should their stories.

We want to ask who is affected, whose voice is missing and what a development means beyond the announcement. We also want room for the books, ideas and experiences that help us understand each other.

title: Reading beyond the headline
subtitle: A note on the space we make for books, essays and difficult questions.
author: ATHENA
body:
EDITOR’S NOTE

Some stories need the pace of a news report. Others need time: to follow an idea, sit with a difficult character, or return to a book with new questions.

ATHENA’s culture section makes space for that slower reading. Literature can help us consider grief, power, girlhood and belonging without pretending that one experience speaks for everyone.

An essay is an invitation to think alongside its writer. Here, that means making a clear distinction between interpretation and evidence, and allowing complexity to remain visible.

title: Who tests AI before children do? A new institute wants to become the crash lab
subtitle: Former Google safety chief Tom Siegel will lead independent tests of AI products used by young people. The project could give families clearer evidence—but funding from AI companies makes transparency central to its credibility.
author: ATHENA
body:
## Archive update — 15 October 2026

On 7 October, after this article was originally reported, the institute published an assessment rating ChatGPT for Teens an “Unacceptable Risk” for users under 18. It said testers ran more than 4,000 prompts before and after the teen mode launched and found that some advertised protections held while others failed. The assessment records important limitations: its two testing windows were sequential, it did not test every product mode, and all testing was conducted in the United States. OpenAI reviewed a draft for factual accuracy but, according to the institute, had no editorial control over the rating. This remains the institute’s assessment, not a regulatory finding. Read the assessment [1].

The Youth AI Safety Institute has appointed former Google trust-and-safety executive Tom Siegel as its founding executive director, placing a veteran of the technology industry in charge of an effort to test AI products before children and families are left to discover their weaknesses themselves.

The institute, created by Common Sense Media in May, says it will develop standards, run product evaluations and publish its findings. Siegel’s appointment was announced on 22 September. In an interview with Reuters, he argued that AI development should slow down and warned that companies risk repeating mistakes made during the growth of social media. Those are Siegel’s assessments of emerging risks—not established findings that AI has already caused more harm than social media. Youth AI Safety Institute [2], Reuters [3].

The distinction matters. Artificial intelligence is already part of many teenagers’ schoolwork and online lives, but evidence about its long-term effects on children remains incomplete. Strong warnings can prompt overdue safeguards; they should not be presented as proof of outcomes researchers have not yet established.

## What “crash-testing” AI would mean

The institute compares its ambition to vehicle crash testing: establish public standards, examine products against them and tell people what failed. Its published methodology says human reviewers test youth-specific, adversarial and multi-turn scenarios, rather than judging a chatbot from a single answer. It divides reviews among general-purpose tools, AI applied to particular activities and products designed specifically for children. Institute methodology [4].

That approach recognises a basic problem with conversational systems. A product may respond safely to a direct question but behave differently after a long exchange, when a user has disclosed distress or when the model has been encouraged to break its own rules. Young people also use the same system for different purposes: homework help, search, companionship and, in some cases, emotional support.

The institute has already published 22 assessments, assigning products ratings from unacceptable to high risk. These labels are the institute’s judgements, not regulatory decisions or findings reached under a universally accepted testing standard. The organisation is itself helping to define the standard it wants others to use. Its authority will therefore depend on whether outside researchers can understand, challenge and reproduce its tests—and whether products are retested when companies update their models.

## Teen use is widespread. The evidence still has limits.

![School pupils using a laptop together.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Kids_with_laptop.jpg/1280px-Kids_with_laptop.jpg)
Primary-school pupils use a laptop during a class on 21 January 2017. Contextual archive photograph: Wikipresence. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kids_with_laptop.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0

A Common Sense Media survey published in August found that seven in ten US teenagers reported using AI for schoolwork. The nationally representative survey covered 1,017 teenagers. Among those who used AI for school, 63% said they had used it to obtain an answer, while 77% reported using it for help that did not simply provide the answer, such as brainstorming or checking work. Only 27% said teachers had talked with them about how AI works. Common Sense Media survey [5].

The findings show reported behaviour among US teenagers at one point in time. They do not measure all children worldwide, verify every use or prove that AI caused a change in learning. They do, however, expose a gap between adoption and guidance: many students are already using tools that schools and families are still learning how to evaluate.

That gap is why independent testing could be useful. Parents and teachers cannot inspect a model’s training data, safety rules or hidden system instructions. Nor can a caregiver realistically repeat hundreds of tests after every software update. Public evaluations could turn vague assurances into questions that can be checked: Does age detection work? How does a chatbot respond when a child mentions self-harm? Does it encourage a young user to keep secrets from adults? Can parental controls be bypassed?

## Independence will be tested by the funding

The institute lists the OpenAI Foundation, Anthropic and Pinterest among its supporters, alongside philanthropic funders. It says it alone controls its research, standards, evaluations and publications—even when a funder makes a product being tested. That commitment is important, but it is also a claim the institute will need to demonstrate through its conduct. Its public funding page does not disclose how much each supporter contributed. Institute funding and governance [6].

Industry funding does not automatically invalidate research. It does create questions that should be answered plainly: Are testing protocols published in enough detail to reproduce them? Can a company see or negotiate a rating before publication? Are unsuccessful tests and dissenting expert views retained? How are conflicts declared, and is there a cap on how much influence any one funder can acquire?

Siegel brings relevant experience to those questions. He joined Google in 2004 and built its trust-and-safety operation before leaving in 2019, according to the institute. That background may help him understand how product decisions are made inside large technology companies. It also means the institute should be explicit about any continuing relationships or conflicts involving companies it evaluates.

## What the companies say—and what remains unresolved

Siegel told Reuters that stronger age verification is needed and argued that Google should allow users to disable AI-generated search features. Google responded that parents can turn off a child’s access to Search entirely and said its AI search tools can support learning. That is not the same as offering a setting that preserves conventional search while removing AI-generated answers.

OpenAI told Reuters that it uses account information, behavioural signals and self-reported age, while acknowledging that no age-assurance method is perfect. The company said it continues to test and improve its systems. Anthropic did not provide an immediate response to Reuters. These statements describe company policies and positions; they are not independent evidence that every safeguard works consistently in real use. Reuters [3].

The institute is not a regulator. It cannot compel a company to provide technical access, correct a dangerous feature or accept a rating. Siegel acknowledged that the work will depend partly on whether companies cooperate. A credible system must therefore be designed to publish meaningful findings even when a manufacturer refuses access—and to identify exactly what could not be tested.

For mothers, fathers, teachers and other caregivers, the promise of independent ratings is not a new obligation to monitor every prompt a child types. Safety cannot rest on the assumption that an adult is always present, technologically expert and able to detect a system’s failure. Companies decide what products can do; schools decide what tools enter classrooms; governments decide which protections are mandatory.

The institute’s most valuable contribution may be to move the question away from whether a family used the right settings and towards whether the product was safe enough to be offered to a young person in the first place. Its own test begins now: showing that an organisation supported by the AI industry can examine that industry publicly, consistently and without allowing access or funding to soften the result.

title: Italy proposes school face-veil ban and classroom limits on foreign pupils
subtitle: Giorgia Meloni calls the measures a route to integration. Their consequences will depend on who is counted, how schools enforce them and whether children retain meaningful access to education.
author: ATHENA
body:
## Archive update — 15 October 2026

The proposal described below advanced after this article was originally reported. On 24 September, Italy’s government approved a decree setting a 30% classroom limit for pupils with limited Italian proficiency and banning full-face coverings in schools. The decree took effect immediately but required parliamentary endorsement within 60 days. It provides exemptions and language-support funding in some cases; Associated Press reported that officials expected about 1,000 classrooms, 0.3% of the national total, to be affected. The later decree therefore resolves several unknowns in the original report, while questions about implementation and equal access remain. Associated Press, 24 September [1].

Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, announced on 20 September that she would bring forward measures banning burqas and niqabs in schools and limiting foreign pupils in individual classrooms. Speaking at her party’s youth festival in Rome, she also proposed compulsory Italian lessons for parents whose children face serious difficulties integrating into school. Associated Press [2].

These are announced proposals, not an enacted school ban verified by ATHENA. The distinction matters for families deciding what the news means for their children today.

Meloni did not give a numerical classroom limit. Her argument was that children struggling with Italian can learn through classmates and teachers, but that a high concentration of such pupils undermines integration. She also framed uncovered faces as a matter of young women’s freedom. Reuters [3].

## Which children would count as “foreign”?

The policy’s central ambiguity is the relationship between citizenship and educational need. Reuters, citing the research foundation ISMU, reports that pupils without Italian citizenship account for 11.6% of school enrolment. That figure measures nationality, not proficiency in Italian. Reuters [3].

A citizenship-based ceiling and a language-support policy therefore answer different questions. The first determines where a child may study; the second should establish what help that child needs. A workable proposal would have to explain how those decisions connect, rather than treating a passport as an assessment of ability.

School leaders have identified a practical obstacle. Antonello Giannelli, president of the national headteachers’ association ANP, described the educational aim as reasonable but questioned how schools could implement it where neighbourhood populations are predominantly foreign. El País, reporting his comments to La Repubblica, says existing guidance recommending a 30% limit has already encountered this difficulty. That figure should not be presented as Meloni’s newly announced cap. El País [4].

Moving children between schools would raise further questions: who pays for transport, how siblings are placed and what happens when nearby schools lack space? Those are implementation questions, not established consequences of a text ATHENA has inspected.

## A face veil is not a headscarf

Meloni named the burqa and niqab. AP reports that she did not mention the hijab, the headscarf that leaves the face visible. Reporting this as a general ban on Muslim headscarves would overstate the announcement. Associated Press [2].

For women and girls, the test goes beyond the government’s stated intention. How would a school respond to a pupil wearing a face veil? Would it offer dialogue and support, impose sanctions or refuse entry? Would the rules cover parents visiting school? The announcement as reviewed does not settle those questions, and the reporting consulted provides no reliable count of affected pupils.

Nor does this draft establish how Muslim students themselves view the proposal. Their choices and experiences cannot be inferred from clothing or replaced by political claims made on their behalf.

Compulsory language learning for parents also needs an accessible service behind it: affordable classes, workable hours and provision for people with caring responsibilities. Without those details, a duty to attend says little about a parent’s ability to comply.

## Education remains the starting point


![An empty blue classroom in a nursery school in Fontevivo, Italy.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/Asilo_Fontevivo_%285%29_sez_blu_interno.jpg/1280px-Asilo_Fontevivo_%285%29_sez_blu_interno.jpg)
An empty classroom at the “Cucciolo” nursery school in Fontevivo, Parma, photographed in 2011. Contextual archive photograph: Vincenzo Mainardi. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Asilo_Fontevivo_%285%29_sez_blu_interno.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0
UNHCR’s current guidance for Italy says children have a right to education regardless of their status, with compulsory attendance from six to 16. Lack of residence registration or previous schooling cannot prevent enrolment. The agency also explains that schools can assist families unable to complete online registration. UNHCR Italy [5].

That is the baseline against which the proposals should be examined. Integration can be assessed through attendance, language progress and participation. The government’s next task is to show how its restrictions would improve those outcomes while preserving children’s access to school—and women’s ability to take part in their children’s education.

title: Iva Jovic returns to Guadalajara—and leaves with a title, not just promise
subtitle: The 18-year-old American defended her Guadalajara crown without dropping a set, adding substance to a season that has already taken her into the world’s top 20.
author: ATHENA
body:
Original reporting date: 21 September 2026.

Iva Jovic has won the Guadalajara Open for a second consecutive year, beating fellow American Peyton Stearns 6-4, 6-2 to claim her second WTA singles title. The WTA’s report, published on 20 September, places the final on Saturday night, 19 September. Jovic is the tournament’s first repeat singles champion. [WTA match report](https://www.wtatennis.com/news/4578948/jovic-goes-back-to-back-in-guadalajara-outduels-stearns-in-all-american-showdown).

For an athlete whose first trophy arrived at 17, the distinction is important: this was a return as the player to beat, not an unexpected breakthrough.

## A final controlled on serve

Stearns never earned a break point. Jovic won 70% of her service points and converted three of her five opportunities to break, according to the match statistics reported by Reuters. Stearns, ranked 60th coming into the final, was seeking a third career title after victories in Rabat in 2024 and Austin earlier this year. [Reuters, 20 September](https://www.reuters.com/sports/tennis/wta-roundup-iva-jovic-repeats-guadalajara-open-champ--flm-2026-09-20/).

The opening set stayed level through eight games. Jovic then broke for 5-4, held to take the set and broke again at the start of the second. She finished with a backhand winner down the line. [WTA](https://www.wtatennis.com/news/4578948/jovic-goes-back-to-back-in-guadalajara-outduels-stearns-in-all-american-showdown).

Those details matter more than the shorthand of teenage talent. Protecting a service game and converting an opening are competitive skills, not personality traits or predictions about a distant future.

![Iva Jovic practices ahead of the 2024 US Open.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Iva_Jovic_%282024_US_Open%29_01.jpg/960px-Iva_Jovic_%282024_US_Open%29_01.jpg)

Contextual archive photograph: Iva Jovic at practice before the US Open, New York, 25 August 2024. Photograph: Hameltion. CC BY-SA 4.0.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Iva_Jovic_(2024_US_Open)_01.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

## From breakthrough to repeatability

Jovic arrived at the 2025 tournament ranked 73rd. She beat Colombia’s Emiliana Arango 6-4, 6-1 in that final, becoming the youngest American tour-level singles champion since Coco Gauff in 2021. Arango had struggled with illness during the match; Jovic acknowledged her opponent’s effort afterwards. That first title carried the promise of a substantial rankings jump. [WTA’s 14 September 2025 report](https://www.wtatennis.com/news/4362990/jovic-becomes-youngest-champion-this-season-with-guadalajara-title).

This year’s defence sits within a broader run: an Australian Open quarterfinal, entry into the top 20 in February and second-week appearances at Wimbledon and the US Open. Jovic described herself as “a more complete and better player” than a year earlier, according to the WTA’s account of her post-match comments. [WTA](https://www.wtatennis.com/news/4578948/jovic-goes-back-to-back-in-guadalajara-outduels-stearns-in-all-american-showdown).

A second trophy cannot guarantee a Grand Slam title, and it should not become a deadline by which a young woman must fulfil other people’s expectations. It does provide something more useful than hype: another result against professional opposition, built on a week of sustained performance.

For girls following her progress, the story is not that success must arrive before adulthood. It is that a young woman’s sporting achievement deserves to be examined on its own terms—with attention to her decisions, execution and development. Jovic’s age is part of this result. Her tennis explains it.
