title: “Great Jeans.” “Just Sports.” What Are Sydney Sweeney’s Adverts Really Selling?
subtitle: Female athletes are challenging Sydney Sweeney’s new Novig campaign, a year after American Eagle’s jeans-and-genes wordplay prompted a different dispute over beauty and race. Both controversies ask who advertising imagines its audience to be—and what happens when a woman’s body becomes the principal way to reach it.
author: ATHENA
body:
Original reporting date: 15 September 2026

Sydney Sweeney’s latest advertising controversy has drawn objections from women whose professional lives are spent in sport. Olympic swimmer Ariarne Titmus and British sprinter Amy Hunt are among the athletes criticising her campaign for Novig, arguing that its sexual imagery diminishes the work behind women’s sporting achievements. Other competitors have answered with footage of themselves training and competing.

The campaign is called ‘Just Sports’. Novig’s website spells out the proposition: ‘No war. No death. No politics. Just sports.’ It is advertising a prediction platform focused on sporting outcomes, rather than markets in other events. Its promotional imagery features Sweeney with sports equipment covering parts of her otherwise unclothed body.

The commercial follows an earlier dispute over American Eagle’s ‘Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans’ campaign, launched in July 2025. These are different advertisements, with different criticisms. The denim debate concerned the use of inherited traits to sell an image of beauty. The Novig debate concerns the use of sexual appeal within sports marketing—and whose interests that representation serves.

Reducing both to another argument about whether Sweeney should cover up misses the substance of the objections. Equally, criticism of a commercial does not establish the actress’s private beliefs or justify abuse directed at her.

## What the jeans campaign said—and why it mattered

American Eagle launched its campaign on 23 July 2025, describing Sweeney as central to a major denim promotion aimed at its Gen Z audience. The company announced billboards, social-media features and a presence on the Las Vegas Sphere. This was a coordinated commercial campaign, with a distribution strategy extending well beyond a single video.

The disputed wordplay moved between ‘jeans’ and ‘genes’. In one video, Sweeney discussed traits inherited from parents, including hair and eye colour, before concluding: ‘My jeans are blue.’ Critics argued that pairing praise for inherited traits with a blonde, blue-eyed white actress evoked racialised beauty hierarchies and, for some, the language of eugenics.

That interpretation needs precise attribution. An advertisement invoking genes does not, by itself, prove that its creators intended to promote racial superiority. The criticism concerned the association the campaign constructed: an admired appearance, inherited characteristics and the suggestion that those characteristics were ‘great’.

A stronger analysis can examine that association without claiming access to anyone’s motives. When a brand uses heredity as part of a beauty joke, audiences may reasonably ask which traits are being elevated and why. Calling the campaign playful does not settle how its language works.

American Eagle’s response was that the campaign concerned jeans and celebrated individual confidence. Sweeney later told People she did not support the views others had connected to it, saying: ‘I’m against hate and divisiveness.’ She also acknowledged that remaining silent had widened the divide. Those statements belong in the account alongside the criticism.

The partnership continued. On 15 April 2026, American Eagle announced a second campaign, ‘Syd for Short’, centred on denim shorts. It also continued a charitable component, promising the purchase price of designated styles to Crisis Text Line, with butterfly details honouring domestic-violence survivors. The donation commitment is relevant context; it neither resolves nor invalidates criticism of the advertising.

![An American Eagle billboard featuring Sydney Sweeney in Times Square](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/American_Eagle_Outfitters_Times_Square_NYC_-_Syd_for_Short.jpg?width=1600)

Contextual photograph: American Eagle’s later ‘Syd for Short’ billboard in Times Square, New York, photographed 12 May 2026 by Nielsoncaetanosalmeron. This is not an image from the 2025 ‘Great Jeans’ launch. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:American_Eagle_Outfitters_Times_Square_NYC_-_Syd_for_Short.jpg Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

## Why athletes are challenging ‘Just Sports’

Novig announced its Sweeney campaign on 9 September. In its launch statement, the company identified her as a strategic partner and equity holder, giving her a financial relationship with the business beyond appearing in an advert. Sweeney described the concept as humorous and playful, intended to focus attention on sport. This was a launch statement, not an apology issued after the backlash.

For the athletes objecting, the problem is what the campaign chooses to make visible. Titmus emphasised the dedication and collective values of sport. Hunt pointed to the physical work of competition, while gymnast Gracie Kramer shared her own sporting footage as a counter-image. Their responses challenge a commercial representation through the work that representation leaves out.

![British sprinter Amy Hunt speaks at an athletics press conference](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Amy_Hunt_at_a_press_conference_during_the_Wanda_Diamond_League_Athletissima_athletics_competition._01.jpg?width=1200)

British sprinter Amy Hunt, one of the athletes who criticised the campaign, at an Athletissima press conference in Lausanne, Switzerland, 20 August 2026. Photograph by Quejaytee. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Amy_Hunt_at_a_press_conference_during_the_Wanda_Diamond_League_Athletissima_athletics_competition._01.jpg Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

The distinction between the product and the imagery matters. Novig is promoting a service for people predicting sporting outcomes; it is not presenting a documentary about female athletes. Yet choosing a sports setting does not place the creative decisions beyond scrutiny. The equipment supplies the sporting context, while the performer’s body supplies much of the visual attraction.

The resulting question is about advertising priorities. What does this company believe will persuade its intended customers to pay attention? And where do women appear in that imagined audience—as participants, knowledgeable spectators, potential customers or an attraction offered to somebody else?

## Choosing sexual imagery does not end the discussion

Sweeney is an adult entitled to make decisions about her image. Treating her as incapable of understanding a provocative campaign would erase her agency. Her disclosed equity role makes that particularly difficult to justify.

But agency and cultural criticism answer different questions. Her participation concerns her decision to take part. Criticism concerns what the finished campaign communicates, how it is distributed and whose experiences it sidelines. Neither question has to cancel the other.

Nor should the athletes’ objections become a demand that women look a particular way to be taken seriously. A sportswoman can enjoy fashion, pose nude or present herself sexually without forfeiting professional respect. The relevant issue is the meaning of a particular image in its commercial setting, rather than a universal rule about how much skin a woman may show.

Sweeney appeared to answer the criticism by sharing ESPN Body Issue covers featuring nude athletes, according to Variety. The posts suggest a comparison, although they should not be treated as a detailed statement of her position.

That comparison opens a useful discussion. Nudity can draw attention to athletic form, express sexuality, sell a service or do several things at once. Evaluating it requires looking at framing, purpose, context and control. The presence of nudity alone proves neither empowerment nor exploitation.

## Follow the business behind the image

Novig’s launch announcement says the campaign will run across digital, social, online-video and outdoor placements during football season. Chief executive Jacob Fortinsky praised Sweeney’s ability to make its message difficult to ignore. The company also says participation is restricted to people aged 21 and older.

Attention is plainly part of the objective. Whether controversy produces durable customer growth is a separate question. Shares, views and arguments cannot establish how many people register, remain active or generate revenue. There is also insufficient evidence to declare that every hostile reaction was deliberately planned.

The business relationship nevertheless matters. Focusing exclusively on Sweeney turns a campaign developed and distributed by a company into a referendum on one woman’s character. It leaves less room to examine the brand’s target audience, creative approvals, financial incentives and responsibility for the finished work.

The same applies to the jeans controversy. A celebrity provides recognition, but a retailer chooses the campaign, pays to circulate it and responds to its reception. Accountability should follow those decisions as well as the face on the poster.

## What women should be able to ask

The two campaigns deserve scrutiny for different reasons. The jeans advert raises questions about inherited beauty and the associations brands create through wordplay. The sports advert raises questions about whose bodies attract attention and whose sporting labour remains outside the frame.

Neither debate requires treating Sweeney as a symbol of everything wrong with advertising. Neither requires dismissing critics as jealous, prudish or unable to understand a joke.

For ATHENA, the sharper question is what these campaigns invite women to recognise about themselves. Are women addressed as customers with knowledge, ambitions and interests? Are they represented as competitors whose work deserves attention? Or is their value to the advertisement primarily the attention their appearance can secure?

A woman can choose an image and profit from it. Other women can still question the story it tells.

## Update — 16 October 2026

Since this article was first reported, Sweeney and Novig have continued the campaign with another provocative advertisement responding to criticism. Powerade has also released a ‘Never Just Sports’ counter-campaign centred on women athletes. The responses reinforce the distinction between a woman’s agency in choosing sexual imagery and the commercial framing used to sell sport.

The Athena Perspective.

title: Destry Damayanti Broke Bank Indonesia’s 73-Year Ceiling. Independence Is Her Next Test
subtitle: Indonesia has installed its first woman central-bank governor and placed another woman in the institution’s second-highest office. The appointments change who is seen at the top of economic power—but do not settle whether the bank can support growth without surrendering its independence.
author: ATHENA Finance & Economics Desk
body:
Original reporting date: 2 September 2026

Indonesia’s House of Representatives approved three economists to lead Bank Indonesia for the 2026–2031 term. Solikin M. Juhro became a deputy governor. Aida S. Budiman moved into the role of senior deputy governor. Destry Damayanti became governor.

For the first time since Bank Indonesia was officially established on 1 July 1953, the person at the top is a woman. The second-in-command is a woman too.

Damayanti’s appointment was approved at a plenary sitting on 1 September after the House finance commission conducted fit-and-proper hearings on 26 and 27 August. She, Budiman and Juhro took their oaths at the Supreme Court on 2 September.

The milestone deserves to be recorded without decoration. Indonesia has placed a woman in charge of the institution that sets its benchmark interest rate, works to defend the rupiah, oversees payment systems and helps safeguard financial stability in Southeast Asia’s largest economy. It has done so after 73 years of male governors.

Yet the appointment did not occur during a period of calm, nor through a visibly wide contest. Damayanti was President Prabowo Subianto’s sole nominee after Governor Perry Warjiyo resigned unexpectedly in July, midway through his second term. Parliament is dominated by parties allied with the president. The rupiah has been one of Asia’s weakest currencies this year, investors have questioned the predictability of economic policy, and a new law has increased both Bank Indonesia’s growth responsibilities and parliament’s influence over financial regulators.

That context does not diminish the first. It explains why the story cannot end with it.

## A historic appointment built on an established career

Damayanti is not arriving at Bank Indonesia as a symbolic outsider. She has been inside its senior leadership since 2019 and served as acting governor after Warjiyo’s departure.

Born in Jakarta in 1963, she studied economics at the University of Indonesia and completed a master’s degree in regional science at Cornell University. Her career has moved through public policy, research, commercial finance and regulation.

She was a senior economic adviser to the British ambassador, taught and conducted research at the University of Indonesia, became chief economist at Mandiri Sekuritas and then Bank Mandiri, chaired an economic task force under the state-owned enterprises ministry, and served on the board of Indonesia’s Deposit Insurance Corporation before joining Bank Indonesia.

She took office as senior deputy governor in August 2019 and was sworn in for a second term in 2024. Those seven years included the economic shock of the pandemic, rapid changes in digital payments and repeated periods of global financial volatility. Markets largely read her nomination as a continuity choice rather than a policy experiment.

That distinction is important in reporting on women’s advancement. A first woman is often introduced as though she appeared suddenly at the summit. The years spent becoming qualified are compressed into a celebratory caption, while the institution’s long history of choosing men is treated as background rather than a decision repeated over generations.

Damayanti did not become capable on the day parliament noticed her. The significant change is that her experience has finally been permitted to carry her into the office that experience traditionally prepares a central banker to hold.

Budiman’s approval as senior deputy governor strengthens the significance. It means the change is not confined to one woman occupying one exceptional chair. Budiman is also an internal candidate with a long central-bank career, including responsibility for international affairs and economic and monetary policy.

Public evidence does not establish that the appointments resulted from a deliberate gender-equality strategy, and neither the president nor parliament should be credited with one without proof. What can be stated is that two of the institution’s most senior posts have now been assigned to qualified women.

That is a measurable break with the past. It is not yet evidence that women throughout Bank Indonesia encounter equal recruitment, pay, promotion or authority.

![Indonesian rupiah banknotes issued after 2000](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Indonesian_Rupiah_(IDR)_banknotes.jpg?width=1600)

Contextual photograph: Indonesian rupiah banknotes in denominations issued after 2000, photographed 5 June 2009 by EvanC0912. The notes are not presented as a current set in circulation. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Indonesian_Rupiah_(IDR)_banknotes.jpg Licence: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/

## The office became vacant under unresolved circumstances

Warjiyo formally stepped down for personal reasons on 25 July. The government did not provide a fuller public explanation, and he did not publicly connect his resignation to political interference.

Reuters separately reported that he had experienced a major disagreement with then-finance minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa over strategies for economic growth before leaving. That reporting raises a legitimate question about the policy climate Damayanti inherited, but it does not prove that the dispute caused the resignation. The distinction should remain intact unless Warjiyo, the government or documentary evidence establishes more.

The market reaction showed why an unexplained mid-term exit matters. On the first trading day after the announcement, the rupiah weakened to 18,000 against the US dollar and the main share index fell. Analysts interviewed at the time warned that the departure could deepen concern about Bank Indonesia’s autonomy.

Damayanti moved quickly into meetings with the finance minister and the president and promised continuity. Her nomination in August helped the currency recover, suggesting that investors regarded an experienced internal candidate as less disruptive than some alternatives. This was a judgement about expected policy, not proof that all doubts had disappeared.

The selection process itself leaves little evidence of rivalry. Damayanti was the only candidate submitted for governor. Reuters noted during her hearing that an Indonesian parliament had not rejected a sitting president’s central-bank nominee since 2008.

A sole candidacy is lawful, and broad political support can reflect confidence in a nominee. It also limits the public’s ability to compare competing accounts of how the bank should manage inflation, currency pressure and government demands.

The correct conclusion is not that Damayanti lacks legitimacy. Parliament approved her under the established process after a public hearing. The correct conclusion is narrower: the process shows consensus around her, not the outcome of an open competition among several tested candidates.

## ‘Stability first’ must survive the demand for growth

Shortly after the parliamentary approval, Damayanti presented Bank Indonesia’s revised outlook. The bank expected the economy to grow between 5.2 and 6 per cent in 2027, compared with the previous range of 5.1 to 5.9 per cent. The new upper limit matched the president’s target and would represent Indonesia’s first 6 per cent expansion since 2012.

She attributed the stronger possibility partly to rising investment, including activity associated with Danantara, the sovereign wealth fund created by Prabowo’s administration. She also supported tighter retention of export earnings and the centralisation of strategic commodity exports, arguing that the measures could strengthen government revenue and the rupiah. Traders and investors have expressed concern that the latter policy could increase state control over resource exports.

At the same time, Damayanti said stability would remain the central bank’s priority. She promised cooperation with government to contain inflation and sufficient liquidity to support the economy, while maintaining that inter-agency coordination would not compromise Bank Indonesia’s independence.

Those promises are not inherently contradictory. Central banks and governments routinely coordinate. Food inflation, for example, cannot be solved by an interest-rate decision alone; transport, harvests, imports, storage and regional supply all matter. A monetary authority can communicate with fiscal officials without taking orders from them.

The danger lies in what happens when the objectives conflict.

Bank Indonesia increased its benchmark rate by a full percentage point between May and June to defend the rupiah, then held it at 5.75 per cent in July and August. Higher rates can support a currency and restrain inflation, but they also increase borrowing costs and may slow investment.

A government seeking rapid growth prefers abundant, inexpensive credit. An independent central bank must retain the authority to choose stability when political leaders would rather have immediate stimulus.

Damayanti’s slightly higher 2027 forecast was not in itself evidence of political submission. Forecast ranges change, and the shift was small. It should nevertheless be tested against incoming data, particularly because the World Bank’s June assessment projected growth of 5 per cent in 2026 and warned that fiscal pressure, higher energy costs, capital outflows and a weaker currency had increased the risks around Indonesia’s outlook.

Independence concerns also extend beyond one forecast. Law No. 4 of 2026, enacted on 17 June, amended Indonesia’s financial-sector framework. It reinforced Bank Indonesia’s obligation to support sustainable economic growth and added attention to real-sector growth and job creation. Reuters reported that the changes also empower lawmakers to issue binding recommendations to the bank and other nominally independent financial authorities.

The president’s nephew, Thomas Djiwandono, became a Bank Indonesia deputy governor earlier this year after leaving government and party positions. His family relationship does not establish that he takes instructions from the president, nor does it make his appointment unlawful. It does create a perception problem at an institution whose decisions must be believed to rest on economic evidence rather than family or party loyalty.

Damayanti cannot resolve every concern about the law or other appointments. She can determine how the board operates within them. Meeting records, consistent explanations, credible forecasts and a willingness to make politically inconvenient decisions will matter more than repeated assurances that the bank remains independent.

Independence is not a sentence a governor says once. It is a pattern the public can observe.

![The Bank Indonesia Museum building in Jakarta](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Bank_Indonesia_Museum_-_Jakarta_(2025)_-_img_12.jpg?width=1200)

Contextual photograph: the Bank Indonesia Museum in Jakarta, 6 May 2025. This is a historic museum building, not the central bank’s current headquarters. Photograph by Chainwit. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bank_Indonesia_Museum_-_Jakarta_(2025)_-_img_12.jpg Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

## A woman at the top is not automatically a policy for women

Damayanti enters a global profession in which women remain unusual at the highest level. OMFIF’s Gender Balance Index, published in April, counted women leading 35 of the 185 central banks it examined—a record, but still only about 19 per cent.

Across central banks, commercial banks, sovereign funds and pension funds, women held 19 per cent of the top positions and the index estimated that parity remained decades away at the current pace.

The scarcity does not mean every woman central banker thinks alike. There is no sound basis for assuming that women are naturally more cautious with interest rates, more compassionate towards borrowers or more resistant to political pressure. Damayanti’s sex cannot substitute for analysis of her votes, forecasts and institutional decisions.

Representation matters for different reasons. It expands the visible route into authority. It challenges the belief that monetary expertise has a male face. It can broaden professional networks and the range of experience present when decisions are debated. It also makes it harder for institutions to claim that no qualified woman is ready the next time a top post becomes vacant.

An IMF pilot study of eight advanced-economy central banks, using 2020 or 2021 workforce information, illustrates the wider promotion problem without supplying a direct audit of Bank Indonesia.

Women made up an average of 44.6 per cent of employees in the participating banks but 32 per cent of senior management and about 35 per cent of economists. The authors also found that women were heavily concentrated in part-time work and certain administrative roles.

Because the sample was small, wealthy-country focused and based on older data, those figures should not be presented as Indonesia’s own. They show the kind of institutional questions that one historic appointment cannot answer.

Bank Indonesia has not published, in the materials reviewed for this report, a current gender breakdown of staff by department, grade, pay, promotion and contract type. Nor did ATHENA find a new gender-equality programme attached to Damayanti’s confirmation.

Absence from the reviewed public record is not proof that no internal data or programme exists. It means the appointment should not be reported as an institution-wide transformation without further evidence.

The bank’s decisions still reach women in concrete ways. Interest rates affect the cost of working capital and household loans. Currency weakness can increase the domestic price of imported food, fuel, medicine and production inputs. Payment-system rules shape whether small traders can participate safely in the digital economy.

Bank Indonesia also works on financial inclusion and small-business development, and the World Bank has identified it as one of the formal institutions involved in initiatives supporting Indonesian women’s entrepreneurship.

These are not women-only policies. Men and women both borrow, save, run firms and absorb inflation. But unequal income, care responsibilities, asset ownership and access to formal credit can make the same economic shock land differently. A central bank committed to public welfare should know who gains access, who pays more and who remains outside the system.

Damayanti does not need to turn every monetary statement into a gender speech. Her institution can publish better sex-disaggregated financial-inclusion data, examine whether credit and payment innovations reach women-owned firms, disclose its own leadership pipeline and ensure that Budiman’s and Damayanti’s rise is not followed by another generation of women stalled below them.

That is how representation becomes a structure rather than an event.

## The first should be recognised—and then allowed to become accountable

Women who enter offices previously reserved for men often encounter two unfair demands at once. They are expected to embody progress for all women, then blamed more broadly if they make an unpopular decision.

Damayanti should not have to prove that women as a group can manage a central bank. Men who held the post were not required to prove the economic competence of their sex.

Equal treatment, however, does not mean ceremonial protection from scrutiny. The weakened rupiah will not stabilise because its defender is a woman. Inflation will not become less damaging because the policy statement announcing it carries a historic name. Investors, workers and households need credible decisions, transparent reasoning and an institution able to say no when political objectives endanger price or financial stability.

The early measures of Damayanti’s tenure are therefore clear. Does the bank explain how it balances the new growth and employment language with its stability responsibilities? Do forecasts change with evidence, or appear to converge automatically with government targets? Are currency interventions, liquidity programmes and cooperation with Danantara reported transparently? Can board members disagree without political retaliation? Does the bank publish enough information for the public to distinguish coordination from control?

There is also a gender test, but it is not whether Damayanti behaves as an imagined ‘female governor’. It is whether her appointment leaves the ladder sturdier for women behind her: more women in economic and market-facing roles, fair promotion, meaningful authority and a process capable of producing several qualified candidates rather than one exceptional first.

Indonesia’s parliament made one part of history. It approved a woman to lead Bank Indonesia and another to serve immediately below her. The years ahead will give those offices meaning.

Damayanti’s gender is not the source of the pressure facing the bank, and it will not determine whether she withstands it. The significance of the moment is that a woman finally holds the same power, responsibility and obligation to be judged on evidence that men have held since 1953.

The ceiling has broken. What happens beneath it will be recorded in interest-rate decisions, the value of the rupiah, the candour of public explanations and the distance Bank Indonesia can maintain between cooperation with government and obedience to it.

## Update — 17 October 2026

In an interview published on 12 October, Damayanti said Bank Indonesia retains full authority over interest-rate decisions even as it works more closely with the government. She said government representatives attend part of the bank’s monthly policy review but have no vote. The assurance directly addresses the central question in this article; its credibility will still depend on the bank’s decisions over time.

The Athena Perspective.

title: Girls Are Being Taught to Fear Wrinkles Before They Have Finished Growing
subtitle: Research has found skincare creators as young as seven using six products on average, while regulators and dermatologists question how adult anti-ageing formulas are marketed to children.
author: ATHENA Beauty & Health Desk
body:
In one skincare video examined by medical researchers, a young creator applied 10 products to her face in six minutes.
As the routine continued, she described discomfort and burning. By the final minutes, a visible reaction had developed on the skin she was supposedly learning to protect.
The contradiction captures the strange bargain now being offered to girls online. A child can be persuaded to injure healthy skin while trying to prevent signs of an ageing process that has barely begun.
In August 2024, Teen Vogue warned that celebrity treatments, restrictive collagen diets, overnight face tape, mouth taping and the relentless promotion of retinol were pushing anti-ageing culture towards teenagers. Its argument was not that young people should neglect their skin. It was that social media had blurred the line between basic care and a fear-driven regimen designed for concerns children did not have.
Two years later, that warning looks less like commentary and more like an early report from a market that was still expanding.
A peer-reviewed study has now measured the products and ingredients in youth skincare videos. British dermatologists are calling for warnings on adult formulas after seeing children with reactions. An Italian regulator has opened Europe’s first investigation of its kind into alleged marketing practices by major beauty companies.
This is not a story about girls becoming unusually vain.
Girls did not invent the belief that a woman’s face loses value as it ages. They did not build recommendation algorithms, commission influencer campaigns, formulate brightly packaged acids or decide that “self-care” should require a shelf of products. Adults created the commercial culture. Children learned its language.
Then adults mocked them as “Sephora kids” for speaking it fluently.

## The warning became evidence

![Rows of skincare products on shelves inside a Brazilian drugstore](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Skin_care_cosmetics.jpg?width=1600)
Contextual photograph: skincare products in a drugstore in Colatina, Brazil, 4 February 2024. Photograph by ArionStar. This image does not show the products or children studied in the article. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Skin_care_cosmetics.jpg Licence: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/

In 2025, researchers published the first peer-reviewed systematic examination of paediatric skincare routines on TikTok.
Two investigators created new accounts identifying themselves as 13-year-olds. They watched, liked and saved relevant posts from the “For You” feed until they had collected 100 unique skincare videos. The creators ranged from seven to 18 years old, and each video had an average of 1.1 million views.
The average routine contained six products and cost an estimated US$168. Only 26.2 per cent included sunscreen. Among the 25 most-viewed videos, routines contained an average of 11 potentially irritating active ingredients; one contained 21. Seventy-six per cent of the videos analysed for ingredients included at least one potential contact allergen.
The study was small and should not be stretched beyond what it measured. It analysed 100 videos gathered during April and May 2024, not every child’s feed. The investigators deliberately engaged with skincare content, so their experience does not show what a completely passive user would receive. Some creator ages had to be estimated from appearance and contextual clues. The research did not establish how many children use these routines, whether the videos caused viewers to buy products or whether watching them directly harmed mental health.
What it did show was the kind of material an account presented as 13 could be taught to expect after expressing interest.
The researchers found that a few likes and saves quickly filled the feed with girls using expensive, complicated routines. The two test accounts also received different recommendations, meaning a parent looking at their own phone may not see what the child’s algorithm is delivering.
The algorithm does not have to announce that six products are compulsory. Repetition performs that work. When every smooth-faced creator appears to cleanse, tone, exfoliate, treat, brighten and seal, an optional ritual begins to look like the minimum required for being a responsible girl.

## The products can create the problem they promise to prevent

Most of the children in the TikTok study did not appear to be treating a visible condition. Only eight of 82 creators had visible blemishes, according to the researchers.
That matters because benefit and risk depend on need.
Retinoids and hydroxy acids are not inherently bad ingredients. Dermatologists prescribe retinoids to adolescents for acne and other conditions. Salicylic acid, benzoyl peroxide and related treatments may be appropriate where hormonal changes cause persistent breakouts. A medically supervised treatment for acne is not the same as a child layering several cosmetic products to prevent wrinkles.
The risk rises when users apply multiple active ingredients at once, unknowingly repeat the same ingredient across several bottles or combine products that increase irritation and sensitivity to sunlight. The Pediatrics study found that the 25 most-viewed routines used an average of three products containing alpha hydroxy acids. For children without acne, the authors concluded that the risk of irritant dermatitis was likely to outweigh any benefit.
Possible outcomes include redness, dryness, burning, peeling, disruption of the skin barrier, increased sun sensitivity and allergic contact dermatitis. Once a person becomes sensitised to an ingredient, avoiding that allergen can affect which soaps, shampoos, cosmetics or occupational products they can use later.
This is why the medical message requires more care than the slogan “retinol is bad for teenagers.” A young person prescribed a retinoid should not stop treatment because of a social-media warning. The problem is unnecessary cosmetic use without an individual diagnosis, especially when several actives are combined.
The American Academy of Dermatology advises most tweens to begin with a gentle cleanser, fragrance-free moisturiser and broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher. It recommends that children avoid cosmetic retinol, vitamin C and exfoliating acids intended for wrinkles, sun damage and uneven tone unless a dermatologist identifies a reason to use an active ingredient. New products should be introduced one at a time.
The simplicity is almost embarrassing beside the industry surrounding it.
Healthy skin does not require a child to perform ten steps before school. Skincare can be care without becoming correction.

## Sunscreen is not an instruction to fear the sun—or age

![An adult applies sunscreen to a child outdoors](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Applying_sunscreen.jpg?width=1600)
Archive health photograph: an adult applies sunscreen to a child outdoors, 1995. Photograph by the US National Cancer Institute. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Applying_sunscreen.jpg Licence: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/

Only about a quarter of the daytime TikTok routines included sunscreen, even while many featured acids that can make skin more sun-sensitive.
That gap reveals how easily the language of health can conceal a beauty hierarchy. Products promising glow, glass, brightness and prevention received centre stage. The basic measure with the strongest long-term health rationale was often absent.
Sun protection is appropriate for children and adults of every skin tone. Its purpose is not to make a child afraid that daylight will ruin her future face. It reduces ultraviolet damage, sunburn and skin-cancer risk. Protective clothing, shade and sunscreen are practical health measures, not a demand for a poreless appearance.
That distinction matters because even good advice can be absorbed into the same anxiety. A child should not be taught that missing one application is a moral failure or that every freckle, line or change in texture represents negligence.
The goal is healthy skin, not the permanent visual performance of childhood.

## Anti-ageing begins by making the future frightening

The physical risk is the easiest part of this story to demonstrate. The cultural harm is harder to measure and may be more enduring.
An anti-ageing product does not merely sell moisture or exfoliation. It identifies age as the adversary. The customer is invited to detect its approach, delay its evidence and interpret visible change as failure to intervene early enough.
For adult women, that message has long operated through a gendered double standard. Men may be allowed to become distinguished, rugged or authoritative. Women are more often asked to become older without looking old.
Now the timeline of vigilance is moving backwards.
The child is not being sold a solution to a wrinkle. She is being sold surveillance of the face that might one day produce one. “Prevention” expands the customer base because it does not require an existing problem. The absence of visible ageing becomes proof that the routine must begin before ageing appears.
Once a girl starts fearing her future face at 10, the industry does not need to find a new customer when she is 40. It has created a consumer relationship that can last for the rest of her life.
Research on how ageing appears on TikTok supports the concern that women’s ageing is still framed primarily through appearance. A 2026 study analysed 300 posts under #aging and #antiaging and found that women were more likely to focus on looking younger or “glowier,” reflecting gendered pressure around visible age. The researchers also found counter-narratives celebrating ageing and challenging stereotypes, showing that social media can resist ageism as well as reproduce it.
No study reviewed for this article proves that watching a skincare routine causes a child to fear ageing. Broader evidence does show that greater exposure to appearance-focused social media is associated with body dissatisfaction, particularly through comparison with edited peers, celebrities and influencers. Much of that adolescent evidence remains cross-sectional, so researchers appropriately warn against assuming a simple one-way cause.
The honest conclusion is therefore not that every child with a serum has a psychological disorder. It is that a developmental period already shaped by comparison is being filled with commercial messages that define normal pores, texture, acne and future age as problems requiring purchase.

## “Self-care” can become unpaid beauty labour

Skincare has qualities that make it particularly effective marketing for children.
It can be described as hygiene rather than beauty, health rather than appearance, discipline rather than consumption. A makeup product visibly changes the face; a serum promises that the change will appear later—or that an unwanted change will never arrive. Failure is difficult to prove because the claim concerns a future that cannot be observed twice.
The ritual can also feel calming, creative and intimate. The Pediatrics researchers found mother-and-daughter routines that appeared to offer bonding, and they acknowledged that beauty can be a form of play, identity and self-expression. One boy in the sample used an elaborate routine in a way that both adopted and disrupted gender expectations.
Those benefits should not be dismissed. Children are allowed to enjoy colour, scent, packaging and imitation. A face mask at a sleepover is not automatically evidence of pathology.
The concern begins when play becomes obligation.
Some creators in the study woke as early as 4.30am to complete their routines before school. Product “hauls” displayed hundreds of dollars of cosmetics beside carefully styled bedrooms and vanities, linking clear skin with wealth, beauty and the ability to consume. A child who cannot afford the products may not simply feel that she owns less; she may feel that she is caring for herself less responsibly.
This is beauty labour arriving before employment: time, attention and money spent managing an appearance that has been declared perpetually at risk.
The word routine helps normalise it. Six products sound excessive when described as a purchase. They sound responsible when described as daily care.

## The ideal is not only young. It is often light, smooth and expensive

The TikTok study identified repeated aspirations towards “porcelain,” “glowy,” “glassy” and “glazed” skin. Researchers also observed language emphasising lighter and brighter skin.
Those words are not identical to an instruction to bleach the skin, and “brightening” products may target dullness or pigmentation rather than skin colour. But the vocabulary can collide with older racial and colourist hierarchies in which lighter skin is treated as healthier, cleaner or more valuable.
For Black and brown girls, the face may therefore be placed under two timelines of correction: it can be judged too dark in the present and at risk of becoming too old in the future.
The standard is also classed. A US$168 routine is not neutral self-care in a household choosing between school costs, food, transport and health needs. Yet social media removes the surrounding income from the frame. The viewer sees a girl of similar age confidently using the products, not the family resources, gifts, sponsorships or debt that may have placed them on the shelf.
This content crosses borders more easily than its safeguards. A girl in Kampala can receive the same beauty instruction as a girl in London or Chicago even when local labels, dermatology access, consumer enforcement and household income are entirely different. The algorithm globalises the aspiration; the cost and the reaction remain with the family.

## Adults built “Sephora kids”—then turned the children into the spectacle

The backlash against young beauty consumers has often focused on behaviour inside shops: messy testers, demanding children, expensive wish lists and preteens who appear too confident discussing adult products.
Some behaviour deserves ordinary boundaries. Testers should not be destroyed. Staff should not be abused. Families can say no to purchases.
But recording children in stores for ridicule does nothing to explain why the products became desirable. It converts girls from targets of a commercial system into the system’s most visible villains.
Children imitate what culture rewards. They watch celebrities undergo extreme procedures, influencers organise shelves by active ingredient, adults describe ageing as “letting yourself go” and brands present skincare as the entry price for confidence. They also observe that beauty expertise can generate views, free products, affiliate income and status.
The child creator is therefore not only a consumer. She can become an unpaid advertiser to other children, whether or not a brand formally sponsors the post.
Peer recommendation is powerful precisely because it does not look like an advertisement. A girl may distrust a corporate commercial and still believe a creator who attends the same grade level, uses the same slang and opens a bottle in a bedroom rather than a studio.
Blame aimed only at the child leaves the profitable adults untouched.

## Regulators are beginning to look beyond parental responsibility

In March 2026, Italy’s Competition Authority opened investigations into Sephora Italia, Benefit Cosmetics and related LVMH companies over possible unfair commercial practices involving children and adolescents.
The regulator said it was examining whether warnings and precautions for products not intended or tested for minors had been omitted or presented misleadingly. It also raised concerns about the alleged use of very young micro-influencers to encourage children—including some under 10 or 12—to buy face masks, serums and anti-ageing creams. The authority linked the concern to what it called “cosmeticorexia,” an obsessive relationship with skincare among minors.
An investigation is not a finding of wrongdoing. Sephora, Benefit Cosmetics and LVMH’s Italian cosmetics business said they comply with applicable rules and would cooperate with the inquiry.
The significance lies in the question being asked. The trend is no longer treated only as a private failure of parenting or taste. A public authority is examining the design of warnings, the route through influencers and the commercial incentives behind premature use.
In Britain, the issue has moved in the same direction. A July investigation by ITV documented children as young as four appearing online with adult anti-ageing products and reported the case of a 13-year-old whose swollen, peeling rash took months to heal after a skincare gathering. The British Association of Dermatologists called for clearer labels when products are unsuitable for children and information about irritation, allergy and longer-term risks.
Labels alone will not solve an algorithmic marketing problem. A warning printed in small type cannot compete with a brightly coloured bottle, a trusted young creator and hundreds of enthusiastic comments. But an explicit age caution would at least interrupt the fiction that every product on an open shelf is appropriate for every customer.

## Protecting girls must not become another way to control them

There is a familiar danger in responding to beauty pressure: adults may turn concern into surveillance of girls.
They may ban every cosmetic, mock a child’s interest, treat femininity as foolish or demand that girls display perfect self-confidence in a culture organised to undermine it. That response repeats the same message in a different form—that a girl’s body and choices are public property.
A better approach begins with curiosity.
What does the child believe the product will do? Where did she hear that claim? Is she treating acne, enjoying a ritual, copying a friend or afraid of looking old? Does she know the difference between an advertisement, an affiliate recommendation and independent medical advice? Can she identify retinol, exfoliating acids and fragrance across several ingredient lists?
For most children without a diagnosed condition, the answer can remain simple: gentle cleansing, moisturiser when needed and sun protection. Acne, eczema, persistent irritation, scarring or changes in pigmentation deserve appropriate medical care rather than influencer experimentation. A child already using a prescribed treatment should follow the clinician’s advice.
Parents and schools can teach advertising literacy without requiring children to leave social media entirely. Retail staff can be trained to explain age suitability and refuse to recommend adult actives as harmless toys. Influencers can disclose payment and stop presenting a personal routine as universal. Platforms can enforce age rules, limit targeted beauty advertising to minors and provide users with a way to reset recommendation feeds that have become saturated with appearance content.
Brands can redesign the proposition itself. Products made for children should serve a genuine skin need, use age-appropriate formulations and avoid promising the prevention of normal adulthood. Packaging that resembles toys should not conceal adult-strength ingredients.
Most importantly, adults can stop describing their own faces with contempt in front of children. A girl learns what growing older means partly by hearing how women speak about themselves.

## A child’s face is not an unfinished problem

The anti-ageing trend has produced a peculiar reversal.
Childhood was once sold to adult women as the beauty ideal they should attempt to recover. Now the maintenance rituals built around that ideal are being sold back to actual children.
The result is not simply premature skincare. It is premature dissatisfaction: the belief that a face must be managed before it has done anything wrong, that ageing is a preventable error and that responsible femininity means beginning the fight early.
Teen Vogue was right to warn that viral did not mean viable. The evidence published since then makes the responsibility clearer.
Children need protection from irritating products. They also need protection from a culture that calls fear self-care, calls consumption discipline and calls the natural evidence of a long life damage.
Skincare should help a young person live comfortably in her skin.
It should not teach her to spend childhood preparing to apologise for leaving it.
ATHENA will continue covering the health and commercial consequences of beauty trends aimed at girls, the regulation of influencer marketing and the cultural systems that turn ordinary development into a marketable flaw.

The Athena Perspective.

title: BeLoud maps women’s experiences of violence. It is not an emergency service
subtitle: The German-built app lets women anonymously place experiences of harassment, stalking, threats, physical assault and fear on a global map. Its rapid growth makes its privacy design, unverified reports and limits as important as its promise.
author: ATHENA Technology & Safety Desk
body:
A woman opens a map, moves a pin and chooses what happened: harassment, stalking, a threat, physical assault, a feeling of being unsafe or something else.

She does not give her name. She does not create an account. The experience can have happened minutes ago or decades earlier. She can say whether the person was known to her and whether it occurred at home, in a relationship, on public transport, at work, online or in another setting.

Then another point appears on a global map.

That is the proposition behind beloud.now, the international version of a German project originally called laut.jetzt. It was launched in April by developer Lydia Ickler to make violence and insecurity experienced by women and gender-diverse people visible, particularly when those experiences never enter a police file, hospital record or official survey.

The app is moving faster than the reporting about it. Google Play showed more than 100,000 downloads on 27 August. Apple ranked it 67th in Uganda’s Lifestyle category, while an Australian publication reported that it had reached number one in that country’s free Lifestyle chart earlier this month. The same publication said the app was displaying 115,908 unique devices and 135,692 documented experiences worldwide at the time it checked. Those usage figures come from the platform and have not been independently audited.
In searches conducted for this article, ATHENA found little substantive journalism about BeLoud beyond that Australian report, the app stores and the project’s own material. The scarcity helps explain why the app is easily misunderstood.

BeLoud is sometimes described on social media as an app for domestic violence, stalking or sexual assault. It can record experiences connected to all three. But it is not a specialist domestic-violence service, an emergency alert, a police-reporting system or a tool that dispatches help.

It is an anonymous testimony map.

That difference is not a semantic detail. It defines both the app’s value and its limits.

## The map gives an unreported experience somewhere to exist

Much of gender-based violence remains outside formal systems.

The World Health Organization estimates that almost one in three women globally—about 840 million women and girls—have experienced physical or sexual violence by an intimate partner, or sexual violence by someone else, during their lifetime. The figure is itself likely to understate the scale because shame and stigma suppress disclosure, especially for sexual violence.
Official data can show only what their collection systems are designed to see. Police figures depend on reporting and recording. Health statistics depend on a survivor reaching care and a provider asking the right questions. Surveys can estimate prevalence, but they are periodic and do not necessarily capture the places, contexts and repeated everyday conduct that shape how women move through a community.

BeLoud lowers the threshold for saying that something happened.

At the reporting date, its six broad categories included conduct that may be criminal, such as physical assault, and experiences that may never fit a criminal charge, such as a diffuse feeling of danger. A user may add an approximate location or submit without one. She may identify the context and indicate possible factors including misogyny, racism or queerphobia. There is no box asking her to prove the experience or defend why it mattered.

For a survivor who does not want to begin a legal process, that can have emotional and political value. The pin says: this did not disappear merely because I remained anonymous.

The collective map may also challenge the fiction that harassment and fear are exceptional. A single incident can be dismissed as misunderstanding. Thousands of accounts suggest a pattern that cities, event organisers, transport authorities and researchers may need to examine.

The project says it is developing an aggregate dashboard for municipalities and event organisers. Partners would see counts across areas and time periods, not individual reports, coordinates or timestamps; at least five entries would be required before an aggregate result appeared. The stated aim is to help institutions identify patterns and improve prevention. The first pilot partnerships are still being prepared.
This is where BeLoud could become more than a screen of points. A city might compare clusters with lighting, transport access, closing times or complaints about a venue. An organiser might change stewarding or safe-exit arrangements. A university could examine whether reports concentrate along particular routes.

But a pin alone does none of those things. Visibility is an input to action, not action itself.

## A pin is testimony—not proof, prevalence or a crime statistic

BeLoud is unusually direct about one central limitation: reports are not conventionally verified. The platform says it documents experiences rather than legal evidence and does not claim to provide complete or representative statistics.

That warning must remain attached whenever its map or totals are published.

The app cannot establish that every reported event occurred as described. Anonymous systems can be spammed or deliberately manipulated. BeLoud limits a device to one submission an hour, uses automated scoring to hold suspicious reports for manual review and lets users flag content. Its rules prohibit false, misleading or person-targeted reports. These measures reduce some forms of abuse; they do not independently corroborate a survivor’s account.
Nor does a dense area necessarily contain more violence than a sparse one. It may contain more app users, better internet access, a social-media campaign, a younger population or people more comfortable recording an experience. A blank part of the map can mean no reports, not no violence.

Time adds another complication. The app accepts historical experiences, including incidents from years earlier. A user can filter reports, but a map combining recent fear with decades-old assault is not a live description of current danger.

The categories also describe very different things. “Feeling unsafe” is real information about how a place is experienced, but it is not equivalent to a physical attack. Harassment may range from words to unwanted sexual contact. “Other” is necessarily ambiguous. Adding every pin into one total can communicate scale while obscuring severity.

Location blurring is designed to protect users. Reports are shifted before storage and displayed imprecisely. That means a point appearing beside a house, school, shop or bar must never be treated as an allegation against the people at that address. A Google Play reviewer complained that a submitted point moved roughly 50 metres; the behaviour they perceived as a mapping failure appears to be the privacy feature working as intended.
The safest description is therefore precise: BeLoud maps what its users chose to document. It does not map all violence, verified crimes or the identities of perpetrators.

## Domestic violence does not fit neatly on a street map

Calling BeLoud a domestic-violence app risks suggesting services it does not provide.

Domestic violence is often a pattern rather than one event: intimidation, surveillance, financial control, isolation, sexual coercion, threats, assaults and post-separation stalking may accumulate across months or years. The danger may come from a person with access to the survivor’s home, phone, children, money and daily routines. Avoiding a marked street does not address it.

BeLoud can record “home” or “relationship” as a context and whether the other person was known. That is significant because it pushes against a safety narrative focused only on strangers in public. WHO defines intimate-partner violence to include physical aggression, sexual coercion, psychological abuse and controlling behaviour by a current or former partner.
Yet the app does not have a distinct domestic-violence category. It also does not offer a separate sexual-assault category in its six principal choices. A survivor must fit the experience into harassment, threat, physical assault, stalking, unsafe feeling or “other,” then use optional context to add meaning.

That simplicity makes reporting fast. It also limits analysis. A policymaker cannot safely infer how many pins represent domestic violence, rape, coercive control or repeated abuse. One survivor submitting one event and another recording one point from a years-long pattern each produce a pin.

The map should not be used as an avoidance guide that teaches women to navigate around dangerous dots. For domestic abuse, the dangerous person may move with the survivor. For stalking, mapping a previous encounter does not predict where the stalker will appear next. And for public harassment, telling women which areas to avoid can shift responsibility from perpetrators and institutions back onto those already restricting their lives.

BeLoud’s best potential use is collective: revealing enough aggregated patterns to demand safer systems. Its weakest interpretation is individual: implying that a woman can prevent violence if she studies the map carefully enough.

## The privacy design contains serious protections—and unresolved contradictions

An app dealing with stalking and abuse should be judged not only by what it collects, but by what an abuser, attacker, data broker, government or security failure could expose.

BeLoud has made several thoughtful choices. It requires no account, email address or name. Reports may be filed without a location. The privacy policy says the precise coordinate is never stored or logged; the server randomly shifts it before storage. Reports sit on servers in Germany under European data-protection law. The project says it uses no advertising trackers, analytics platforms or social-media pixels. Users can view and delete their own entries through a device-generated token without opening an account.
The same detailed policy, however, exposes discrepancies in the project’s simpler public promises.

On 27 August, the homepage said an exact location “never leaves the device.” The privacy policy then said the exact coordinates were transmitted over HTTPS to the server and shifted there before storage. Both statements cannot describe the same technical journey.

The homepage also promises that reports contain no device identifiers. The detailed policy explains that the app generates a random UUID whose cryptographic hash is stored, and that a platform-specific device ID such as an Android Instance ID may also be stored with a report to detect repeat submissions. The policy distinguishes these technical tokens from directly identifying personal device numbers such as an IMEI or advertising ID. That distinction may be legitimate, but “no device identifiers” is too absolute for the processing later disclosed.

On 27 August, Google Play introduced a third inconsistency. Its developer-supplied Data Safety panel says the app may collect location and device or other IDs and currently labels the data as “not encrypted.” BeLoud’s privacy policy says report coordinates travel over encrypted HTTPS. The store disclosure may be outdated, may refer to a different part of the data flow or may be wrong; the public material does not resolve which. Google explicitly notes that developers supply these declarations.
None of these discrepancies proves that BeLoud is exposing users. They do mean a survivor cannot obtain one consistent answer to a basic question: what exactly leaves my phone, in what form, and for how long?

ATHENA found no published independent security audit, open technical assessment or peer-reviewed evaluation of BeLoud. The app is only months old and has been changing quickly; its current privacy policy was revised on 21 August. An independent audit would test the implementation rather than asking users to rely on promises, reconcile the public wording and assess how the system behaves under attack.

There are also forms of safety beyond data storage. A domestic-abuse perpetrator may monitor a partner’s phone, app list, browsing history or notifications. Research on safety technology has warned that location tools can be misused by abusers and that personal-safety apps operate without consistent accreditation or regulation. In a UK review, researchers found that 45 candidate apps failed to function as marketed after repeated testing, demonstrating why app-store availability is not itself evidence of reliability.
ATHENA found no public BeLoud documentation of a disguised icon, quick-exit function or guidance for users whose devices may be monitored. That does not establish that every user needs those features. It does show why BeLoud should resist being marketed as a comprehensive domestic-violence tool.

## An anonymous map protects disclosure and limits response

Anonymity is BeLoud’s defining strength. It is also why the app cannot send help.

The platform does not know who placed a pin and does not collect contact details with a report. It cannot call the survivor, preserve a witness statement, arrange medical care, begin a risk assessment or tell a police unit that someone may be in immediate danger. The app stores an account of an experience, not a pathway back to the person who had it.

Its app-store description explicitly says it is for awareness only and is not intended for emergency reporting or contacting law enforcement. That warning should appear prominently wherever BeLoud is recommended, particularly in short social-media posts that might otherwise call it a “safety app.”
BeLoud added in-app counselling and hotline resources in August, but its published version notes specify services only for Germany, Austria and Switzerland. The app is available much more widely. Apple’s Uganda listing offers English and 37 other languages, yet neither Luganda nor Swahili appears in the listed options.
That gap matters. A global map can accept an account from Kampala while offering no visible Uganda-specific route to medical care, shelter, legal advice, psychosocial support or police protection.

## Uganda already shows the difference between visibility and referral

Uganda has its own example of a different design choice.

SafePal was created by young Ugandans with UNFPA support to let survivors confidentially report gender-based violence and connect them to psychosocial, legal and medical services. UNFPA said submitted cases could be routed to organisations including ActionAid, the Naguru Teenage Information and Health Centre, the Centre for Domestic Violence Prevention and the Uganda Police Child and Family Protection Unit. Unlike BeLoud’s anonymous pin, SafePal’s process asked for a telephone number so a service provider could contact the survivor.
The comparison is about architecture, not a current endorsement. SafePal’s Google Play listing was last updated in October 2023, and ATHENA has not independently verified the present coverage or response time of its service network. The listing describes confidential sexual-violence reporting linked to nearby response services.
BeLoud sacrifices follow-up to maximise anonymity. SafePal’s model sacrifices some anonymity to permit contact and referral. Neither choice is automatically correct for every survivor.

A woman who wants only to leave a record may reject a system that asks for her number. A survivor needing post-rape care, safe accommodation or protection from a violent partner needs more than a public dot. The ethical design question is not which app “wins,” but whether users understand which problem each is built to solve.

In Uganda, BeLoud would become more useful if it partnered with credible local women’s organisations, added local languages, placed verified country-specific support inside the app and made the boundary between mapping and reporting impossible to miss. Any partnership would need to preserve the promise that individual pins and timestamps are not handed to institutions.

## What BeLoud must prove next

Rapid adoption demonstrates demand. It does not yet demonstrate impact.

The project’s next stage should be measured against questions that its download count cannot answer:

— Can an independent security assessment confirm that exact locations are discarded as promised and that stored tokens cannot reasonably be linked back to survivors?
— Will the project reconcile its homepage, privacy policy and app-store disclosures in clear language?
— How many submissions are withheld, flagged or removed, and under what moderation standards?
— Can aggregate analysis distinguish reporting activity from the prevalence of violence and communicate selection bias honestly?
— Do municipal partners actually change lighting, transport, staffing, venue practice or prevention policy after seeing a pattern?
— Can support information expand country by country without turning the app into a directory of outdated services?
— Will survivors, domestic-violence specialists, disability advocates and local women’s organisations help govern the design rather than merely supply its data?
— Can the app add discreet-use guidance and accessibility information for people whose phones are monitored or who use assistive technologies? Apple currently says the developer has not identified supported accessibility features.
## Update — 17 October 2026

BeLoud has changed since this report was first published. The project’s current homepage now says that coordinates are randomly shifted before storage, replacing the earlier statement that the exact location never left the device. Its privacy notice, dated 5 October, says an exact coordinate is sent over encrypted HTTPS and shifted on the server before storage; it also discloses the use of a hashed app token, a platform-specific device identifier where available, short-lived hashed IP data for rate limiting, Apple App Attest or Google Play Integrity checks, and temporary server logs.

The app has expanded from six to nine principal categories, adding emotional violence, rape and suspected drink spiking. Its October releases added shorter map time filters, supporter subscriptions and revised terms concerning anonymised data used in analyses for cities and organisations. The homepage now states more plainly that the map contains documented experiences, not verified crimes or an objective danger assessment.

Those revisions answer some of the wording problems identified in August. They do not turn the app into an emergency service, independently verify anonymous reports or establish that the map measures the prevalence of violence. ATHENA has not independently audited the app’s code, data handling or security implementation.

Those questions are not an argument for abandoning the project. They are what taking it seriously looks like.

BeLoud has captured something institutions routinely fail to offer: a place where a woman can say an experience mattered without first surrendering her identity, submitting to cross-examination or deciding whether it meets a legal threshold.

That is not a small contribution.

But no survivor should mistake the act of placing a pin for an emergency call, a police report, evidence preservation, medical care or a safety plan. No journalist should turn the map into a ranking of dangerous neighbourhoods. No city should cite crowdsourced points as a substitute for listening to survivors, funding services and holding perpetrators accountable.

The app’s name asks women to be loud. The responsibility cannot end there.

If thousands of anonymous experiences are now visible, the next question belongs to institutions: what will they do with what women have shown them?

ATHENA will continue examining BeLoud’s growth, its privacy and security claims, the development of municipal partnerships and whether global visibility is being converted into local protection for women.
